To address the potential difficulties visually impaired children face in articulating their learning challenges, both blind adults and visually impaired children were involved in the study, with the adults reflecting on the difficulties they encountered in their childhood learning. Due to their lack of visual input, visually impaired children rely solely on tactile perception  to  recognize  the  shape  of  Braille  dots,  limiting  their comprehensive  understanding  of  text  and  its  meaning.  While  most visually impaired children retain their auditory and cognitive abilities, the  absence  of  visual  cues  for  large,  untouchable  objects,  such  as "mountains"  and  "trees,"  complicates  their  image  cognition.  Braille learning typically requires significant time and effort, and the inability to effectively associate text with real-world objects and concepts hampers  learning  efficiency  and  comprehension.  This  prolonged  learning process often leads to boredom and a loss of interest, further exacerbating low learning efficiency. Improving the Braille learning experience and enhancing the learning process for visually impaired children thus became a key motivation for designing innovative learning tools.

Feedback from teachers also revealed numerous challenges in Braille instruction. Current teaching aids, often manually crafted by teachers, help  visually  impaired  children  to  some  extent,  but  they  are  timeconsuming to produce, difficult to scale, and insufficient to meet classroom demands. Furthermore, the tactile learning materials available in schools fail to fully represent the appearance of objects, leading students to misunderstand the content. This not only affects teaching efficiency but also increases teachers ' workload. To support better classroom instruction  and  Braille  lesson  preparation,  there  is  an  urgent  need  to develop intelligent, user-friendly teaching aids that simplify the Braille teaching process and improve educational outcomes.

Based on the needs of the visually impaired and their teachers, this study seeks to design a multimodal learning tool that integrates tactile, auditory, and visual perception. By combining these sensory modalities, the  tool  aims  to  help  visually  impaired  children  learn  Braille  more efficiently.  The  integration  of  different  sensory  inputs  provides  them with richer information, enhancing their understanding of Braille and its meaning while addressing the challenge of associating text with realworld  objects.  Additionally,  the  tool  offers  intelligent  teaching  support,  streamlining  lesson  preparation  and  enabling  more  effective teacher-student interaction in the classroom.

## 3.2. Interaction system

The  interaction  process  defines  how  visually  impaired  children engage with the assistive tool, forming the core framework of the system (Fig. 3).

First, visually impaired children read aloud from a Braille book they are touching. The system then uses speech recognition technology to analyze the spoken content, and AI-based image generation technology automatically creates related scene or object images. These images are formatted in black and white, with pixel-style processing to match the hardware ' s tactile display.

Fig. 3. Product interaction framework.



The final output is tailored to the sensory needs of visually impaired children  and  includes  both  tactile  and  auditory  outputs.  The  tactile output consists of raised dots corresponding to the generated image, allowing children to perceive the shapes and contours of the objects they are reading about through touch. The auditory output complements this by providing relevant sound effects and voice narration, enhancing the multidimensional experience of text comprehension.

For example, when a child presses the voice button and reads aloud, "a mountain," and confirms with the enter button, a corresponding scene is generated -a tactile image displaying the contours of a mountain. The child can touch and feel the height and shape of the mountain, while Braille representing "a mountain" is displayed below. Sounds of birds chirping and wind blowing through the mountain trees are played to heighten the sense of realism.

## 3.3. Hardware design

We divided the touch display into two sections: the upper part displays pixel-based images, while the lower part is reserved for Braille. This  design  reflects  a  deep  understanding  of  how  visually  impaired children  learn,  allowing them to combine tactile exploration of both images and text for a more comprehensive learning experience. On the right  side  of  the  touch  screen,  control  buttons  are  added,  including power, record, stop, page navigation, and volume adjustment buttons. A small speaker is placed in the upper-right corner to support the future implementation of multimodal interaction.

Discussions  with  teachers  from  schools  for  the  visually  impaired helped finalize the overall size of the product, as well as the dimensions and spacing of each tactile dot. Each dot measures 5 mm x 5 mm, with a 1 mm gap between them. The total size of the product is approximately 360 mm in length, 210 mm in width, and 30 mm in height -comparable to a laptop, making it portable and convenient for class learning scenarios. The tactile image display adopts a raised, positive-relief design, which enhances tactile perception for visually impaired users.

Referring  to  earlier  research  on  electromagnetic-driven  tactile display devices, we employed Arduino, an open-source microcontroller platform widely used for controlling electronic devices, along with a multi-channel relay and micro magnets to create a system capable of controlling the elevation of six magnetic dots. In this system, Arduino is responsible for managing the on-off states of the electromagnetic circuits, enabling the precise raising and lowering of Braille dots and tactile images (Fig. 4).

## 3.4. Software design

To achieve efficient language-to-image conversion, a software system  was  developed,  which  is  based  on  Python  and  Unity  (a  crossplatform  game  engine  used  for  creating  both  2D  and  3D  interactive applications including games and simulations). The system consists of two  main  components:  a  Unity-based  front-end  responsible  for  user interaction and visual output, and a Python back-end that processes data and executes core functions.

## 3.4.1. Unity front-end design

The Unity front-end focuses on providing an intuitive and responsive user interface. After reading a Braille text, the user inputs speech via a microphone, engaging  interactively  in  the  image  generation  process. The visual display uses a dynamic grid of blocks, where the height of each block (ranging from 0 to 1) is adjusted based on the generated image,  simulating  the  pixel-like  representation  of  real-world  objects. This design mirrors the physical tactile pixel image creation process, enhancing the experience for sighted users and offering them control over visual interaction.

## 3.4.2. Python back-end architecture

The back-end system, built using Python and the Flask framework, processes  the  speech  data  transmitted  from  the  Unity  front-end.  The system employs Baidu ' s speech recognition API to convert speech into text, selected for its superior accuracy and performance in processing Chinese. Once converted, the text undergoes custom algorithmic optimization to generate prompts suitable for image creation. These prompts are used to call OpenAI ' s DALLE-3 model, with specific instructions for "simple, child-friendly, black-and-white pixel-style images." The prompt also  generates  music  that  aligns  with  the  theme  of  the  image.  The resulting images are then processed using OpenCV (an open-source library used for computer vision tasks, such as image and video processing,  enabling  machines  to  understand  and  analyze  visual  data)  for pixelation, binarization, and size adjustments to ensure seamless integration with the Unity block array.

This  system  not  only  demonstrates  an  efficient  speech-to-image conversion  process  but  also  integrates  auditory  feedback  through music output. By combining visual, tactile, and auditory elements, it introduces  an  innovative  multimodal  interaction  model,  highlighting the  system ' s  broad  application  potential  and  promising  development prospects (Fig. 5).

## 4. Methodology

This section outlines the participants, settings, and materials used in the  study,  followed  by  an  overview  of  the  materials  and  procedures employed. Lastly, we describe data collection, analysis, and usability metrics.

Fig. 4. Product design.



## 4.1. Participants

The study received approval from the University Ethics Committee (H20230365I). The participants comprised five sighted children (mean age = 9.2, 3 boys and 2 girls) and fourteen visually impaired children (mean age = 9.4, 9 boys and 5 girls), recruited with the assistance of teachers from a school for the blind. All visually impaired participants met  the  following  inclusion  criteria:  (1)  congenital  blindness,  (2) enrollment in a school for the blind for over one year, (3) blindness not caused by other diseases, and (4) working at age-appropriate cognitive and  communication  levels.  The  sighted  children  were  required  to demonstrate  age-appropriate  cognitive  and  communication  abilities. Informed  consent  was  reviewed  by  the  participants ' guardians,  who were assured that participants could rest or withdraw at any time. After addressing all questions from the guardians or participants, the guardians signed the consent forms. Meanwhile, another researcher set up the equipment.

The  purpose  of  testing  with  sighted  children  was  to  determine whether  the  generated  images  aligned  with  their  cognitive  understanding  of  objects.  Following  their  positive  feedback,  the  usability testing with visually impaired children commenced. Participants were observed  in  two  locations:  fourteen  visually  impaired  children  at  a school  for  the  blind,  and  five  sighted  children  at  a  local  elementary school. Each participant received a $20 gift card as compensation. Data collection took place between April and May 2024.

Fig. 5. Example of multimodal interaction of TaleVision.



## 4.2. Materials

The primary tool used in this study was the "TaleVision" product, designed to generate tactile images and corresponding sound effects by large language models (LLMs). The system was programmed to produce touchable  representations  of  various  objects,  animals,  and  simple scenes, accompanied by audio descriptions and sound effects to provide a multimodal sensory experience.

## 4.3. Experimental procedure

The experiment comprised five stages (Fig. 6). Following the principle  that  visually  impaired  children  are  capable  participants,  we communicated directly  with them rather than  their  guardians,  using age-appropriate language. Various options were provided to familiarize the  children  with  the  equipment  before  obtaining  their  consent  to participate.

In the pre-experiment phase (Part A), sighted participants received a brief introduction to the product and its operation. First, a two-minute subtitled video explaining the product ' s usage and the tasks involved was shown. Participants then engaged in a blindfolded simulation of the learning  process  of  visually  impaired  children,  interacting  with  the hardware to experience the product ' s overall size, material, and functionality.  They  touched  the  display  image  of  a  "puppy,"  speculating about the object on the screen, aided by audio cues. Afterwards, they removed their blindfolds and used the system ' s voice input and image generation functions.

In  Part  B,  visually  impaired  participants  received  guidance  from teachers, along with a brief introduction and operational instructions.

Fig. 6. Experimental flow.



Each  visually  impaired  participant  had  five  minutes  to  familiarize themselves  with  the  product ' s  buttons  and  interaction  methods.  Researchers explained what participants would experience and perform during the study -such as voice input of words or sentences, pressing the image generation button, and interacting with the tactile display. During the pre-test, participants could ask questions, and they were free to withdraw from the experiment for any reason.

First,  voice  the  words  from  your  textbook  into  TaleVision.  Then, explore the touchable images generated and listen to the corresponding sound  effects.  Participants  were  asked  to  describe  the  objects  they perceived and provide feedback on their understanding of the images. Teachers guided the participants through specific tasks and were asked to comment on how the tool supported or challenged their instructional methods. Researchers recorded the participants ' behaviors, operational steps, and reasons for task failures. Participants were allowed to take breaks if needed, and researchers invited them to continue when ready.

In  Part  D,  visually  impaired  participants  were  instructed  to  input complex descriptive phrases via voice commands, such as "a pavilion on a mountain" or "a boat passing by several mountains on the water." They then followed the same procedure as in Part C. Researchers documented their performance, behaviors, and any operational challenges.

After completing the experiment (Part E), participants filled out a user experience rating scale and  satisfaction survey, specifically designed to assess engagement, satisfaction, and ease of use. Visually impaired students were assisted in orally completing the forms. Finally, structured  interviews  were  conducted,  asking  participants  questions such as: "Did you enjoy using this product?" "What improvements would you suggest?" and "At what point did you experience difficulties?"

## 4.4. Data and metrics

The study gathered data from the pre-test conducted with sighted children. Specifically, we presented seven commonly taught words in class: "dog," "cat," "flower," "mountain," "child," "tree," and "boat." The sighted children, blindfolded, were asked to touch the images displayed by the product and guess the objects represented. Their accuracy rates were recorded.

Data  collected  from  the  visually  impaired  children  included:  (a) quantitative data, such as participant satisfaction and user experience, and (b) qualitative insights derived from researcher observations. Due to the sensitivity of participant identities and school policies, researchers manually  recorded  events  in  digital  form,  as  video  or  photographic documentation was not permitted.

Our analysis focused on four key metrics: (a) participant satisfaction with  the  product,  (b)  their  user  experience,  (c)  overall  performance during  product  interaction,  and  (d)  reasons  for  interruptions  or  task failures. These metrics are described in detail below:

## 4.4.1. Participant satisfaction

At the end of the experiment, subjective satisfaction was assessed using  a  modified  Visual  Analogue  Scale  (VAS)  tailored  for  visually impaired  children.  The  VAS  is  a  simplified  psychometric  system designed to collect individual perceptions of specific experiences. This adjusted scale included three smiley faces, each representing different satisfaction levels: a sad red face for "not at all," a neutral yellow face for "somewhat," and a happy green face for "very much liked" (Wong and Baker, 2001) (Fig. 7). The faces, with high-contrast colors, were easily perceptible for visually impaired children, and each had a tactile mouth to aid comprehension. Touching the mouth and its orientation (downturned,  straight,  or  upturned)  helped  children  understand  the  corresponding expression. After being shown the smiley faces one by one and allowed time to explore them, participants were asked, "Did you enjoy interacting with this product?" Children provided responses by either touching or pointing at a face, or by answering verbally. Researchers recorded their responses at the conclusion of each session.

Fig. 7. VAS scale (Visually Impaired Child Friendly Version).



## 4.4.2. User experience

The user experience of visually impaired participants was assessed using the User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) (Schrepp, 2015). Researchers verbally conveyed the questions and options to ensure clarity and accuracy in expressing participants ' feelings about the product. The six  dimensions  of  the  UEQ  (Attractiveness,  Perspicuity,  Efficiency, Dependability, Stimulation, and Novelty) were retained, but the presentation  was  adjusted  to  align  more  closely  with  the  participants ' actual interactions. Researchers paid particular attention to the participants ' reactions to tactile feedback, audio cues, and the overall interaction process, ensuring that these aspects were reflected in the UEQ scores. A 7-point Likert scale was used for each dimension, defined as follows:

- Attractiveness: Measures participants ' overall satisfaction and emotional response to the product.
- Perspicuity:  Evaluates  the  product ' s  ease  of  use  and  clarity  in  its functionality.
- Efficiency:  Assesses  how  effectively  participants  could  complete tasks using the product.
- Dependability: Measures the product ' s predictability and the level of control participants felt during use.
- Stimulation: Reflects the enjoyment and positive emotions elicited by the product.
- Novelty: Assesses whether the product provided a unique and innovative experience.

## 4.4.3. Task performance

This metric assessed participants ' operational skills and  task completion rate during product use. The research team observed and recorded the number of tasks completed within 30 min, interruptions during  tasks,  and  instances  where  participants  disagreed  with  the generated images. The task performance of visually impaired participants was indicative of their ability to identify objects using the product and provided insight into its applicability in educational settings.

## 4.4.4. Interaction performance

We observed and recorded conversations between visually impaired children and their teachers during interactions. These interactions were categorized into 1) Interactive operations; 2) Judgments about images; 3)  Characterizing  objects  and  expressing  ideas.  Given  the  potential technical limitations and the specific needs of the target population, it was anticipated that participants might face challenges during product use. Therefore, the study also documented instances where learning was interrupted or tasks were unsuccessful. Reasons for these interruptions were classified into (1) difficulties in tactile recognition, (2) cognitive overload from multimodal inputs, and (3) excessive complexity of the product ' s feedback. This metric aimed to identify barriers to the learning process and provide insights for product optimization, such as simplifying image complexity or adjusting the frequency of audio prompts.

We employed an abductive content analysis method to analyze the recorded  data  in  NVivo  (Version  12;  QSR  International)  (Graneheim et al., 2017; Timmermans and Tavory, 2012). In each group, the first author coded the records, aiming to understand how visually impaired children,  with  teacher  assistance,  engaged  in  learning  and  behavior. This  process  involved  reviewing  the  records  line  by  line,  extracting relevant excerpts, and identifying codes (children = 14, teacher = 2), with a focus on what visually impaired children attempted to accomplish and how they did so. Subsequently, sub-themes related to the methodology were identified ( n = 6). The authors then collaboratively refined these codes and sub-themes, which were organized into broader themes ( n = 3) concerning the interaction between visually impaired children and teachers within the three main components of the product. Examples of data extraction are provided in Appendix File 1.

## 5. Results

## 5.1. Product testing with sighted children

Preliminary  data  from  five  sighted  children  participating  in  the product test revealed an overall accuracy rate of 65.71 % in identifying tactile  images.  The  highest  recognition  rates  were  for  "flower"  and "boat," both at 100 %, while "tree " and "mountain" were recognized 60 % of the time, and "dog " only 40 %. More complex figures, such as "child,"  had  a  significantly  lower  recognition  rate  of  20  %,  whereas simpler natural objects like "flower" and "boat" had higher accuracy. This suggests that simple line-drawn images are more effective for tactile recognition, whereas more intricate images may require further optimization to improve identification accuracy among visually impaired children.  Given  that  prior  literature  indicates  sighted  children  are generally less proficient in tactile perception compared to their visually impaired counterparts, we hypothesize that visually impaired children may  possess  greater  tactile  recognition  abilities  for  simpler  images. Based on these insights, we proceeded with a formal usability experiment involving visually impaired children.

## 5.2. Usability testing with visually impaired children

## 5.2.1. Quantitative analysis of usability testing

Fourteen  children  participated  in  a  30  min  interaction  with  the product, and the results indicate a high level of overall satisfaction. The average satisfaction score among the participants was 2.6 (SD = 0.50), with 60 % expressing very high satisfaction. In terms of task performance, children successfully completed an average of 2.9 (SD = 0.77) tasks involving image generation from individual words. However, their performance in sentence-based tasks was limited, with most participants completing  only  one  sentence  task,  suggesting  that  large  language models  may  not  yet  be  suitable  for  generating  complex  images  for visually impaired children. Regarding errors, most children experienced 2 -4 task interruptions, reflecting the adequacy of the product ' s button configuration in maintaining their focus. A few children experienced higher  interruption  rates,  primarily  due  to  unfamiliarity  with  the directional buttons. Additionally, several children exhibited instances of image misidentification, with the highest misidentification rate being two instances per child. For example, some children mistook "mountain" for "cloud".

An  analysis of the relationship between  satisfaction and  interruptions  reveals  an  inverse  correlation  between  these  two  factors. Children who reported higher satisfaction (e.g., Children 5, 6, 10, and 13) generally experienced fewer interruptions, suggesting that smoother task flow with minimal disruptions positively influenced their overall experience. For instance, Child 6, who encountered no interruptions, exhibited a high satisfaction score and successfully completed multiple word tasks, reinforcing that reducing interface-related disruptions enhances user satisfaction. Conversely, participants with higher interruption  rates  (e.g.,  Children  4,  9,  and  12)  reported  lower  satisfaction, implying that frequent task disruptions due to unfamiliarity with controls  diminished  their  engagement  and  positive  perception.  Notably, Child  4  experienced  the  highest  number  of  interruptions  (6)  and  reported  lower  satisfaction,  emphasizing  the  need  for  more  intuitive tactile  navigation.  A  similar  pattern  emerges  when  examining  task completion. Children who completed more word tasks (e.g., Children 1, 5, 6, and 13) tended to report higher satisfaction, while those with fewer completed tasks (e.g., Children 4, 9, and 12) demonstrated lower satisfaction, highlighting the connection between successful task execution and positive user experience. Interestingly, sentence completion rates remained consistently low across participants, regardless of satisfaction levels, suggesting that the complexity of sentence-based tasks remains a significant challenge (Fig. 8).

These findings suggest that improving interface familiarity through training, introducing adaptive tactile prompts, and providing personalized interaction pacing could reduce interruptions and further enhance satisfaction in future iterations of the product.

## 5.2.2. Experience feedback

The fourteen participants provided comprehensive feedback based on six dimensions of the User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) (Fig. 9). The product received particularly high scores for attractiveness (2.0, SD = 0.96), clarity (1.8, SD = 0.70), and novelty (2.4, SD = 0.50), reflecting strong user satisfaction and an appreciation for the product ' s innovative features.  Participants  highlighted  that  the  interactive  combination  of touchable  images  and  auditory  feedback  made  the  learning  process engaging  and  provided  a  novel  experience  compared  to  traditional Braille learning tools.

However, the efficiency score was relatively low (1.1, SD = 0.77), indicating that participants experienced delays and operational complexity  when  interacting  with  the  system.  Some  participants  reported that the response time for generating tactile images was longer than  expected,  which  disrupted  the  learning  flow.  Suggestions  for improvement included optimizing the system ' s  processing  speed  and simplifying the interface to facilitate faster, more intuitive interactions.

The dependability score (1.8, SD = 0.80) suggests moderate user confidence in the system ' s performance consistency. Participants noted occasional  errors  in  tactile  image  generation  and  the  need  for  more precise  haptic  representations.  To  address  these  concerns,  future  enhancements should focus on improving system reliability through more refined 3D modeling and robust error-checking mechanisms.

While the product ' s novelty received the highest score (2.4, SD = 0.50), a few participants suggested that the range of touchable images could be expanded to include more complex shapes and real-world objects, further enriching the learning experience. The stimulation score (1.8,  SD = 0.63)  indicates  that  users  found  the  product  engaging, although  some  suggested  adding  more  interactive  features,  such  as multi-sensory exercises, to sustain long-term engagement.

In  comparison  to  the  benchmark  derived  from  the  UEQ  database -which includes 163 applications across various categories, such as  business  software,  online  services,  and  mobile  applications -the product performed above average in attractiveness and novelty. However,  it  fell  short  in  efficiency  and  dependability,  highlighting  areas where  technical  optimization  and  user  interface  enhancements  are needed. These findings underscore the product ' s potential while identifying  specific  aspects  requiring  improvement  to  better  serve  the learning needs of visually impaired children.

## 5.2.3. Usability experiment: qualitative analysis

## 1.  Language Visualization

Overview: Language visualization is an innovative technique that uses  large  language  models  and  generative  AI  technologies  to transform  textual  descriptions  into  tactile  images  for  visually impaired  children.  In  this  process,  the  system  generates  corresponding images based on the text, with the complexity and level of detail directly influencing the children ' s comprehension and learning  outcomes.  The  children  primarily  expressed  two  points: "What benefits do I find in the generated image?" and "Why do I like or dislike this image?"

## Uncertainty in Generation

"I tried inputting the word ' puppy ' twice... but the resulting images were different each time -one simple and the other complex -which caused me some confusion. When generating images from sentences, the results are often highly complex, making them difficult for me to understand."

This  statement  highlights  a  key  challenge  in  applying  text-toimage  models  for  visually  impaired  children -the  need  for  finetuning  to  reduce  variability  in  generated  images.  Simple  outlines and  structures  are  easier  for  the  children  to  recognize,  whereas complex scenes or excessive details may cause confusion. Additionally, when voice inputs include multiple nouns or when more than two objects need to be generated, the resulting images often become too pixelated or abstract for clear interpretation.

## Diversification of objects

"It ' s fascinating... no matter what word I say, it responds with an image.  For  instance,  when  it  generated  a  monster,  I  got  my  first tangible concept of what it looked like... I can share these moments with my family."

The richness of generated images is also central to enhancing the learning  experience.  By  allowing  visually  impaired  children  to explore  and  interpret  these  images  freely,  the  system  encourages creativity and fosters a more active role in understanding content. Offering varied inputs can help generate a broader range of image scenarios, catering to diverse learning needs.

## 2.  Human- computer Interaction Process

Overview: During interaction, visually impaired children focus on

Fig. 8. Quantitative analysis of data from usability experiments.



Fig. 9. Data from the subject user experience scale.



constructing  their  own  technological  practices.  However,  due  to varying levels of technical literacy, we found that their product use practices were inconsistent. Many teachers attributed this disparity to the children ' s lack of exposure to electronic devices in their daily lives. We observed that the children developed different methods of interacting with the product through tactile and verbal feedback. The following  sections  explore  their  varying  attitudes  toward  product design.

## Simplification

"The five buttons are very helpful... it keeps everything organized because I can ' t quickly understand the function of each one... AI is unfamiliar to me. We need time to comprehend it."

By optimizing system responsiveness and feedback mechanisms, the product can more quickly perceive and respond to the children ' s actions,  ensuring they receive timely feedback and reducing frustration.  Standardizing  operational  procedures  is  a  key  aspect  of simplification,  streamlining  complex  steps  so  the  children  can quickly  grasp  and  remember  the  process,  ultimately  easing  the cognitive load required to learn new devices.

## Standardization

"It ' s important that this system benefits our care services... but if I want to revisit an image... once it ' s gone, it ' s gone."

This statement underscores the need to establish a unified design framework that ensures new products are compatible with the children ' s familiar usage patterns. Such standardization not only facilitates seamless transitions between  different devices but also improves their overall user experience with digital products.

## 3.  Teacher-Student Interaction in Learning

Overview: During the teacher-student interaction phase, visually impaired children use the product with the guidance of their teachers, resembling a traditional classroom setting. Their tasks include touching images, discussing their appearance with the teacher, and articulating their understanding of the images. Teachers guide the students  in  recognizing  object  shapes  and  simultaneously  nurture their  independent  learning  and  expression  abilities.  We  observed that through teacher-guided interaction, visually impaired children deepen their understanding of the learning content by integrating external information and validating internal knowledge.

## External Information Supplementation

"I  find  that  exploring  object  features  with  students  helps  them better understand... I guide them to think about what certain parts are and what they ' re used for, then offer explanations afterward... these interactions prompt the children to ask questions, aiding their memory  retention...  the  sound  effects  are  engaging  too,  keeping them focused on the task."

During  teacher-student  interactions,  visually  impaired  children receive additional details about the objects depicted in the images. For instance, when touching an image of a tree, the teacher might explain  its  species  or  the  shape  of  its  leaves.  This  additional information  helps  the  children  build  a  more  complete  cognitive picture, compensating for the limitations of tactile feedback alone. Furthermore,  combining  auditory  descriptions  or  relevant  sound effects enhances the clarity of the information. For example, when touching an image of a cat, the teacher might play a recording of a cat ' s meow. This multi-sensory approach reinforces recognition and memory retention, significantly improving learning efficiency.

## Internal Knowledge Validation

"When I touched the umbrella image, I never realized it was shaped like that... I usually only touch folded umbrellas or stand beneath open ones... the teacher said this image shows the umbrella from the side... it gave me a new perspective I hadn ' t considered before."

This  statement  illustrates  how  visually  impaired  children  deepen their understanding by connecting the learning content to real-life experiences. Teachers guide them to recall past encounters with the object, such as touching real items or participating in related activities. This method enables the children to link abstract tactile images with actual objects  and  experiences,  fostering  knowledge  internalization.  Additionally,  the  children  are  encouraged  to  translate  what  they  have learned into their own language and understanding, thereby expressing their cognitive grasp of the subject matter.

## 6. Discussion and recommendations

## 6.1. Discussion of results

The objective of this study was to evaluate the usability of a multimodal perception integration product, based on large-scale models, for enhancing image cognition among visually impaired children. Through both qualitative and quantitative analyses, we discovered that the majority  of  participants  effectively  utilized  this  innovative  interactive product to recognize objects in their environment. Specifically, 60 % of the visually impaired children expressed satisfaction with the product, which demonstrated high levels of novelty and attractiveness within the user experience framework. Consequently, we addressed the following research questions:

RQ1:  Can  large-scale  models  serve  as  a  technical  foundation  for graphic cognition educational products tailored to visually impaired children?

Large-scale  models  exhibit  substantial  potential  in  empowering graphic cognition educational products. The images generated by these models facilitate the understanding of abstract concepts among visually impaired children, particularly through a multimodal perception system that  integrates  tactile  and  auditory  stimuli.  This  integration  enables children  to  better  perceive  and  comprehend  image  content  that  is otherwise inaccessible (Zhang et al., 2017). However, the complexity of the generated images poses a significant challenge. Our observations indicated  that  large-scale  models  struggle  with  visualizing  complex short phrases, resulting in cognitive confusion due to the excessive aggregation of elements within the images (Tekli et al., 2018). Controlling image  complexity  appropriately  can  mitigate  confusion  during  the cognitive process. Additionally, fine-tuning these models is essential to ensure that the generated images are better aligned with the practical needs of visually impaired children. In summary, the inherent flexibility of  large-scale  model  technology  also  allows  for  diverse  input  types, fostering children ' s imagination and facilitating a richer image generation experience.

Compared to existing tactile display technologies, such as the APH Monarch and Dot Pad, our approach using large-scale models introduces greater flexibility and adaptability. While the Monarch relies on preexisting  Braille  books  and  the  Dot  Pad  requires  pre-defined  visual input (Hu et al., 2022; Rao et al., 2021), our product can dynamically generate tactile representations from diverse input sources, reducing the reliance  on  pre-programmed  content.  This  dynamic  capability  better accommodates  the  spontaneous  learning  needs  of  visually  impaired children. However, it is also essential to address the challenge of image complexity  and  improve  model  fine-tuning  for  more  accurate  and comprehensible outputs.

RQ2: How do visually impaired children collaborate with teachers while  using  the  product,  and  what  is  the  manifestations  of  their interaction?

The collaboration between visually impaired children and teachers in  utilizing  the  product  constitutes  a  process  of  information  complementarity and knowledge co-creation (Gadiraju, 2023). Teachers provide  supplementary  information,  such  as  detailed  explanations  and contextual backgrounds of the images, while leveraging the multimodal perception system (tactile and auditory) to enhance the learning experience.  This  interaction  transcends  mere  one-way  information  transmission;  it  involves  teachers  guiding  the  children ' s  perceptions  and facilitating the transformation of real-world objects into cognitive understanding. Teachers help overcome the limitations of tactile cognition by offering external information, whereas  children  deepen  their comprehension  through  continuous  interaction  and  feedback,  ultimately  constructing  a  unique  knowledge  system  during  the  product usage (Cuturi et al., 2016). The essence of this interaction lies in the integration of external information with internal knowledge validation, thereby  progressively  unifying  sensory  experiences  with  cognitive processes.

Unlike  static  materials  that  rely  on  fixed  content  delivery,  our product allows for real-time adaptation and teacher-guided exploration. This dynamic process fosters a more personalized learning environment where both tactile and auditory channels are integrated. Nevertheless, further  studies  are  required  to  examine  how  these  collaborative  interactions evolve over longer periods and to identify best practices for optimizing teacher-child cooperation.

RQ3: What are the experiences, views, and preferences of visually impaired children and teachers regarding the touch interface input method?

Visually impaired children and teachers exhibit distinct experiences and preferences concerning the touch interface input method. Simplification emerges as a core element in enhancing the product experience, particularly for visually impaired children. Enhancing the responsiveness of the touch interface and standardizing operational procedures are crucial for improving usability (Kieras, 1988; Xu et al., 2018). Concurrently,  standardized  design  ensures  that  the  product  aligns  with  the interaction  methods  of  digital  devices  commonly  used  by  visually impaired  children,  thereby  making  operations  more  intuitive  and consistent  (S ´ anchez,  2008).  Visually  impaired  children  prefer  touch screen inputs that are easy to operate and highly responsive, whereas teachers prioritize design strategies that adapt to the children ' s usage habits and provide adequate informational feedback. This dual perspective  on  touch  screen  input  reflects  the  children ' s  need  for convenient operation and the teachers ' emphasis on product operability and effective interaction methods.

Compared to other smart educational tools, such as speech synthesis devices  and  screen  readers  (Radecki  et  al.,  2020;  Ma ´ ckowski  et  al., 2023), our touch-based interface offers a multisensory experience that combines  tactile  exploration  with  auditory  feedback.  While  screen readers primarily provide auditory access and lack tangible engagement, our product enhances the sensory interaction by allowing children to actively manipulate and interpret image content. This approach aligns with prior research emphasizing the importance of sensory integration in  fostering  cognitive development (Mascle et al., 2022; Slade et al., 2021). However, future iterations should continue refining the touch interface to ensure consistency and accessibility across diverse educational contexts, addressing both the children ' s need for simplicity and the teachers ' need for efficient instructional tools.

## 6.2. Design recommendations

Based  on  the  findings  of  this  study,  we  propose  several  design recommendations:

## ' Systematic Design for Learning, Not Just One-time Interactions '

When  designing  products  for  visually  impaired  children,  it  is imperative  to  move  beyond  one-time  interactive  experiences  and develop  a  comprehensive  learning  system.  During  the  experimental phase, visually impaired children indicated an inability to revisit previously  completed  images,  suggesting  that  simplicity  should  not  be achieved by reducing functionality (Markopoulos et al., 2008). A complete system should encompass features relevant to the learning process, such as saving and recording previously learned images and content for future review and deeper understanding. This approach enables visually impaired  children  to  build  long-term  memory  through  continuous learning rather than relying solely on isolated experiences.

## ' Necessity of Fine-tuning Large-scale Models '

While large  language  models  demonstrate  significant  potential  in image generation, their default outputs may not always align with the specific learning needs of visually impaired children. Therefore, finetuning  these  models  to  address  the  unique  requirements  of  this  demographic is  essential  (Ruiz  et  al.,  2023).  Training  the  models  with extensive annotated image data tailored for visually impaired children can enhance the models ' understanding of the children ' s needs, particularly concerning contour clarity and tactile feedback recognizability. Additionally,  implementing  adaptive  algorithms  that  continuously adjust image details based on feedback from visually impaired children ensures  the  generation  of  images  that  are  more  educationally  meaningful  and  appropriate  for  their  cognitive  development  stages  (Zeng et al., 2024).

In our study, we identified several key failure points, including high interruption rates due to unfamiliarity with the task interface, image misidentifications  such  as  mistaking  a  "mountain"  for  a  "cloud,"  and limitations in tasks that require more complex contextual understanding. These challenges underscore areas where the model ' s performance could be improved.

To address these issues, we propose a focused fine-tuning approach that specifically targets these failure cases. First, we recommend using a dataset tailored to these problems, incorporating multimodal data with child-friendly  descriptions  and  clear  object  visualizations.  Relevant datasets  include COCO-Captions ,  which  provides  diverse  object-text pairs,  and Conceptual  Captions ,  which  includes  broader  object  and scene descriptions. Additionally, for improving accessibility, we suggest leveraging datasets like VizWiz , which is designed for visually impaired users  and  emphasizes  clear,  easily  recognizable  object  shapes.  By manually marking cases of misidentification and expanding the dataset with  ambiguous  or  unclear  examples,  we  can  improve  the  model ' s ability to disambiguate between similar concepts. Furthermore, capturing user interaction logs will help us understand where children encounter difficulties, allowing the model to be adjusted for more accurate guidance and error correction. Additionally, we plan to explore tactile  data  resources  such  as  the TGIL repository,  which  offers  a collection of 2385 tactile graphics templates that can be used to create graphics or be embossed for classroom use. This resource could provide a  foundation  for  further  enhancing  accessibility  through  touch-based learning.

In terms of fine-tuning methodology, we aim to use data augmentation techniques to enhance the model ' s ability to handle ambiguous prompts,  as  well  as  contrastive  fine-tuning  to  differentiate  between visually similar objects. We also intend to implement instructional finetuning,  where  structured  prompts  and  responses  help  guide  children step by step through tasks, addressing difficulties as they arise. Lastly, by using interaction logs, we can reinforce the model ' s  ability  to  detect when additional guidance is needed, reducing instances of navigation errors. While a fully developed cross-modal tactile-visual dataset specifically  designed  for  visually  impaired  children  is  not  yet  widely available, we plan to explore datasets like the Natural Scene Braille Image Dataset (which  contains  images  with  Braille  labels)  and GelSight ,  a dataset developed by MIT researchers using tactile sensors to categorize textures like fabric, wood, and sandpaper. Additionally, the Touch and Go dataset,  which  supports  multimodal  tactile-visual  learning,  could help in improving touch-based interactions within the system. Through this  targeted  approach  and  by  leveraging  these  resources,  we  are confident that we can improve the model ' s performance and its ability to function effectively in educational settings.

' Transition from 2D to 3D for Enhanced Object Cognition '

Interactions with visually impaired children and visually impaired children  revealed  that  while  some  can  recognize  flat,  cartoon-like shapes, they often struggle to associate these shapes with real-life objects, such as dogs or cats. This indicates the limitations of 2D images in conveying complex and realistic objects. A key design recommendation is  to  develop  images with 3D effects, which can facilitate easier and more direct associations between tactile shapes and familiar real-life objects  for  visually  impaired  children  (S ´ anchez  and  S ´ aenz,  2006). Furthermore, visually impaired users expressed a preference for finer and smaller surface textures on the interactive interface, as heightened tactile  sensitivity  makes  overly  large  grains  detrimental  to  their perception of details. Adopting finer grain designs can provide richer tactile  information,  enabling  users  to  discern  subtler  differences  and accurately identify images.

Future  iterations  of TaleVision will  employ  advanced  AI-driven techniques  to  generate  more  detailed  and  accessible  tactile  outputs. We  plan to utilize AI-based 3D model generation tools (e.g., Hunyuan3D,  Nerf,  or  Depth  Anything,)  to  create  corresponding  3D models from 2D images (Fig. 10). By sampling and stratifying the height values  across  the  3D  model  surface,  we  will  reconstruct  the  surface morphology through variations in block heights, allowing for a more accurate tactile representation. Additionally, we will explore monocular depth estimation models (e.g., DPT and MiDaS) to extract depth maps directly from 2D images, enabling the tactile display to represent multilayered  object  contours.  This  dual  approach,  combining  3D  model generation and depth estimation, will allow for adaptive scaling and enhanced tactile feedback. To optimize user experience, we will also implement a hybrid 2.5D model that emphasizes critical object features while  simplifying  non-essential  areas,  ensuring  a  balance  between tactile  clarity  and  structural  complexity.  Furthermore,  we  plan  to introduce  dynamic  height  control,  allowing  users  or  instructors  to customize  the  tactile  resolution  based  on  individual  sensory  needs. These enhancements will provide a more immersive and precise learning experience, facilitating a clearer understanding of complex visual concepts for visually impaired children while maintaining adaptability to diverse educational contexts.

## ' Essential Role of Teacher Involvement in Learning '

Another critical insight is the indispensable role of teacher involvement in the learning process of visually impaired children. Teachers are not  merely  auxiliary  support  but  act  as  central  guides,  providing personalized  instruction  and  immediate  feedback  to  facilitate  deeper understanding of learning content (Mountapmbeme and Ludi, 2021). This  guidance  is  particularly  vital  when  using  multimodal  sensory interaction products, where visually impaired children rely on tactile and auditory senses in lieu of vision. Timely intervention by teachers can significantly enhance learning outcomes (Rosas et al., 1997). However, without teacher guidance, the effectiveness of the product in promoting autonomous  learning diminishes considerably. Observations from testing  and  usage scenarios indicated that visually impaired children often experienced confusion and a slower learning pace in the absence of teacher guidance. This underscores the necessity of designing additional features and tools that support teacher involvement, such as comprehensive training materials and detailed product usage guides, ensuring that  teachers  can  proficiently  utilize  the  product  to  assist  visually impaired children in their learning journey (Niwagaba, 2014).

Fig. 10. 3D "tree" display in the unity interface.



## 7. Limitations

Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, due to the specialized nature of the participants, our sample size was limited to 14 visually impaired children. However, from a usability perspective, a sample of this size is sufficient to identify the majority of usability issues (Nielsen and Landauer, 1993). Second, institutional policies at the school for the visually impaired restricted the use of video or photographic recordings during the experiments. This limitation hindered the capture  and  analysis  of  detailed  participant  behavior  and  reactions, particularly non-verbal communication cues. Digital records alone may have omitted crucial contextual information. Third, while the images generated by the large model were fine-tuned for the study, there were still variations in image quality that could not be fully mitigated. Future research will focus on more specialized model training for generating images tailored to the needs of visually impaired children. Additionally, the backend system experienced delays, with image generation times for a single word ranging from 10 to 15 s, which may have contributed to user disengagement.

Finally, this study focused exclusively on short-term user experiences and  learning  outcomes.  We  did  not  assess  the  long-term  cognitive development or Braille literacy improvements that could result from extended  product  use.  Future  research  should  employ  randomized controlled trials to track the progression of visually impaired children ' s image recognition abilities, supported by quantitative data to verify the product ' s efficacy.

## 8. Conclusions and future work

This study demonstrates that integrating multimodal perception into assistive learning tools can enhance visually impaired children ' s ability to associate tactile and auditory inputs with Braille. The findings indicate that participants were generally able to grasp the connection between generated tactile graphics and verbal descriptions, yet several key challenges emerged. Issues such as the complexity of AI-generated images,  the  precision  of  tactile  representation,  and  the  role  of  teacher guidance  significantly  influenced  usability  and  learning  outcomes. Although the children exhibited strong engagement with the system, frequent  interruptions  and  operational  difficulties  highlighted  areas requiring further refinement.

A critical insight from this study is that while multimodal integration enhances learning, the effectiveness of tactile representations remains contingent on the clarity of image generation and the adaptability of the system to different user needs. The reliance on teacher facilitation also underscores  the  necessity  of  structured  instructional  support.  In  this regard, developing a more adaptive learning platform -one that allows children  to  review  previously  learned  content  and  interact  with  a personalized curriculum -could substantially improve learning continuity and retention.

Future work should prioritize several key areas. First, a more systematic learning platform is needed -one that allows visually impaired children to save and review previously learned content rather than being limited to one-time usage. Second, to address the precision of image generation, further fine-tuning of the model and more responsive feedback mechanisms should be explored to improve recognition accuracy. Furthermore, the involvement of teachers remains indispensable in the learning  process  for  visually  impaired  children.  Developing  a  standardized teacher support system is essential to facilitate their guidance in product usage. Lastly, large-scale, long-term studies should be conducted to evaluate the impact of this product on the cognitive development and learning outcomes of visually impaired children.

## An Artificial Intelligence Tool for Accessible Science Education

Jacob Watters

Metropolitan State University of Denver

Mellissa Weinrich

University of Nothern Colorado

## April Hill

Metropolitan State University of Denver

## Cary Supalo

Independence Science

## Feng Jiang*

Metropolitan State University of Denver

Abstract: One  of  the  most  important  issues  in  accessible  science  education  is  creating  a laboratory workspace accessible to blind students or students with visual impairments (VI). Although these students are often provided access to the science lectures, they are usually denied full participation in hands-on laboratory work. Current solutions to this problem focus on providing special accommodations such as asking sighted lab partners to complete the hands-on work. Although the accessibility of laboratory devices in modern science education has been improved in recent years, students with VI often remain passive learners. In this work, we developed a new artificial intelligence tool, the MSU Denver Virtual Lab Assistant (VLA), using Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon Alexa Skills Kit (ASK), Alexa smart speaker, and a microcontroller (Raspberry Pi). The VLA can be used as a virtual assistant in the lab in combination with other access technologies and devices. The VLA allows students with VI to perform the hands-on laboratory work by themselves simply using voice control. The VLA can be accessed through any smartphone or Amazon Echo device to assist general science lab procedures. The VLA is designed to be applicable to different science laboratory work. It  is  also  compatible  with  other  common  accessible  electronic  devices  such  as  the  Talking LabQuest (TLQ). We believe that the VLA can promote the inclusion of learners with VI and be beneficial to general accessible science education work.

Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Virtual Assistant, Accessible Science Education

* Corresponding Author, Feng Jiang (fjiang@msudenver.edu)

## ISLAND 2020 ARTICLE



## 1. BACKGROUND

According  to  the  statistics  provided  by  the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2020), people with  a  disability  are  less  likely  to  work  as Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) professionals than those with no  disability  (19.9  percent,  compared  with 24.9 percent). This suggests that students with disabilities  are  disproportionately  discouraged  from  pursuing  STEM  education  and employment.  For  youth  with  visual  impairments (VI), artificial barriers encountered in public school science laboratories (e.g., insufficient hands-on materials, few teachers who understand  tactile  learning,  lack  of  access to resources) may hinder their entry into the STEM workforce  (Supalo,  2005).  This  lack of access to experiences with direct, handson laboratory work leads to the marginalization  of  students  with  disabilities  in  science. In the case of students with VI, the lack of vision requires this population to have spatial awareness and be familiar with the layout of the  laboratory  workspace.  Often,  students with  VI  lack  the  ability  to  read  essential information  (e.g.,  procedural  details,  safety data,  etc.)  required  to  effectively  participate in the STEM laboratory (Field et al., 2003). A common solution to this problem is to pair the student with VI with a sighted lab partner, who is called a 'directed assistant' (Miner et al., 2001). This assistant is expected to carry out  all  tasks  requested  by  the  student  with VI with the exception of any task that would violate safety protocols. This system puts the student with VI in the role of an expert while the assistant is a subordinate. However, students with VI who are early in their science education may not feel qualified and/or expe -rienced to serve in the role of expert. More importantly,  the  directed  assistant  approach creates  a  passive  laboratory  experience  for the  student  with  VI,  who  is  excluded  from participating  in  the  hands-on,  active  aspect of science laboratory learning. The shift from the directed assistant approach to an independent approach in a hands-on way to promote interest in STEM careers is needed in science education for students with VI (Supalo, 2012).

Access technology (AT) solutions are widely used  to  help  involve  students  with  VI  in science  learning  (Rose  et  al.,  2005).  The modern science learning environment is becoming  more  equipped  with  accessible and  inclusive  technologies,  such  as  digital textbooks or learning materials, online course  management  systems,  smartphones, and tablet computers equipped with text-tospeech and voice dictation tools. These tools help students with VI greatly, while still not solving some fundamental problems faced in the laboratory workspace. Most AT solutions are effective at transmitting text-based infor -mation  or  generating  the  voice  explanation of  collected  data.  However,  they  are  unable to  convey  general  lab  settings,  interactively answer questions, give general guidance of  lab  procedures,  perform  calculations,  or pause after dictating a task until the student is ready to move to the next step. In a laboratory environment, it is common for students with VI to have more anxiety and fear due to the complexity of the lab procedures and the unknown status of all lab materials and devices. Human assistants can reduce stress and  fear  in  such  an  environment  but  often take over the operating role of students with VI. Hence, a 'smart assistant' with the ability to provide all procedural information step by step, answer general questions, perform calculations,  assist  in  acquiring  and  recording experimental data, and monitor the status of a measurement device is needed.

Unlike  the  aforementioned  approaches,  an artificial intelligence (AI)-based 'smart assistant'  can  improve  the  accessibility  of the  laboratory  environment while maintaining  the  operating  role  of  students  with  VI. AI is proving itself to be a robust, innovative 21st-century  technology  that  has  boundless applications in today's world. In the arena of science education, the use of AI in the science laboratory is in its infancy. The greatest difference between traditional AT tools and AI tools is whether the software or devices are equipped  with  self-learning  abilities.  Tools with  self-learning abilities  can  provide  a more  interactive learning  experience  and continually  improve  themselves  based  on user  interactions.  We  developed  the  MSU Denver Virtual Laboratory Assistant (VLA) using multiple Amazon Web Services (AWS), an  Alexa  smart  speaker,  and  a  microcontroller (Raspberry Pi) connected to other lab devices. The VLA is equipped with all public Amazon Alexa skills and one new self-developed Alexa skill designed for general science laboratory work. All Amazon Alexa skills can constantly  improve  themselves  while  being used by numerous Amazon customers every day. The self-developed skill enables VLA to read  and  interpret  the  traditional  laboratory document,  thus  generating  interactive  voice responses to assist the laboratory work.

In this paper, we introduce the related tools, hardware, and AWS services used in our work and explain how they were utilized to build the  VLA. We also describe the unique features we have designed for our VLA, which make it adaptable to different lab procedures and compatible with other electronic devices. Finally,  conclusions  and  future  work  directions are given.



## 2. DESIGN OF THE VIRTUAL LAB ASSISTANT

## 2.1 Overview of Virtual Lab Assistant

The VLA system consists of four main components  working  together  to  create  a  single cohesive tool that greatly improves the accessibility of the laboratory environment. These components include an Alexa smart speaker, a  custom  Alexa  Skill  that  acts  as  a  virtual AI lab assistant, a Talking LabQuest (TLQ) which  allows  for  accessible  data  collection and  statistical  analysis  ('Talking  labquest', n.d.),  and  a  Raspberry  Pi  which  allows  the Alexa Skill to interact with the TLQ, effec -tively connecting all the components together. The Alexa skill contains all of the software making up the VLA. This skill code is hosted in an AWS Lambda rather than a server, thus allowing the software to be easily maintained with no server upkeep. The skill has several intents that allow students to perform various lab  tasks  with  the  assistance  of  the  VLA tool.  Students  use  an  Alexa  smart  speaker (or  any smart device such as a smartphone) to provide verbal input to the VLA skill. The input is passed through the Utterance Profiler, which allows the VLA to infer which intent to trigger based on example phrases defined in the intent schema. This allows students to interact with the VLA using natural language rather than memorizing specific keywords or phrases. It has the ability to dictate a lab procedure one step at a time, to pause until the student is ready, to list required materials, to provide guidance on using the tool, to navigate  the  lab  procedure,  etc.  Custom  laboratory procedures can be entered into our VLA Readable Format and uploaded, allowing the tool  to  be  used  with  any  lab  procedure.  A Raspberry Pi microcontroller acts as an Alexa Gadget and serves as a connection between the TLQ, the VLA tool, and the Alexa smart speaker, thus allowing hands-free control of the  TLQ.  Together,  these  four  components work in conjunction as a Virtual Lab Assistant  System  to  create  an  accessible  laboratory environment. The overall design of the VLA system enables hands-free control in a science  lab  environment,  which  is  ideal  for students with VI.



## 2.2 Tools Used in the VLA

## Alexa Skills

Alexa Skills are voice-enabled apps for Alexa.  Anyone  can  build  a  custom  skill  by creating  an  Amazon  developer  account  and using the Alexa Skills Kit ('Alexa Skills Kit,' n.d.). Skills can be uploaded to the Alexa Skill Store, where they can be enabled and used on any person's Amazon Alexa account.

## Intents, Utterances, and Slots

Intents,  utterances,  and  slots  are  the  tools used to build an interaction model between a user and an Alexa skill. An Alexa Skill is a collection of intents and slots which are triggered by user utterances. An intent defines the intended action for the Alexa skill to execute. A student could ask the VLA to begin a lab, triggering the begin lab intent which would read the first step in the lab procedure. Slots allow for variable information to be included in  the  intent.  They  are  optional  arguments that  further  define  the  functionality  of  an intent.  An  example  interaction  is  illustrated in Figure 1, in which the user triggers a 'get status' intent that returns the status of a lab device. A pH sensor slot could be added as a slot to this intent allowing the user to get the status of the pH sensor specifically.

Currently, there are 12 intents and two slots which are listed in Table 1. There is a 'material'  slot  that  allows  a  student  to  specify  a piece of lab equipment and a 'LabTitle' slot that  allows the user to specify which lab to open.

We plan on adding support for intents such as calculate,  verify  answers,  check  status,  and ask  TLQ,  which  will  have  many  slots  that will allow for verbal control of the TLQ using the VLA Alexa skill.

Intents are defined in a JavaScript Object Nota -tion (JSON) structure called the intent schema. The intent schema outlines the intents and slots of the skill as well as examples of what phrases should  trigger  each  intent.  The  intent  schema only  defines  the  basic  details  of  the  skill's intents.  The  JavaScript  (JS)  skill  code,  which implements the functionality of the intents, is not part of the intent schema but exists in an AWS Lambda and is executed on demand.
