## Empowering Individuals With Visual Impairment: A Digital Braille Solution for Learning the Urdu Language

## FARZANA JABEEN AND MEHVISH RASHID, (Member, IEEE)

Faculty of Computing (FOC), National University of Sciences and Technology, Islamabad 44000, Pakistan

Corresponding author: Farzana Jabeen (farzana.jabeen@seecs.edu.pk)

This work was supported by the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST) under Grant NUST-22-41-32.

This work involved human subjects in its research. Approval of all ethical and experimental procedures and protocols was granted by the Ethics Review Committee of the Internal Board of NUST.

ABSTRACT In today's digital era, smartphones have become an integral part of education and learning. The unification of smart devices with assistive technologies such as screen readers, voice-based navigation, and object detection, including the use of wearable devices, has significantly enhanced the abilities of individuals with disabilities. Despite these advancements, there is a notable gap in the realm of comprehensive and indigenous digital learning apps tailored for individuals with visual impairments. Traditional education for visually impaired students heavily relies on the Braille system, which required extensive training and continuous support from educators and professionals. This dependency poses a significant barrier to the availability of dedicated learning environments for this specific demographic. Addressing this challenge, our research proposes a digital solution named ''Chasham'' designed around the Braille system, specifically tailored for the Urdu language. This innovative solution involves mapping Braille codes to their corresponding Urdu alphabets and letters. Incorporating voice output further facilitates users in identifying typed letters and words. The Chasham includes various quizzes and exercises to assess and enhance student learning skills. To ensure the effectiveness and usability of the proposed solution, a 3-week user study was conducted involving 50 visually impaired students to evaluate Chasham's usability and validity. The preliminary results of this study are promising and indicate a positive impact on student learning experiences. This research represents a significant step towards filling the void in comprehensive digital learning tools for visually impaired individuals, particularly in the context of education. Integrating the Braille system into a digital learning environment for the Urdu language is a novel and thoughtful approach. It leverages technology to overcome traditional barriers and enhance the learning experience.

INDEX TERMS Braille, visual impairment, accessibility, human computer interaction in education, Urdu language tutor.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Human vision is regarded as the most crucial sense for an individual's overall well-being as it facilitates us to perceive the world around us. However, unfortunately, around 285 million individuals worldwide are estimated to suffer from blindness [1], with 1.12 million [2] of them residing



The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Orazio Gambino .

in Pakistan. Blindness can be caused by various factors, such as diseases, injuries, or other medical conditions. This impairment of sight significantly reduces an individual's ability to see and thus limits their movement and efficiency in performing daily activities [3]. Visually impaired individuals often require the assistance of walking aids such as canes or other people to navigate, avoid obstacles, and locate objects. Therefore, it is imperative that we work towards providing adequate care and resources to support visually impaired indivisuals to ensure they have a better quality of life.





Education is essential for both individuals with visual impairments and those with a sighted eye. Although obtaining education comes naturally to many, it presents significant challenges for the visually impaired [4]. Not with standing these obstacles, individuals with visual impairments possess the same inherent qualities and capabilities as their sighted counterparts, including remarkable cognitive abilities. Nevertheless, their visual limitations often impede their capacity to engage in reading and writing activities comparable to those who are sighted [5]. Consequently, they frequently rely on external assistance, such as auditory means of learning. New technologies like screen readers, voice commands, touch feedback devices, and Braille displays have made it easier for visually impaired students to learn, especially when it comes to reading and writing [6]. These tools can read out Urdu alphabets aloud. They help with correct pronunciation by using voice features. They also allow students to feel the Urdu letters through Braille devices. By using these technologies in learning apps, many difficulties faced by visually impaired learners can be removed. This helps students become more independent and confident in learning Urdu [7]. Nonetheless, with access to appropriate resources, individuals with visual impairments can enhance their education through the aid of adaptive technologies, specialized training, and community support. By facilitating these necessary provisions, visually impaired individuals can cultivate their intellectual potential more effortlessly, contributing to an improved quality of life and an increased likelihood of attaining greater independence [8].

Urdu holds a prominent status as a widely spoken and comprehended language, bearing significant influence within Pakistan. It stands as the national language of Pakistan, embraced by a substantial portion of the populace as their primary means of communication [9]. Serving as an intrinsic component of Pakistani culture and identity, the Urdu language assumes a pivotal role in shaping the education landscape of the nation. Notably, Urdu finds extensive employment within Pakistan's educational sector, thereby fostering a rich educational literary heritage. The focal point of this study revolves around devising a solution capable of mitigating the challenges confronted by individuals with visual impairments, thereby enhancing their access to Urdulanguage education. Through the provision of an accessible and user-friendly application, those afflicted by visual impairments can elevate their level of autonomy and engage more actively in societal endeavors.

Contribution The main contributions of this study are outlined below:

- Development of a specialized system to aid visually impaired individuals in comprehending and utilizing the Urdu language effectively.
- Introduction of ''Chasham,'' an innovative Braille application designed to offer assistance to visually impaired individuals.
- Creation of a hardware-based Braille system that complements and enhances the functionality of the Chasham application, further supporting visually impaired users in their language learning and communication endeavors.

Paper Structure -The introduction is presented in Section I above. The subsequent sections of this paper are structured as follows: Section II offers a comprehensive literature review related to the study's topic. In Section IV, an overview of the proposed methodology is provided, encompassing the mobile application's outline, the tools employed and application interface with braille codes for Urdu glyphs in this framework. Section V details the implementation and results, including the braille keyboard and display, along with the circuit and usability testing of the proposed application and finally, the paper concludes in Section VI.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

This review of the literature focuses on numerous research concerning assistive technology for visually impaired persons who speak or read Urdu. By offering access to information and instruction, the studies hope to bridge the gap between the visually impaired and the sighted. There several methods of assistive technology, such as voice output systems [10], Braille translation [11], and interactive learning tools [12]. The goal of these research is to improve the learning experience, communication, and information access for visually impaired people in Urdu-speaking areas. While these studies provide useful information, several drawbacks, such as limited sample numbers, must be addressed in future study.

The article presented in [13] details a system that has been developed to assist visually impaired individuals by providing voice output in the Urdu language. To create this system, the researchers built three custom datasets, each with a specific purpose. The object-dataset contained 5,5446 images of various objects such as cups, glasses, and books. The currency dataset comprised 25,626 images of Pakistani notes, and the day-night dataset contained 640 images. The system was trained using the ResNet-18 model, which has 71 layers, to evaluate these datasets. By using this model, the system could recognize and identify the objects in the images, read the currency notes, and differentiate between day and night. The voice output in Urdu language would then provide the visually impaired individual with the necessary information.

The authors of the paper [14] have developed a context-sensitive translator that can optically recognize Braille codes for the Urdu language. This technology aims to bridge the gap between partially sighted and sighted individuals by providing a means of translating Braille into Urdu. To achieve this, the authors first developed Braille codes for the Urdu language. They then scanned the Braille and used Optical character recognition (OCR) to recognize the Braille characters [15]. To ensure accurate translation, the authors also devised a deterministic Turing machine for context-sensitive translation. This machine uses a set of rules to analyze the context of the Braille characters and generate an appropriate output in Urdu. The output can then be read by sighted individuals, allowing for greater communication and understanding between those who are visually impaired and those who are not.

The authors of [16] have developed a self-teaching system that uses image processing and voice recognition to educate visually impaired children. The system is designed to be interactive, allowing children to learn in a more engaging and immersive way. The researchers have devised a mechanism to create a highly efficient Text-to-Speech (TTS) system in [17]. The main idea behind this system is to recognize handwritten Urdu characters and then convert them into audible human speech. To achieve this, the researchers used advanced handwriting recognition technology to accurately identify each handwritten Urdu character. Once the character was recognized, it was then processed and converted into a corresponding speech signal using sophisticated signal processing techniques, another same kind of study was presented in [18], for efficient TTS and voice conversion.

A comprehensive evaluation of the usability and accessibility of the real-time Braille application was conducted [19]. This app offers a new touchscreen Braille input method that allows users to tap anywhere on the screen, making it easier for visually impaired individuals to type Urdu Grade 1 and Grade 2 characters. The system was tested for speed, accuracy, error rate, and user satisfaction to assess its overall performance. In an other study, authors have created a web-based Urdu Braille Translator and interactive learning tool with the aim of improving the learning experience of Urdu Braille for parents of visually impaired children in [20]. The tool is designed to be user-friendly and interactive, enabling parents to easily translate Urdu text into Braille and learn the Braille system themselves. To evaluate the effectiveness and usability of the tool, a study was conducted with 15 parents of visually impaired students. In [21], the study demonstrates that most sighted individuals can learn whole-word Braille reading. This study is the first to show that adults with intact visual systems can acquire such a complex tactile skill when provided with the right motivation and approach. The study outlined five objectives, one of which was to examine the effects of tactile training on children. Another objective was to explore the impact of visual cues-based training on children.

The purpose of the research, presented in [25], was to investigate the accessibility of information for university students with visual impairment in higher academic institutions in Lahore, Pakistan. The study utilized a qualitative research design with interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) to explore the phenomenon. Participants were selected through purposive sampling from higher academic institutions, and face-to-face interviews were conducted with 15 visually impaired students using an interview guide. The aim was to gain insight into the actual experiences



of visually impaired students in accessing information in academic settings. In [22], the researchers have proposed an enhanced algorithm for the backend processing of a previously developed touchscreen-based Braille text entry application. The application is utilized to collect Braille Urud data, which is then transformed into Urdu text. For this particular research, Urdu Braille Grade 1 data was collected for 39 different classes comprising 144 cases for each class. A project was developed to address the challenges faced by visually impaired individuals in terms of language barriers in [23]. The goal of the project is to provide them with access to digital information using software that can communicate with them in the Urdu language. The project aimed to develop an intelligent system that utilizes voice recognition and image processing techniques to allow visually impaired individuals to interact with digital content in Urdu. This system was designed to be user-friendly and accessible, with the aim of promoting equal access to information for all individuals, regardless of their visual ability.

Amobile electronic Braille alphabet trainer was developed that improved learning outcomes among partially sighted children by integrating auditory and sensorimotor feedback [26]. Chen et al. [27] proposed a low-cost, refreshable Braille display with a haptic touch-reading system using CHAI3D, achieving a 95.5% accuracy rate in Braille recognition. Another study [28] introduced an IoT-driven OCRBraille system that converts printed text into real-time Braille output, promoting independence for visually impaired and deaf-partially sighted users. Similarly, an AI-powered Braille display system was developed to integrate refreshable Braille hardware with voice-interactive AI and cloud platforms, enabling real-time access to digital educational content for partially sighted learners [29]. The literature presented covers various studies related to assistive technology for visually impaired individuals, specifically for those who speak or read Urdu. These studies aim to bridge the gap between the visually impaired and the sighted by providing accessibility to information and education. These studies highlight the importance of assistive technology for visually impaired individuals and demonstrate various approaches to improving accessibility to education and information. However, some studies have small sample sizes, limiting the generalizability of their findings. However, the studies serve as a starting point for further research in the field of assistive technology for visually impaired individuals.

## A. SUMMARY OF THE LITERATURE

The review of the literature gives an overview of numerous studies that focus on the development and application of assistive technology to help visually impaired people in Urdu-speaking countries. These investigations examine several methodologies, such as voice output systems, Braille translation, interactive learning tools, and web-based translators, all with the goal of increasing communication, information accessibility, and education for the visually impaired. Although the study provides useful insights, some studies have drawbacks, such as small sample sizes, which may restrict the generalizability of their conclusions. Nonetheless, the assessment emphasizes the importance of assistive technology in bridging the gap between visually impaired people and the sighted, opening the way for future advances in this critical subject. ## III. EXISTING METHODS AND APPLICATION FOR VISUALLY IMPAIRED CHILDREN

## A. TRADITIONAL METHODS

When visually impaired students learn Braille, each step is critical. It assists them in becoming more familiar with Braille and understanding how it works. They begin when they are very young, and as they grow older, they learn more about reading and writing in Braille.

## 1) SIXER

When visually impaired students first begin learning Braille, they use a tool known as the Sixer. Students can touch and feel the Sixer's six pins in a 3 × 2 pattern. This helps their fingers become more adept at detecting Braille dots. They took a lot of practice to understand how the dots represent letters, numbers, and symbols. This greatly aids in their learning of Braille. Sixer takes different amounts of time for different students, but it usually takes about 2.5 years to become proficient. They improve their ability to recognize Braille patterns without the assistance of a teacher as they practice. The Practice of Sixer is important because it helps students improve their sense of touch and their comprehension of Braille. This makes them feel more confident in themselves and better prepared to learn more difficult Braille skills, such as reading and writing more difficult things. visually impaired students learn important skills that will help them read and write with their fingers by using the Sixer. This prepares them for a lifetime of touch-based learning.

## 2) BRAILLE BOX

Students progress from using the Sixer to using something called a Braille Box. This tool assists them in learning a language and understanding the Braille alphabet for various languages [30]. Students master the use of the Braille Box to read and write in the language they are learning in about three months. Students begin to learn the Braille alphabet and understand how the characters feel at this stage. The Braille Box has a grid with raised dots in the cells. These dots correspond to particular letters, numbers, and symbols in the language.

For about three months, teachers assist students in learning how to use the Braille Box. They spend a lot of time practising reading and writing with it. They can understand the language's characters by touching the raised dots. This helps them improve their reading and writing skills. Students improve their ability to use the Braille Box on their own with more practise. They can convert written text to Braille and back again. This allows them to use a variety of educational resources and participate in school activities in the language they are learning.

Using the Braille Box not only improves their language skills, but it also increases their confidence and ability to do things on their own. They are able to write well and perform well in school. This helps them succeed in school and gives them more opportunities to learn. visually impaired students learn how to understand a language through touch by mastering the Braille Box. This enables them to communicate, read books, and perform well in school. This aspect of their Braille education is a significant step towards becoming fluent in a language and learning on their own.

## 3) FRAME

Frame is the next tool students use in their Braille learning journey. It's similar to a board with a page on it. The Frame helps them in writing paragraphs and doing homework in the same way that other students use paper. It allows them to complete written tasks. Students in the Frame stage learn two important skills: reading and writing in Braille. They practice reading raised dots on one side of the board, while writing words and sentences on the other. This allows them to practice reading and writing in a constructive way. The Frame helps students improve their Braille reading and writing skills. They can use it to write paragraphs and complete assignments.

This boosts their confidence and allows them to express themselves in writing.

Students improve their reading and writing skills by using the Frame frequently. They improve their ability to connect the dots and read written material. This part of their Braille education prepares them to learn more and do well in school. Using the Frame demonstrates that we care about visually impaired students and want them to succeed in school. We know they need a variety of learning methods, and the Frame helps them read and write more effectively. It provides them with a safe environment in which to practise and learn.

## 4) PERKINS BRAILLER

As visually impaired students learn more Braille, they begin to use a device known as the Perkins Brailler. It's a unique machine that functions similarly to a typewriter for Braille. It has keys for the six Braille dots, and each key is shaped like a dot. Students can use it to record their ideas and thoughts in Braille [31]. The Perkins Brailler performs critical functions such as adding spaces, correcting errors, and moving to the next line. Students can feel the dots and know what they're writing when they use it. This enables them to write effectively. For visually impaired students, learning to use the Perkins Brailler is a significant step. It improves their ability to move their hands and fingers, as well as their ability to write Braille. However, it is important to note that the Perkins Brailler is quite expensive, costing between 100 and 200 thousands PKR. This makes it difficult for many students and families to obtain one. This price makes it difficult for all visually impaired students to have equal access to this useful tool.

## B. EXISTING DIGITAL APPLICATIONS

In today's rapidly changing digital world, technology has created new avenues for partially sighted children to learn and receive assistance. There are numerous digital apps designed specifically for them. These apps help them learn more effectively and make school more enjoyable. They use touch and sound to help children learn Braille, become smarter, and think more clearly. These apps aim to help partially sighted children succeed in school and learn more about the world. This section will discuss some important apps designed for partially sighted children. We'll see what they do and how they contribute to school.

## 1) BRAILLE BUZZ

The Braille Buzz App is a special app designed to help partially sighted children learn Braille. It has fun activities and makes cool sounds. Children can play while learning how to use the app and read Braille letters [32]. This app is compatible with a variety of Braille machines, including APH's Chameleon 20TM and Braille Trail Reader LETM. It makes reading Braille more enjoyable.

## 2) BRAILLE BEE

Braille Bee is an innovative digital application that helps visually impaired children learn in a variety of ways. It has

many unique features to assist them. They can learn from various word lists, such as special signs, common words, and words for different seasons. The app supports various types of Braille, including simple and advanced, as well as regular print. It is designed to accommodate how each child prefers to learn [33]. Braille Bee can also speak out loud using VoiceOver and works with Braille machines that can display the words. The app is entertaining and educational because it includes music, talking, and activities.

## 3) TOUCH AND LEARN

Touch and Learn is another app designed for partially sighted children. This app allows children to use their fingers to touch and hear objects on the screen. It allows them to learn about various topics in a fun way. They can even sense shapes and animals on the screen. Touch and Learn teaches a variety of topics, including numbers and more. This app assists children in learning by utilising their senses and thinking abilities [34]. It makes learning enjoyable and assists partially sighted children in improving their feeling and thinking abilities.

## IV. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

Proposed methodology offers a transformative approach to Braille education for visually impaired children. Through the Chasham application, children can access a comprehensive range of Braille lessons and track their progress. By seamlessly connecting the application to a device via Bluetooth, children can engage in interactive learning experiences, gaining hands-on experience with Braille characters. With a user-friendly interface, audio support, and backend database integration, our solution empowers visually impaired children to learn Braille at their own pace, fostering independence, improving literacy skills, and enhancing their educational journey. Our innovative solution is poised to make a significant impact in the lives of visually impaired children, providing them with a powerful tool for inclusive and accessible education. To visualize the logical view of our proposed system, refer to Figure 1.

## A. MOBILE APPLICATION

Our mobile app, Chasham, prioritizes user experience and simplicity to facilitate a smooth learning journey for IEEE AccesS'



FIGURE 2. Architecture of the system.



visually impaired children. Its intuitive interface enables easy navigation, granting access to a diverse range of Braille lessons and exercises tailored to enhance their skills. Through Bluetooth integration, the app enables effortless control and interaction with connected devices, providing a tactile learning experience. Figure 2 depicts the system architecture. Chasham surpasses traditional methods by incorporating progress tracking and saving features. Children's achievements and advancements are automatically recorded and stored as they complete exercises and lessons. The app includes a comprehensive dashboard for guardians or teachers to monitor their development, offering valuable insights into their learning journey and identifying areas that require attention.

## B. TOOLS

Our project employed a robust tech stack that encompassed various technologies to build a powerful and efficient solution. The following technologies were utilized:

## 1) FLUTTER

We utilized the Flutter framework as the foundation for our mobile application. Flutter's cross-platform capabilities enabled us to create a visually appealing and interactive user interface for both Android and iOS platforms. With Flutter, we could achieve a consistent user experience and streamline the development process.

## 2) FIREBASE

Firebase served as our backend and database management platform. We leveraged Firebase's real-time database, authentication services, storage, and hosting capabilities. This allowed us to securely store and retrieve data, implement user authentication, and ensure efficient data management within our application.

## 3) PROTEUS

Proteus, a versatile simulation software, played a pivotal role in the hardware component of our project. We utilized Proteus to design and test the functionality of our Arduino-based hardware device. Through Proteus, we could create virtual prototypes, simulate hardware behavior, and verify the compatibility of our hardware with the software solution.

FIGURE 3. Login screen of the application.



## 4) ARDUINO

Arduino served as the hardware platform for our project. We designed a braille keyboard and display using Arduino, incorporating DPDT push buttons for the keyboard and servo motors for the braille display. This hardware integration allowed for seamless interaction between the mobile app and the physical device.

## B. CIRCUIT

The circuit implementation is a vital aspect of our Braille learning device as it integrates multiple components and modules to form a functional and user-friendly system. The Arduino Mega microcontroller board, utility buttons, Braille input module, PCA9685 motor driver, HC-05 Bluetooth module, and external power supply are integrated to provide seamless interaction, accurate Braille input, precise motor control, and wireless connectivity with the mobile application. By understanding the role and interaction of each component, the reliability and efficiency of the device can be better appreciated.

Thecomponents used in our Braille learning device include the Arduino Mega microcontroller board, push buttons for user interaction, DPDT buttons for Braille input, the Motor Driver PCA9685 for controlling Braille dots, the Bluetooth module HC-05 for wireless communication, and an external power supply to meet the current requirements of the motors. The Arduino Mega was chosen for its extensive digital pins and processing capabilities. Push buttons facilitated intuitive user interaction, while the DPDT buttons represented the Braille cells. The Motor Driver PCA9685 facilitated precise motor control, and the Bluetooth module HC-05

## C. USABILITY TESTING

A detailed study is conducted to evaluate the usability and effectiveness of a real-time Braille self-learning application. The study involved 50 visually impaired students aged between 8 and 17 years, with no prior experience in Braille (see Table 4). To ensure fair representation across age groups, participants were divided into 10 groups, each consisting of 5 students. The grouping was based on stratified random sampling to ensure age diversity. Each group participated in structured testing covering alphabets, words, sentences, and random content. The study spanned a period of three months and involved 10 tasks/tests, each designed to examine a specific learning aspect. All 50 students completed each task and provided feedback. A detailed explanation of these tasks is presented in Table 2. Figure 11 visualizes the improvement in test performance: while many participants initially struggled with correctly responding, their scores significantly improved over time as they practiced using the app.

This study was conducted in collaboration with a special education institute, and ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Review Committee of the Internal Board of NUST prior to the start of the study. Each participant voluntarily signed an informed consent form prior to the user study. The Urdu writing was crucial for the journey of the participants. Using an Urdu-to-Braille converter, the participants translated familiar Urdu content into Braille format. This helped them connect what they knew about writing with

TABLE 3. Reliability check.

the sensation of Braille. Then, using what they already knew, they learned how to use Braille online. This transition from linguistic familiarity to tactile learning marked a key milestone in their progress. This study demonstrated how the combination of technology and learning can make Braille easier to learn. Furthermore, it revealed that multimodal teaching strategies can significantly enhance the learning outcomes of students with visual impairments.

## D. RELIABILITY STATISTICS

In general terms, a reliability assessment is typically carried out using Cronbach's Alpha and implies the measurement of internal consistency or the extent to which a set of items measures a single unidimensional latent construct. In other words, it helps determine if the items in a measurement instrument produce consistent measurements of one underlying concept.

Table 3 shows the results of reliability testing and offers Cronbach's Alpha value-a numerical scale from 0 to 1. The value in this case is 0.929. Values closer to 1 indicate higher reliability. In general, a Cronbach's Alpha of 0.7 or greater is considered satisfactory for research purposes. The number of items analyzed in the reliability test is 10.

Cronbach's Alpha [35] value of 0.929 indicates an excellent level of internal consistency. This implies that the questionnaire items are highly reliable in measuring the intended concept.

Moving on to Table 5, it provides information related to the gender distribution of the participants. Out of the 50 students, 28 were male (56%) and 22 were female (44%). This nearequitable gender representation allows the study to draw conclusions applicable across genders, further strengthening the generalizability of the findings.

## F. ANOVA TESTING FOR USABILITY

The user study involved 50 visually impaired students, aged 8 to 17 years, who had no prior knowledge of Braille. The participants were divided into 10 groups, each consisting of 5 students. This structure ensured consistency across groups, enabling meaningful comparison of performance outcomes. The diverse age range helped evaluate the Braille learning application's usability across cognitive and motor developmental levels.

The study aimed to evaluate the usability and effectiveness of the Braille learning application by evaluating the performance of the participants in recognizing Braille alphabets, forming words, understanding sentences and handling random Braille input. The evaluation was carried out over three months and included the following key steps :

- Pre-Test Preparation: Participants were introduced to the Braille application and trained in its functionalities.
- Testing: Participants completed a series of tests designed to measure their performance in identifying Braille alphabets, forming words, and understanding sentences. These tests were sourced from basic Urdu language textbooks for visually impaired learners.
- Data Collection: Scores for each category (Alphabets, Words, Sentences and Random) were recorded and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of the learning application.

## 1) CRITERIA FOR CHOOSING ALPHABETS, WORDS, AND SENTENCES

The alphabets, words, and sentences used in the tests were chosen to cover a wide range of difficulty levels. This ensured comprehensive assessment of both foundational and advanced Braille reading skills.

- Alphabets : Individual Braille letters for Urdu were carefully selected to include a balanced mix of simple and complex Braille symbols, representing common and less frequently used letters in the Urdu language. All Urdu alphabets were included in the selection.
- Words : A combination of commonly used and more complex words was selected, sourced from basic Urdu language textbooks specifically designed for differently abled learners. These words were chosen to assess students' learning performance.
- Sentences : The sentences were formed using the selected words from basic Urdu language textbooks tailored for differently abled learners. This approach enabled us to evaluate the participants' ability to comprehend and interpret complete thoughts in Braille, which is a more advanced skill compared to recognizing individual words or letters.

## 2) ANOVA TEST RESULTS AND SIGNIFICANCE

Table 6 presents scores for four key categories: Alphabets, Words, Sentences, and Random, each assessed by 10 distinct groups. This table is crucial in understanding the usability and effectiveness of the application in helping participants learn Braille. It reflects skill acquisition in both structured and unstructured learning tasks.

To determine whether there were statistically significant differences between performance in different types of tests, we performed an ANOVA. The results of the ANOVA test are presented in Table 7. This analysis provides insight into the variation between different types of tests and assesses whether differences in mean scores are statistically significant.

Here, SV stands for Source of Variation, SS represents Sum of Squares, DF denotes Degrees of Freedom, and MS

TABLE 8. Comparison of claims and evidence with previous studies.

indicates Mean Square. The ANOVA test results show that there is a significant difference in performance between the different types of tests, with an F-value of 8.95 and a p-value less than 0.01. This indicates that the performance variations are unlikely to be due to random chance, confirming that the different types of tests significantly affect the results. These findings suggest that certain tasks are more challenging or better aligned with the learning objectives of the Braille application, providing valuable insights for further refinement and development of the application.

## 3) ACCURACY AND ERROR MEASUREMENT

The performance of each participant was evaluated in terms of accuracy and errors. Accuracy was determined by the percentage of correct answers in all categories, while errors were calculated based on the number of incorrect or unattempted answers.

- Accuracy : The overall accuracy scores were 87%, expressed as percentages, and varied among the groups. Group 2 achieved the highest accuracy at 90%, closely followed by Group 3 with 89%. In contrast, Groups 4 and 6 had the lowest accuracy rates, at 77% and 73%, respectively. This variation highlights the differences in proficiency levels among the participants in recognizing and translating Braille symbols.
- Errors : The error rates were 13%, calculated as a percentage of total attempts, and were highest for Groups 4, 6, and 9, with error rates of 23%, 27%, and 26%, respectively. These high error rates indicate significant challenges in correctly identifying and interpreting Braille symbols.

## G. DISCUSSION

The completion of our Braille learning solution represents a significant milestone in our project, and we are thrilled to share the results of our endeavors. In this section, we will dive into the implementation results, highlight key insights from user testing and feedback, and engage in a comprehensive discussion regarding the implications and significance of our findings. Through meticulous testing and evaluation, we have observed promising results that underscore the effectiveness and usability of our Braille learning solution. Visually impaired students and educators have provided overwhelmingly positive feedback, expressing greater participation, improved Braille literacy skills, and increased independence in their learning journeys. The user-friendly design of our mobile application, complemented by the tactile features of the hardware device, has allowed students to effortlessly navigate lessons, complete exercises, and track their progress.

The integration of a comprehensive database system has proved instrumental in delivering personalized learning experiences for each student. The ability to monitor individual progress, provide customized lessons and exercises, and generate informative reports has empowered educators to effectively track student performance and make informed instructional decisions. In addition, we reflect on the challenges encountered during the development and implementation phases and discuss potential avenues for future improvements and advances. Our solution represents a significant step towards harnessing technology to enrich the learning experience of visually impaired students, and we acknowledge the need for continued research and development to refine and expand its capabilities.

The results obtained from the implementation of our Braille learning solution demonstrate its efficacy in improving Braille literacy, fostering independent learning, and promoting inclusivity in education. The positive user feedback and the potential for widespread adoption underscore the value and relevance of our solution to address the unique needs of visually impaired students. Through ongoing discussions and collaborations, we strive to further optimize our solution, ensuring its accessibility, impact, and empowerment within the visually impaired community. Table 8 summarizes the main claims of this study, supported by the corresponding evidence and interpretations of the researchers, along with comparisons to previous research. This structured overview highlights the validation of our approach and situates it within the existing body of knowledge.





## VI. CONCLUSION

The development and implementation of our Braille learning solution have yielded promising results, demonstrating its potential to revolutionize Braille education for visually impaired students. By combining a user-friendly mobile application, a tactile hardware device, and a comprehensive database system, we have created an inclusive and holistic learning experience that empowers students to independently master Braille, improving their language skills, and expanding educational opportunities. Positive feedback and successful user tests validate the effectiveness of our solution in addressing the unique needs and challenges faced by visually impaired students during Braille learning. The intuitive design of the mobile application, along with the tactile features of the hardware device, has played a crucial role in fostering student engagement, facilitating skill development, and instilling a sense of empowerment and independence. These findings have practical implications for schools, rehabilitation centers, and special education programs, as they highlight how affordable, portable, and accessible digital tools can be integrated into the curriculum to support independent learning. Educational institutions can adopt this solution to supplement traditional Braille teaching, reduce the dependency on specialized instructors, and enable learners to practice at their own pace. However, certain limitations should be acknowledged. The study sample was limited to 50 participants within a specific age range and region, which may affect the generalizability of the results. Looking to the future, several avenues for further improvements and enhancements are being explored. Our focus is on refining the user experience of the mobile application by incorporating additional features and functionalities based on user feedback and using emerging technologies. This will not only enhance the usability of the system, but will also help establish a scalable framework for deploying similar tools in diverse linguistic and educational contexts. This includes investigating options for voice assistance, multilingual support, and incorporating gamification elements to make the learning process more interactive and enjoyable.

## Encouraging Vision-Impaired Students to Learn Information Technology Using an e-Learning Platform

R. G. G. Anuradha , A. P. Rangodage , K. A. G. T. Nimthara ,

P. S. L. T. Cooray , Anuradha Jayakody , and Pipuni Wijesiri

Abstract Asignificant number of visually impaired children are currently studying in Sri Lanka. But in this technological era, this visual impairment is a huge challenge for visually impaired children to get education and to get a good job opportunity. Due to their condition, visually impaired students can't choose a career that fits their preferences and goals. And also, learning IT is more tough for those students because of their visual impairment. In order to overcome this challenge, providing an opportunity to learn through an e-learning platform which includes a broad collection of learning resources that are related to Information Technology. 14 years and above visually impaired students selected as the target audience and this e-learning platform will be specialized based on information technology. Here students can study Python programming, information security, and business management for IT. This e-learning platform will customize the educational experience by suggesting proper modules depending on each learner's requirements and interests using a voice-based chatbot. Emotion detection technology also creates a positive learning environment and offers emotional assistance. Students with vision impairments can learn the fundamentals of programming such as pseudo codes and flow charts with the help of voice commands. Individuals can also use hand gestures for assessments, which increases user friendliness and involvement of the user. This comprehensive project aims to empower visually impaired individuals in Sri Lanka and realize their potential for future success.

## 1 Introduction

In the current global environment, the frequency of visual impairments is a major concern, affecting an estimated 191 million people globally, of whom 10.8 million individuals are completely blind [1]. Within this large population, there is an important section of Sri Lanka that faces different challenges. When our research team visited The Ceylon School for the Deaf and Blind (CSDB) and The Employer's Federation of Ceylon, we found out there are difficulties that Sri Lankan visual impairments face especially in the education and work sector, even though they have skills equivalent to their sighted rivals. These difficulties highlight the critical requirement for coordinated initiatives to guarantee fair chances for people with visual impairments, especially in fields such as computer programming, information security, and business management for IT [2, 3].

Research highlights the exceptional learning abilities of the visually impaired population, particularly in technology-related fields [4]. Acknowledging this basic capacity, a customized learning environment has been created to support their interaction with contemporary technology and remove the obstacles preventing them from taking advantage of education and employment opportunities. This research project aims to close the gap between aspiration and reality by providing visually impaired learners with the tools and resources they need to pursue their passions and make valuable contributions to their country.

This study is fundamentally motivated by the belief that every person should have an equal chance to prosper in a world that is becoming more technological, regardless of physical constraints. This application is more than just technological advancements; they are tools of empowerment that provide people the confidence and competence to successfully navigate the complexity of the digital world. Through the integration of an AI chatbot, voice-based flowcharts and algorithms learning, emotion-detecting technology, and interactive assessments using hand gestures, this research aims to improve learning outcomes and encourage comprehensive development in visually impaired individuals. It is imperative to recognize the possible constraints and difficulties that may arise from this undertaking, such as problems with technological accessibility, social complexities, and resource limitations. This research project is an attempt to address the differences in work and education that visually impaired people, especially those in Sri Lanka, encounter. It is evidence of the ability to overcome obstacles and realize human potential through creativity, inclusion, and tenacity. We hope to establish a society in which every person, regardless of social or physical barriers, has the chance to achieve success.

## 2 Literature Review

There is some research that focuses on creating chatbots for e-learning platforms because they can be considered an important innovation in the education field. Teachers face difficulties when it comes to giving attention to each student. As a solution, some studies suggest creating chatbots because they can work with multiple students at a time. Additionally, students can get an interactive learning experience using chatbots [5]. However, these chatbots can't be used by visually impaired students, because they can't use technologies like normal students. As a solution for that problem, we can use voice-based chatbot. Our proposed system presents the realization of a voice-based chatbot for supporting visually impaired students to identify the most suitable module for them and their knowledge level based on the selected module. Additionally, they can use this chatbot to ask questions related to anything in the world [6]. Radolfo, Felippe, and Carlos have researched how to give algorithmic knowledge to vision-impaired children. Theoretical parts like basic algorithm concepts, basic programming, and the theory of flowcharts are taught to vision-impaired children using screen readers. They use screen reading software such as DOSVOX [7], JAWS [8], and NVDA [9] which allow visually impaired students to access text and images on computers. Also, use flowcharts to teach by physically touching their shapes and they read the algorithms by using screen readers. The process in this research paper is commendable. However it can be difficult for a vision-impaired child to do all these things alone, so there should be a teacher or a guide who has knowledge about this. While researching about the vision impaired/ blind children of the selected age group, the teachers of CSDB said that if we can teach concepts like basic algorithms, basic programming, and flowcharts interactively to the children even without using a screen reader it would be very valuable. Further, while gathering facts to create an e-learning system suitable for vision-impaired children, the CSDB told us that even though fully blind children learn about flowchart symbols, they do not have much understanding of them, so we should teach them the algorithm concept of flowcharts. Partially blind children should be taught all things like flowcharts and algorithms. There is no need for screen readers due to the theory lessons related to these through a video series so that all vision-impaired individuals can understand them in general. After that, it is possible to listen to the questions of the quizzes given to test the knowledge of vision-impaired children through Text to Speech (TTS).

Johnson et al. (Famuyide and Akindoju [10]) focused on using the Universal Design Model (UDM) as a guide in the creation and assessment of an online voiceassisted examination system (OVAES) [10]. Their study emphasizes how crucial it is to modify technology to meet the unique requirements of visually impaired students. With capabilities such as keyboard navigation and audio support, OVAES showed encouraging results in improving content comprehension and enabling self-assessment tasks. However, when completing the module assessments and responding to questions, our system uses hand gestures.

Sharma et al. explore applying convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to identify facial emotions [11]. The study focuses on the importance of facial expressions in social communication and their importance to interactions between humans and computers. Using the FER 2013 dataset as its training set, the ResNet9 model showed 63%accuracyinidentifyingdifferentemotions.Furthermore,aGUIdesktopprogram for real-time emotion recognition has been developed, demonstrating the usefulness of the suggested methodology. To address this concern, our system detects six main emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Neutral, Surprise, and Fear) to properly identify individuals with visual impairments during the final web assessment through the web camera using CNN and OpenCV2.s.

This research paper compares a learning platform for the visually impaired with existing systems like JAWS, NVDA, and DOSVOX. Traditional platforms focus on screen reading, while the proposed platform combines voice commands with an AI chatbot for more independent interaction between blind and partially impaired users. Our platform offers interactive learning with voice-based flowcharts and algorithms, catering to the cognitive and emotional needs of visually impaired students, bridging the gap between traditional accessibility technologies.

## 3 Methodology

In our proposed e-learning system includes a voice-based chatbot specifically designed to identify the suitable module to learn and the knowledge level of visionimpaired users. Implementing voice-based chatbot includes several steps such as data gathering, machine learning model training, and natural language processing (NLP) techniques.

We have conducted discussion sessions and surveys with teachers and students of the CSDB in order to gain an understanding of the requirements of a voice-based chatbot and to clarify the effectiveness of this method. And also got the help of them to gather datasets and to create questions for stages of chatbot.

When creating intents, divided the responses based on questions. In this step, the most frequent answers that visually impaired students were defined. Then preprocessed the gathered data using methods like tokenization and lemmatization. To increase chatbot's accuracy of output we used NLP techniques including Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK). Tokenization is the process of dividing a text into smaller tokens. Lemmatization is the process of reducing words to their base form.

Several machine learning methods were experimented in order to find out the best model for chatbot. Initially, tested Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models. However, we finally selected Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models because of their higher classification accuracy when identifying intents according to user inputs (Fig. 1).

To implement the system, we used speech recognition library to translates voice inputs to text and used Google Text-to-Speech (GTTS) library to deliver the output as voice. As an additional feature linked the ChatGPT API into our chatbot system.

Fig. 1 Artificial neural network



Because of this integration users can ask any question. There are several significant methods and techniques in providing the proposed solution in the voice selection and answer selection research part. In our web app, when vision-impaired children are given 4 answers to the question, they give the voice command one, two, three, or four as the answer. If the correct answer is 2, when the voice command is given as 2, the SVM machine learning model predicts the corresponding answer. The answer predicted by the model is displayed by STT and the user can listen to the answer given by TTS.

The data set related to this process was created as follows. About 4000-5000 audio clips of people pronouncing one, two, three, and four have been obtained from different voices and the data set needed to train the model has been created. Audacity software has been used as a software tool for this purpose. In addition, there are some special requirements for creating the data set. These audio files should be in WA V format. The sample rate of the audio clip should be 44,100 Hz. Audio recording time duration should be 3 s. And the amplifier/voltage of the audio signal should be between 0.5-1. In the real-time audio recording preprocessing section, the audio clip is cropped with a length of 3 s and low frequencies are cut by basic noise cancelation. The data set is created by this kind of process.

Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) are used for data extraction in speech and audio processing tasks. They capture key aspects of human speech while eliminating extraneous information. MFCCs are extracted from Voice Activity Detection speech segments, providing compact and discriminative features for classification models. Support Vector Machine (SVM) is used for classification and regression in high-dimensional feature spaces (Fig. 2).

Fig. 2 Support vector machine



The retrieved MFCC features from the labeled speech samples corresponding to distinct answers (e.g., 'answer 1', 'answer 2', etc.) would be used to train the SVMclassification model in your case. The trained SVM model learns to categories fresh incoming speech segments into one of the predefined classes using the patterns collected by the MFCC features. Before creating the SVM model, two other models, CNN and LSTM, were tried to do this audio processing and classification, but due to the accuracy of the SVM model being relatively higher than the other two and the use of less computational power, it was used for our research (Table 1).

The interactive assessment evaluates and improves visually impaired individual's understanding by utilizing hand gesture technologies. Users can interact with the evaluation tool by using hand gestures to answer questions and get feedback on their replies. Through the use of this approach, the evaluation process will be more inclusive and accessible for individuals with visual impairments, enabling them to have an active role in learning activities pertaining to business management, information security, and basic programming. The evaluation tool gives visually impaired individuals an interesting and creative approach to demonstrate their comprehension of different concepts and topics through the use of hand gesture technology. Moreover, a model was developed, and its architecture was optimized to utilize the minimum computational power effectively after undergoing modifications. The accuracy of the model is 99%. Additionally, the integration of libraries like MediaPipe, OpenCV, NumPy, Pandas, scikit-learn, and Keras with TensorFlow can enhance the functionality of an assessment tool, improving accuracy and effectiveness. This combination of technologies ensures a robust web-based application infrastructure, benefiting visually impaired individuals and enhancing their learning experience (Fig. 3).

We have invited seven visually impaired members to gather data. We captured their finger movement within 10 min. After that trained the model using that data. We have used a variety of hand gestures and movements to test the robustness of the model across different scenarios.

To support visually challenged individuals during their final online web assessments, this research investigates the design, implementation, and success of a web application coupled with visual technologies such as web camera-based emotion recognition. The study uses a mixed-methods approach to integrate qualitative insights with quantitative data analysis. Depending on the chosen implementation, the React.js and Node.js front-end, supported by a MongoDB database, records both audio (such as pitch and MFCCs) and possibly video data from the web camera [12]. These features are analyzed by deep learning frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch, Keras, Pandas), which then extract emotions and categorize them into specific groups (Happy, Sad, Fear, Angry, Neutral, Surprise). These categories are evaluated using a scoring system, which helps to determine the student's general emotional state throughout the test.

Furthermore, the primary focus of this project is to utilize deep learning to categorize emotions, Support Vector Machines (SVM) can be investigated as a backup classification technique in future versions. Additionally, the integration of Natural Language Generation (NLG) could facilitate the provision of customized feedback to individuals, taking advantage of their assessment results and emotional condition. Potential connections between emotions and assessment performance are investigated using data analysis methods including Item Response Theory (IRT) and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT). This method seeks to overcome the difficulty of identifying emotions in individuals who are visually challenged by making use of both visual signals and, if used, facial expressions that are recorded by the web camera. In the end, the system aims to give insightful information about individuals' feelings, boost their self-esteem and online web assessment experience, and potentially improve visually impaired individuals' learning experiences in programming, business, and security after O/L and A/L examinations.

The data was annotated with the appropriate emotions. Using TensorFlow or PyTorch, a CNN model was trained to map retrieved features to emotions. Predicting a user's emotional state could be used to customize interactions and information with a voice assistant, possibly providing support or changing the way they communicate. The goal of this project is to improve accessible technology experiences by better understanding emotion detection for people with impaired vision. Each participant contributed a 1.5-min keynote video recording. It consisted of six different emotions (Happy, Sadness, Fear, Neutral, Anger, Surprise). Then a 40-s video recording of the left and right sides, separated by frames, was also contributed (Fig. 4).

Epochs represent the number of times the entire framed emotions images dataset is processed. Positive training and validation accuracy indicate a well-defined model. Preprocessing includes noise reduction, feature extraction, and data enrichment. Python-based deep learning tools like TensorFlow and PyTorch are used to prepare the data. Performance is assessed using measures like accuracy, F1-score, and confusion matrices.

Fig. 4 Accuracy of emotion detection model



## 4 Result and Discussion

Multiple machine learning and deep learning models were experimented with in the implementation of e-learning platform to find the best methods for different components of the proposed system. Based on accuracy level Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) are the most effective modules. The selection of models causes to successful implementation of the e-learning platform. Completely blind and partially blind users can use the application with minimal help from guardians and screen readers.

Our study offers a thorough and novel method for meeting the educational needs of people with visual impairments, especially in the area of information technology. The incorporation of voice-activated chatbots, facial recognition software, and hand gesture interactions highlights our dedication to diversity and ease of use. We have included user testing and feedback systems that continuously inform modifications to guarantee the platform's usability and efficacy. To evaluate the viability and efficacy of our solutions in actual educational settings, preliminary pilot studies have been carried out, including testing phases with visually impaired students from the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, Sri Lanka. These studies have yielded important insights into the practical implementation of our solutions. In order to obtain long-term funding and support for the project, possible collaborations with governmental and non-governmental groups are also being investigated. Taking on issues connected to internet connectivity and access to devices among visually impaired individuals in Sri Lanka is also a priority, with strategies in place to mitigate these barriers and ensure broader accessibility (Tables 2, 3 and 4).

This research suggests a voice-based learning platform for visually impaired users, focusing on lighter background colors and larger letter sizes. The platform's userfriendly interface reduces the need for guardians and screen readers, making learning more accessible. The emotion detection technology makes learning more personalized. Interactive learning modules simplify complex IT topics, especially those requiring voice commands and hand gestures. This innovative approach encourages visually impaired students to pursue IT courses and provides self-assurance in using digital technologies. The program shows promise in enabling visually impaired individuals to achieve their academic and professional goals in the IT industry.

## 5 Conclusion and Future Work

The research aims to meet the educational needs of visually impaired individuals in the digital era by creating accessible web apps for Python programming, business management, and information security. Conversational chatbot technology and emotion recognition technology improve learning experiences and foster flexibility and trust. Future research can expand accessibility and empower visually challenged individuals in Sri Lanka by adding language learning features, Braille conversion tools, enhanced evaluations, customized learning pathways, and a community forum for peer-to-peer encouragement. Through the process of this research, we expect to expand accessibility and empower visually challenged individuals in Sri Lanka more than ever. In the future, researchers can add a feature to learn the content using other languages. It will help to serve a wider audience. And also, can add Braille conversion tools to convert the module content and learning material so that users can experience their familiar method of learning. To improve user experience, can create enhanced evaluations and customized learning pathways. And last, a community forum will encourage peer-to-peer encouragement and support. These new paths aim to transform the process of obtaining IT skills into something accessible and strong.

Abstract -In  the  field  of  education,  Teachers  of  Students with  Visual  Impairments  need  to  read  and  review  student's Braille homework. Reading Braille consumes a lot of teachers' time and energy. We propose an end-to-end solution to translate Braille into Chinese. Our approach uses a deep learning method to detect and recognize Braille in images and translate them into Chinese and mathematical formulas. Finally, we reconstruct the translation results into the style of the input Braille image. Our approach is able to adapt to more complex Braille images and make  the  translation  results  easier  to  read  and  understand, significantly  improving  the  speed  of  reading  Braille  for  nondisabled.

For instance,  Minghu  Jiang  [5]  proposed  a  method  to  convert Braille into Chinese. They used the N-Best search algorithm to translate Braille into Chinese characters.

Keywords-Braille, Braille Education, Object Detection, Chinese Braille, Braille Translate

## I. INTRODUCTION

According to a report by the World Health Organization, there are currently 284 million people in the world who are visually  impaired.  Braille  education  is  an  important  part  of learning Braille. Reading and writing Braille is one of the tools used by visually impaired people to access information and communicate with others who use their tactile nerves [10].

However, there are some difficulties with Braille education in practice. Most of the Teachers of Students with Visual Impairments (TSVI) are non-disabled. Reading Braille is difficult for them. They read Braille slower than their native language and they take a great deal of time to read students' Braille. The huge cost of learning Braille also prevents nondisabled  from  getting  involved  in  Braille  education.  Most parents of visually impaired children also do not understand Braille. They are unable to provide adequate assistance in the development of their children. These problems have hindered the development of Braille education.

Much of the work in the past has been aimed at helping non-disabled join Braille education more easily. Most of the past work has been devoted to the interconversion of different languages  to  Braille.  Some  work  has  translated  books  into Braille to make reading materials more accessible to visually impaired. For instance, Taekeun Park [9] proposed a method for automatically translating scanned images of printed books Past  work  on  Braille  translation  has  not  always  been feasible in Braille education. Most of them only support the translation of Braille text, ignoring other types of Braille that may be present in a Braille document. For instance, A Chinese Braille examination paper may contain not only Chinese but also  tables  and  pictures.  Once  the  input  Braille  contains meaningless Braille text used to describe the structure, it can significantly reduce their translation effectiveness.

We solve this problem for Braille translation with a new process that eliminates the user input step and recognizes the Braille image scanned by the scanner directly. Then we use deep  learning  approaches  to  analyze  the  structure  of  the Braille image, dividing it into sections according to the type of  Braille.  For  each  type  of  Braille,  we  design  different processing methods to translate them.

We propose an end-to-end Braille-to-Chinese translation system, named "Read Light". We use deep learning techniques to recognize Braille in Braille Document images and  abstract  the  layout  information  of  documents  from  the recognition results. Then we translate the recognized Braille into Chinese or mathematical formulas according to the rules of Braille dot transcription (including Chinese and mathematical  Braille)  of  the  National  Standard  for  Braille. Our  method  was  able  to  translate  Braille  image  containing both Chinese Braille and mathematical Braille, while experiments showed that this also improved the accuracy of translation in some cases. In order to verify the usability of the system,  five  subjects  were  interviewed  and  the  system  was evaluated in detail and in depth. The results showed that our system significantly improved the speed of reading Braille for non-disabled, thus improving the effectiveness of Teachers of Students with Visual Impairments.

## II. RELATED WORK

## A. Braille Detection and Recognition

Past  approaches  have  mainly  used  machine  learning methods to detect Braille dots. Shanjun Zhang[13] used fast dynamic thresholding and image histogram to detect Braille dots. Then they grouped obtained Braille dots according to the horizontal  coordinates  (x-coordinates)  and  assigned  Braille dots  into  3x2  grid  by  calculating  average  distance  between groups. Renqiang Li [6] used Haar and Adaboost method to detect  Braille  dots  in  images  and  make  post-processing processes similar to the above. Their method got F1=97 at the Braille  dot  level.  These  methods  are  very  sensitive  to  the setting of thresholds and processing of combining Braille dots into Braille characters requires that images are not seriously skewed.

With the development of deep learning, neural networkbased methods surpass machine learning methods in various fields.  For  the  first  time,  Ilya  G.  Ovodov  [8]  was  able  to directly  detect  character-level  Braille  using  a  deep  learning algorithm. The method got F1=99.8 at the Braille character level  and  F1=99.9  at  the  Braille  dot  level  based  on  deep learning methods. Neural network-based methods are not only more accurate than traditional methods, but also more robust. The method can accept little deformation of images.

## A. Overview

Our method receives images scanned by the scanner and uses deep learning techniques to detect and recognize Braille dots in the image. Elements in Braille image are then detected and classified. For each Braille point, we assign it to one type: Chinese, mathematical or table. We design different processing methods for each of the different types. Finally, the translation results are reconstructed according to the position of the Braille dots to produce easily understood visual results. Fig. 1 illustrates the architecture and procedure of our system.

Fig. 1. Framework of End-to-End Braille Translation System(Red words are translations of Chinese words)



## B. Braille Character Detection and Recognition

This  stage  focuses  on  detecting  and  recognizing  the position information and dot information of Braille characters. We follow the approach of Ilya G Ovodov [8] using RetinaNet [7] object detection method to detect the position and classes of Braille characters in parallel. We consider Braille character as a rectangle. RetinaNet  network  directly predicts the coordinates  of  the  four  corners  of  the  rectangle  to  which Braille character belongs and the category of each character. A Braille character consists of a 3x2 rectangle with the first column numbered 1, 2, 3 from top to bottom and the second column  numbered  4,  5,  6.  The  character  class  is  a  string describing Braille dots information. Braille dot number in the string means that the position is dot and Braille dot number not in the string means that there is no dot. For example, '126' means that positions numbered 1, 2, 6 have dots and positions numbered 3, 4, 5 have no dots. To improve the accuracy of the model, we reduce the size of candidate anchors based on the a priori knowledge of Braille but do not significantly affect the speed  of  inference.  The  result  of  Braille  recognition  is  the cornerstone  of  the  whole  translation  system.  Accuracy  of detection  directly  and  significantly  affects  the  translation results.  Because  Errors  will  be  amplified  in  subsequent process.

## C. Table Structure Detection

Braille  images  may  contain  Braille  Characters  used  to describe the structure of table. We use CenterNet [4] object detection  method  to  detect  tables  in  the  input  images.  Its

## B. Braille Translation

Letters and Braille can be mapped one to one the other because the number of letters in most languages is less than the number that Braille can represent. K. Sasindu Anuradha [1] mapped Braille characters to English letters and Sinhala one by  one,  and  then  rearranges  them  into  readable  text.  The translation accuracy in the general case is 85.30%. Ju-Xiao Zhang [12] created a Chinese Braille dictionary and used a binary  language  model  lexicon  to  solve  the  one-to-many problem  in  Pinyin  to  Chinese  characters  mapping.  Minghu Jiang[5] used N-Best method to find the maximum possible N Chinese character sequences. The best sequence is selected as the result by calculating the scores of these sequences in   word graph. The method has 94.38% translation accuracy.

## III. METHOD

detection strategy of segmenting key points is well suited for detecting  wired  forms  in  Braille  document  images.  These Braille characters are detected and then removed from Braille character  detection  and  recognition  results.  These  Braille characters  are  not  involved  in  the  subsequent  translation process. They are only converted into HTML table elements in visual output.

## D. Text Translation

The Chinese national standard of Mandarin Braille defines the conversion rules for Chinese Braille. Chinese Braille is a phonemic alpha representation. The conversion process can be divided into two steps: from Braille to Pinyin and from Pinyin to  Chinese  characters.  We  use  a  nondeterministic  finite automaton (NFA) to accomplish the transcription of Braille sequences  to  intermediate  states.  In  practice,  we  found  a serious one-to-many confusion problem in conversion process. Braille  has  only  64  different  dots  in  total,  which  cannot represent numbers and symbols in mathematical formulas one by  one.  Same  Braille  square  has  different  meanings  in different  cases.  We  add  a  backtracking  mechanism  to  the automaton when state  transition  is  uncertain.  When  system fails to determine what Braille represents, one choice, such as the  letter "a", is  tried  first.  If  the  conversion  fails,  the backtracking mechanism is activated.

We design  end-to-end  encoders  and  decoders  based  on Transformer [11, 3] to transcribe pinyin into Chinese characters according to Chinese Braille rules. Model directly segments  and  translates  consecutive  pinyin  sequences  into Chinese character sequences.

In addition, many abbreviation rules have been designed in the Braille standard in order to simplify Braille writing. We try to recover omitted symbols during the automatic machine transcription. For omitted symbols that are difficult to recover, further attempts are made to recover them in model's encoders and decoders.

## E. Math Formula Translation

Chinese mathematical Braille is a one-dimensional formula. Besides defining the braille for numbers  and mathematical  symbols,  some  auxiliary  braille  parties  are defined in the rules to represent the structural information of the formula. We still use NFA to convert it from Braille to a one-dimensional form. It is the same as the Chinese. Then we designed a set of symbol generation rules based on the LaTeX structured algorithm to transcribe one-dimensional mathematical formulas into LaTeX formulas directly according to the rules of Chinese mathematical Braille and the rules of LaTeX formula.

## F. System Implement

We have developed a visualization system to implement our approach. The system takes an image as input and detects Braille  dots  and  Structure  in  input  Braille  image.  Based  on position information in structure detection result and Braille character detection and recognition result, Braille describing the structure is removed from result. Remaining Braille is fed into the NFA, which attempts to convert the Braille into either pinyin or mathematical formulas. Pinyin sequence generated by the NFA is fed into Transformer-based decoder. Mathematical formulas are transcribed into LaTeX formulas according  to  rules  we  have  designed.  Finally,  Chinese  and LaTeX sequences are output as a result for visualization. In order to make  result of translation easier to read  and understand. We sort translation results by rearranging them according to the order in which Braille characters are written in the input image. We use positional information obtained in Braille detection and recognition to connect translation results to Braille dots.  Each  word  is  then  transcribed  into  an HTML(HyperText  Markup  Language)  element  in  top-tobottom order and rendered by the browser for output.

## IV. EVALUATION

We  used  30  scanned  images  from  Chinese  junior  high school textbooks as our test data, including Chinese, mathematics ， geography and political science subjects. We use  the  Character  Error  Rate  (CER)  metric  to  evaluate  the translation  accuracy  of  the  system,  which  uses  Levenshtein Distance of two sequences to evaluate the similarity of two sequences. The lower CER score indicates better translation performance.

## V. CONCLUSION

We  have  designed and implemented an end-to-end solution  to  translate  images  of  scanned  Braille  documents. Our approach detects Braille text and document structure from the  image  and  reconstructs  outputs  after  translation.  Our approach produces results that are much closer in semantics and structure to the original Braille documents.

We  designed  a  visualization  system  to  implement  the process we proposed. The system receives a scanned image, performs the process of detection and translation, and finally renders translation result through browser and Latex.

Our evaluation shows that our method not only significantly improves the accuracy of translation in images containing  tables  and  mathematics  but  also  improves  the speed  of  reading  Braille  for  the  average  person.  We  are convinced that our method is useful in many areas, especially in the field of education of visually impaired students.

## Enhancing Accessibility: Automated Tactile Graphics Generation for Individuals with Visual Impairments





Citation: Dzhurynskyi, Y.; Mayik, V.; Mayik, L. Enhancing Accessibility: Automated Tactile Graphics Generation for Individuals with Visual Impairments. Computation 2024 , 12 , 251. https://doi.org/10.3390/ computation12120251
