Abstract: This study addresses the accessibility challenges faced by individuals with visual impairments due to limited access to graphic information, which significantly impacts their educational and social integration. Traditional methods for producing tactile graphics are labor-intensive and require specialized expertise, limiting their availability. Recent advancements in generative models, such as GANs, diffusion models, and VAEs, offer potential solutions to automate the creation of tactile images. In this work, we propose a novel generative model conditioned on text prompts, integrating a Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer (BART) and Vector Quantized Variational Auto-Encoder (VQ-VAE). This model transforms textual descriptions into tactile graphics, addressing key requirements for legibility and accessibility. The model's performance was evaluated using cross-entropy, perplexity, mean square error, and CLIP Score metrics, demonstrating its ability to generate high-quality, customizable tactile images. Testing with educational and rehabilitation institutions confirmed the practicality and efficiency of the system, which significantly reduces production time and requires minimal operator expertise. The proposed approach enhances the production of inclusive educational materials, enabling improved access to quality education and fostering greater independence for individuals with visual impairments. Future research will focus on expanding the training dataset and refining the model for complex scenarios.

Keywords: accessibility; visual impairment; tactile graphics; generative model; machine learning; artificial intelligence

## 1. Introduction

The modern advancement of an inclusive society underscores the importance of integrating people with visual impairments into all aspects of social life. The challenges of socializing individuals with such disabilities span several factors that hinder their education and active participation in society. Particularly, people with visual impairments face limited access to information, as a substantial portion of materials is available solely in standard printed or digital formats. This challenge is further compounded by the growing amount of information presented in graphic form, which aims to enhance comprehension for the general audience. These barriers restrict opportunities for people with visual impairments to access quality education and pursue professional growth [1-3]. This issue has become particularly pressing, as shown by data from the Vision Loss Expert Group [4]: In 2020, approximately 295 million people worldwide were affected by vision impairment, and this number is projected to rise to 703 million by 2050.

In addition, an analysis [5] of the activities of publishing and printing industry enterprises specializing in educational and instructional literature (such as textbooks and manuals) for people with visual impairments has identified several challenges related to the creation and adaptation of images and illustrative material, which are especially critical for this type of publication. Key difficulties faced by these enterprises in creating or adapting graphic content include a shortage of qualified specialists with the technical skills necessary for producing tactile graphics, the additional time and financial investment required to train such specialists, and the high labor intensity and costs associated with producing or adapting tactile images. Also, the analysis indicated that production complexity is a major factor contributing to the limited availability of tactile graphics.



## 2. Related Work

Efforts to automate tactile graphics generation have largely focused on transforming visual content into tactile representations. These approaches can be categorized into methods that rely on direct image-to-tactile transformations and those that incorporate semantic processing.

## 2.1. Direct Image-to-Tactile Transformations

Models such as those described by Way, Barner, and others [6-9] utilize edge detection algorithms like the Canny edge detector. These techniques aim to extract contours and boundaries from visual content and render them into tactile formats. While straightforward, these methods suffer from challenges such as spurious edges and omitted critical details, which hinder the comprehensibility of the tactile output. Furthermore, these edge-based methods fail to accommodate the semantic requirements of tactile graphics, often including extraneous elements or insufficient simplifications that impede interpretation by touch, which violates the requirements for tactile graphics [10,11].

## 2.2. Semantic-Based Approaches

Recent advancements in semantic segmentation and object detection have enabled more nuanced methods [12,13]. The Pic2Tac system exemplifies this trend by employing state-of-the-art computer vision techniques such as Mask R-CNN for object detection and PiCANet for saliency detection. Pic2Tac translates salient objects into tactile 'icons' and fills background regions with predefined patterns, thus addressing some of the limitations of edge-detection methods. However, its reliance on preexisting visual content (photographs) restricts its applicability when such content is unavailable. Moreover, the patterns used for backgrounds are predefined and may not adequately represent complex scenes.

Another notable approach by Pakenait˙ e et al. [12,13] combines object detection and salience analysis to create tactile collages. While effective for specific applications, this method often struggles with providing adequate background context, leading to ambiguities in the interpretation of foreground elements.

## 2.3. Advancements in Generative Models

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [14] and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [15] have been explored in image synthesis, but their application in tactile graphics remains nascent. GANs, for instance, excel in generating high-resolution images, but often require extensive training datasets and struggle with generating discrete patterns suited for tactile media. Diffusion models [16] offer promising avenues, but have yet to be tailored for accessibility-focused use cases.

## 2.4. Comparison with Our Approach

The methods described above either focus on transforming existing visual content into tactile formats or utilize limited sets of predefined tactile elements. In contrast, our approach combines the strengths of Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer (BART) [17,18] and Vector Quantized Variational Auto-Encoder (VQ-VAE) [19] to produce tactile graphics that meet accessibility standards while being computationally efficient and scalable. This integration represents a novel application of generative modeling in the domain of tactile accessibility. This innovation not only streamlines the production process but also enhances accessibility, as it enables the creation of tactile graphics solely from descriptive text.

Our method integrates a BART with a VQ-VAE, uniquely partitioning the latent space into independent text and graphic embeddings. This architecture ensures that the generated tactile graphics adhere to the specific requirements of accessibility while allowing for greater variability and customization. By leveraging generative models rather than static transformations, our approach introduces a level of adaptability and semantic richness that previous methods lacked.

## 3. Text-Conditioned Tactile Graphics Generative Model

The transformation of semantic text descriptions into tactile representations builds upon theories of latent space partitioning and generative modeling. Specifically, methods such as BART and VQ-VAE have proven effective for mapping high-dimensional data into interpretable outputs suitable for tactile exploration. The subject of its modeling is the process of converting text information into graphic information. To accomplish this, the embedded space of the transformer, which was formed during language modeling on pretraining task, was divided into two independent embedded spaces-text and graphicsinstead of a shared one.

In this study, the developed model was trained using the parameters presented in Tables 1 and 2 for the VQ-VAE and BART models, respectively. At the same time, the parameters of the BART's text-embedded space remained the same as during language modeling.

Before generating text tokens using the BPE [20] tokenization model, the original text components are normalized to achieve a uniform format, including converting all uppercase letters to lowercase.

This means that the decoder generates one graphics token per iteration, considering the context of the previously generated graphics tokens. where e g i is the i -th element of the vector sequence of the graphic embedded space E g , e g j ; j &lt; i are previously generated vectors of the graphic embedded space; h g is the hidden state of the decoder; dz is the size of the final sequence e g ⊆ E g ; and Decode ( · ) is the transformer's decoding operation, defined within [17].

Decoding occurs in an iterative manner until the sequence e g size is equal to dz (i.e., the size of the latent space vector of the VQ-VAE model). Once the decoding is complete, the resulting sequence of vectors of the graphics-embedded space e g is converted by a linear layer and Softmax function into a sequence of probability distributions from which the element with the highest probability is selected, determining the selected graphics token:



where g is the generated sequence of graphic tokens of size dz and e g i ∈ e g is an element of the vector sequence of the graphics-embedded space E g .

In the next step, on the basis of graphic tokens (6), a sequence of latent quantized vectors is formed, zq , which is defined by the Formula (7). Each graphic token: 1 ≤ gi ≤ K ; i = 1 . . . dz , is the positional number of the quantized vector in the 'codebook' of the VQ-VAE model:



where Z is the set of latent quantized vectors, or 'codebook'; zq ⊆ Z is a sequence of latent quantized vectors; gi ∈ g is a graphics token; and dz is the size of the sequence of latent quantized vectors.

The final step is the generation of tactile graphics using a sequence (7) with a VQVAE decoder:



where zq is the sequence of latent quantized vectors; ImDecode ( · ) is an image-decoding operation based on latent representation defined within [19]; and Y is a generated tactile image.

## 4. Method

4.1. Dataset

Language modeling was conducted using the BrUK corpus [21], a collection of Ukrainian texts sourced from various domains. Unlike textual datasets (i.e., corpora), which are widely accessible, tactile graphics samples are significantly less common. One of the main challenges in modeling tactile graphics generation using machine learning is the limited availability of publicly accessible samples, as the tactile graphics production industry is far less developed compared to traditional publishing.

To address this limitation, a collection of plant and animal images from the APH Tactile Graphics Library [22] was selected as the primary dataset for training the model. Additionally, the dataset was augmented with 41 custom tactile image samples, bringing the total to 179 samples. These custom samples, derived from simple illustrations of animals, were previously used by a Ukrainian institution specializing in preschool education for children with visual impairments. The samples were reviewed by field specialists and have been integrated into a range of books for visually impaired children. Tactile graphics samples are effectively represented as grayscale rasterized images, pre-processed to enhance the model's performance. This was achieved by quantizing their pixel values from the [0, 255] range into a finite set of discrete values (i.e., a 'palette') using the following formula:



where x is the original value of the pixel color in the form of a vector of dimensions from 1 to 4; P is a pre-defined color palette, one of which color values the target pixel acquires; n is the size of the pixel color vector; and ´ x is the quantized value of the color of the original pixel.

## 4.2. Training

Initially, the language-modeling process focused on training the BART encoder to establish the textual embedding space. However, it is important to clarify why we chose not to use an existing pre-trained Transformer model for fine-tuning and instead conducted the modeling independently. The primary reason was the specific requirement to perform modeling for the Ukrainian language, for which no suitable pre-trained models were available from publicly accessible sources. Consequently, this step is not mandatory and can be reproduced using any existing Transformer model trained on generation tasks.

The training process leveraged the pre-trained encoder from BART and the 'codebook' and decoder from VQ-VAE, which were excluded from the training graph. Instead, the BART decoder was trained to operate within its own graphics embedding space, while the VQ-VAE encoder was not utilized at this stage.

Given the limited number of samples in the tactile graphics dataset, the training process was conducted over 35,000 iterations. The hyperparameters utilized during training are summarized in Table 3.

To address potential annotation ambiguities, such as between 'a stretching cat' and 'a cat', we designed an evaluation framework that prioritizes semantic understanding using the CLIP Score metric, which accounts for partial matches. Additionally, the dataset was revised to include multi-label annotations, allowing for broader descriptions (e.g., both 'a stretching cat' and 'a cat'). This was complemented by data augmentation with varied textual descriptions to improve model generalization. Finally, a qualitative human evaluation phase ensured that semantically valid predictions were not unfairly penalized, enhancing the robustness and flexibility of the model in real-world scenarios.

## 4.3. Evaluation Method

The model's performance was evaluated separately for each of its components: BART and VQ-VAE. The Cross-Entropy (10) metric was used to assess how effectively the model converted text prompts into corresponding graphic tokens, while Perplexity (11) measured the level of uncertainty in the model's predictions.





where Q is a corpus distribution and P is an empirical distribution.

The model's evaluation, which assessed its ability to reconstruct the original image and synthesize new ones, was performed by calculating the Mean Square Error (MSE) in both the image space and the low-dimensional latent space, as well as the Fr é chet Inception Distance.

## 5. Results

## 5.1. Experiment

This section presents the results of the experiment through examples of tactile images generated by the developed model. The generation process was performed using the 'greedy search' method, which identifies the shortest path in a directed graph representation of the generation process to synthesize the corresponding image. These examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the variable synthesis capability of the complex tactile graphics generation model, showcasing its ability to produce tactile images based on text prompts of varying descriptions. This text-prompt-based generation approach significantly enhanced the controllability of the process, making it both convenient and accessible, even for individuals without expertise in tactile graphics production.

The results of the experiment include samples of generated tactile graphics images based on various types of text prompts, such as monosyllabic prompts, prompts with numerals, and prompts with epithets. These samples are presented in Figure 2.

5.4. Quantitative Metrics The evaluation results are shown in Table 5. The CLIP score value, according to Formula (14), for the obtained model was equal to 23.7. At first glance, the result may seem bad; however, an explanation was found for this. The CLIP model used to calculate the CLIP  Score  was  trained  on  a  diverse  range  of  image  samples,  including  realistic  and graphically complex images, as it was designed for general-purpose applications. HowThe evaluation results are shown in Table 5. The CLIP score value, according to Formula (14), for the obtained model was equal to 23.7. At first glance, the result may seem bad; however, an explanation was found for this. The CLIP model used to calculate the CLIP Score was trained on a diverse range of image samples, including realistic and graphically complex images, as it was designed for general-purpose applications. However, it has been found that the CLIP model-at least in its publicly available versions-is not well-suited for calculating CLIP scores on simple, graphic images such as tactile graphics.

## 6. Discussion

The current training dataset consists of relatively simple images, such as animals, plants, and basic objects. However, one limitation of the model lies in its potential difficulty in scaling to more complex images, such as those with intricate details (e.g., architectural blueprints or detailed scientific diagrams). The model's ability to capture fine-grained details is constrained by the size of its latent space and the number of hidden layers in the VQ-VAE architecture. Generating complex tactile graphics may require a more detailed representation, which could introduce inefficiencies or inaccuracies without modifications to the model architecture.

Furthermore, while the model performs well with simpler prompts (e.g., 'a cat' or 'a tree'), it faces challenges when handling more complex and nuanced prompts (e.g., 'a group of children playing soccer with a spotted ball'). As the semantic complexity and length of the prompt increase, the transformer's encoding of textual information becomes more demanding. This can result in difficulties disentangling and representing all elements of a complex scene in tactile graphics form, potentially leading to information loss or oversimplification.

In terms of computational requirements, training the proposed model-which combines the BART Transformer and the VQ-VAE-requires substantial resources. The autoregressive nature of the model and the dual processing of textual and graphical latent spaces make training computationally expensive. This process demands powerful GPUs or TPUs, significant memory capacity, and extended training times, particularly as the dataset size increases. Scaling the model to handle larger datasets or higher-dimensional image outputs poses additional challenges without access to advanced computing infrastructure.

The hyperparameters listed in Table 3 were chosen based on a combination of empirical tuning and best practices from prior studies in related fields. The batch size, in particular, was set to 2 due to the high dimensionality of the inputs and the computational constraints of the hardware used during training. While larger batch sizes are often preferred for their ability to improve gradient estimation stability, our experiments showed that the chosen configuration achieved acceptable performance without overloading available resources.

We acknowledge the potential of more advanced hyperparameter optimization techniques, such as Bayesian optimization, to explore and identify more effective configurations. These methods could enable the model to converge faster or achieve improved performance by systematically searching a broader parameter space. While the current study focused on manual tuning to balance resources and performance, integrating automated optimization tools in future work represents a promising direction for further improving the model's effectiveness.

Nevertheless, while the training process of the proposed model is computationally intensive and time-consuming, due to the high dimensionality of the inputs and the complexity of the machine learning process, the inference phase remains efficient. This is achieved through the compact latent space of the VQ-VAE (8 × 8 dimension), which minimizes the computational load during decoding. Additionally, the autoregressive BART decoder generates graphical tokens iteratively, but the manageable size of the latent space (64 elements) ensures that the process remains lightweight and fast. The model's focus on producing simplified and clear tactile graphics, rather than photorealistic images, further optimizes inference time, making it practical for real-world applications on resourceconstrained devices.

Ethical considerations are paramount in the development of tactile graphics to ensure that the generated images accurately represent the intended information. For visually impaired users, tactile graphics serve as a primary means of interpreting visual content. Any distortion or inaccuracy in the generated graphics could lead to misunderstandings. For instance, oversimplification or omission of critical details in a tactile graphic could provide an incomplete or misleading representation. To address this concern, it is essential to rigorously validate model outputs against established standards for tactile graphics.

Additionally, soliciting feedback from visually impaired users is crucial to ensure that the tactile representations are both accurate and comprehensible.

Currently, effective methods for assessing the quality of tactile graphics include expert evaluations, focus groups, and user testing. However, we believe it is crucial to explore the development of an automated tool for assessing the quality of tactile graphics. Such a tool could, for instance, function as a discriminator within a GAN architecture, providing an objective and scalable approach to evaluation. The development of such a tool is a challenging task, as it must address both the technical specifications and the quality standards, which imply that tactile graphics should be compatible with the following properties:

- Legible: The convexity of forms, protrusions of points, signs, lines, and textures defining highlighted surfaces must be easily recognizable by touch;
- Understood: The reader must clearly grasp the idea conveyed by the author through the illustration;
- Substantial: The illustration must correspond to and enhance the text it accompanies;
- Attractive: The illustration should feel pleasant to the touch and evoke interest. Such images encourage visually impaired readers to engage with them, even if it requires effort;
- Continuous: The reader should seamlessly follow the graphic element without losing their place or searching for the next tactile component;
- Useful: Illustrations must convey meaningful information to the user. Decorative elements that merely enhance aesthetic value should be avoided, as they can interfere with readability.

## 7. Conclusions

Our proposed method introduces a novel approach to generating tactile graphics directly from textual descriptions, leveraging a Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer (BART) and a Vector Quantized Variational Auto-Encoder (VQ-VAE). By redefining the latent space architecture to separate textual and graphical embeddings, the model ensures precise semantic mapping from text to tactile graphics. This innovation eliminates the reliance on visual input, distinguishing our work from existing methods like Pic2Tac, which depend on photographs or predefined tactile libraries.

Additionally, our adaptation of VQ-VAE optimizes the generated outputs for tactile accessibility by prioritizing legibility and simplicity over photorealistic detail. The end-toend text-to-tactile pipeline significantly reduces production time and expands accessibility use cases, enabling the automated generation of educational materials for visually impaired users. These contributions establish our approach as a transformative solution in tactile graphics generation, addressing key limitations of prior methods while demonstrating real-world applicability.

This technology has the potential to bridge the accessibility gap in educational materials, enabling visually impaired individuals to better engage with subjects that rely heavily on visual content, such as science, mathematics, and geography. By providing automated tactile graphics, the technology promotes greater independence in learning and supports participation in inclusive classrooms and professional settings.

Akey direction for future research involves expanding the size and diversity of the training dataset. This will enhance the model's generalization capabilities and ensure its stable performance across a broader range of scenarios.

Abstract -This  paper  explores  the  challenges  faced by visually impaired students in educational settings. The research  introduces  a  smart  glass  system  based  on  YOLOv8 and Internet of Things technology, leveraging advancements in computer vision and machine learning. This system offers realtime object detection and comprehensive voice feedback, facilitating  independent  learning  in  subjects  such  as  science, math, and financial transactions. The effectiveness of YOLOv8 has been proven through extensive training and analysis using a  comprehensive  dataset.  By  integrating  text-to-speech  and speech-to-text technologies, the smart glass system is reshaping inclusive  education  and  underscores  the  importance  of  equal learning opportunities for visually impaired individuals worldwide,  promoting  independence,  removing  educational barriers,  and  fostering  interest  in  STEM  subjects  among visually impaired students.

Keywords-visually impaired students, artificial intelligence, machine learning, YOLO, IoT, education, object detection

## I. INTRODUCTION

People use their eyes for nearly every activity and study. However, some individuals are unfortunately deprived of this ability.  The World Health Organization estimates that there are currently 284 million visually impaired people worldwide,  including  39  million  who  are  blind  [1].  In  Sri Lanka, about 1.7% of the population is blind, approximately 364,000 people [2]. A survey revealed that among the study population,  1.6%  had  severe  visual  impairment  and  15.4% had some form of visual impairment [3]. The Ceylon School for  the  Deaf  and  Blind,  established  in  1912,  marked  the beginning of education for the blind in Sri Lanka [2]. Despite an overall literacy rate of 92.5%, Sri Lanka, as a developing country, faces challenges with Braille literacy. According to the Ministry of Social Welfare, 71% of people who are blind or visually impaired have attended school at some level, yet only  6% have advanced beyond the G.C.E. Ordinary Level [4]. Therefore, it is crucial to enhance the educational system for visually impaired students by making it more accessible and engaging, thus increasing their interest in learning.

The  research  problem  addressed  in  this  context  is  the development of assistive technologies to enhance the education of visually impaired students. These students face challenges in science, math education, and object recognition. The aim is to leverage advancements in computer vision, machine learning, and accessibility R. A. K. M. Ranasinghe Department of Software Engineering Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Malabe, Sri Lanka kushanmigara@gmail.com

D. K. S. Savishka

Department of Software Engineering Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

Malabe, Sri Lanka

supunsavishka2017@gmail.com

technologies  to  create  innovative  solutions  that  improve accessibility  for  blind  individuals.  Currently,  the  favourite learning  tools  among  visually  impaired  students  include embossed images, real objects, and braille books. Traditional methods, which are time-consuming and often fail to engage students, result in low interest in learning. However, the time required  to  get  acquainted  with  new  technology  can  be reduced, potentially increasing learning interest among visually impaired students. It is generally more difficult for visually  impaired  students  to  learn  than  for  their  sighted peers.  According  to  teachers  at  schools  for  the  deaf  and blind,  learning  science  and  mathematics  poses  additional challenges. Enhancing  memory  retention  and sustaining attention  among  visually  impaired  students  can  be  more effectively  achieved  through  engaging  activities  rather  than traditional  methods.  These  activities  not  only  strengthen memory  but  also  maintain  focus  throughout  the  learning process. However, it is vital to acknowledge potential risks, particularly concerning the tactile learning of geometric and scientific objects, which may pose injury hazards. Additionally,  the  discomfort that  visually  impaired  students experience  when  using  money  highlights  the  necessity  for early financial literacy training. Such programs equip students  with  essential  skills  and  confidence,  facilitating smoother financial transactions.

Recognizing the significance of technology in education, a  smart  educational  app  paired  with  an  Internet  of  Things (IoT) device proves invaluable for supporting the learning of visually impaired students. Object detection, combined with a user-friendly mobile application, offers an effective solution  for  enhancing  learning  activities  and  outcomes  for these students.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Research into learning systems for the blind has captivated  scholars  for  decades.  According  to  a  meaningful study,  the  ancient  Egyptians  were  pioneers  in  addressing issues concerning visually impaired learners [1].  Every advancement in this field owes its existence to the meticulous research conducted by experts. Research continues,  with  new  technologies  being  integrated  into  this domain each day. Lowenfeld emphasized the importance of educating blind children to help them understand the world, gain  confidence,  and  feel  acknowledged  and  embraced  as unique individuals [2].

Significant strides in assistive technology have profoundly  impacted  our  scientific  understanding  of  object detection for blind students. Initially, efforts  to  convey information  about  objects  primarily  focused  on  touch  and auditory modalities. Tactile aids such as raised-line drawings and tactile graphics were developed to help visually impaired individuals  understand  shapes  and  diagrams.  Over  time, these  aids  evolved  to  include  3D  models  and  embossed pictures,  offering  a  more  tangible  representation  of  objects [3].

Although  71%  of  blind  children  are  schooled,  only  6% progress  beyond  the  G.C.E.  Ordinary  Level  [4].  Scoring  in subjects  like  science  and  math  is  particularly  challenging, with  only  29%  and  43%  respectively  [5].  Enhancing  the desire  to  learn  mathematics  in  blind  students  presents  a formidable  challenge.  Blind  students  typically  recognize money by touch and use a special braille system. They tend to  learn  better  through  hands-on  activities  rather  than  notetaking.

Historically, object detection for the blind relied on basic image processing techniques and rule-based algorithms. However, the integration of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has significantly improved the accuracy and efficiency of these systems. CNNs excel in image detection by autonomously learning features from raw data [1]. Additionally, the advent of You Only Look Once (YOLO), a real-time  object  detection  system,  has  further  enhanced  the effectiveness of CNNs in object recognition for the visually impaired.  Renowned  for  its  speed  and  precision,  YOLO  is particularly well-suited for real-time applications that require rapid and accurate object recognition.

One of the key gaps highlighted is the lack of infrastructure  and financial resources in schools,  which hampers the proper implementation of technology. This issue is compounded by inadequate training for teachers and staff, limiting effective technology integration into the curriculum and  ultimately  restricting  blind  students'  access  to  essential information and knowledge [4]. Despite technological advances, findings often lack generalizability, contain methodological  flaws,  and  exhibit  biases,  which  challenge their  credibility  [5].  Addressing  these  challenges  requires more comprehensive research, as well as increased collaboration among researchers, educators, and technology developers to bridge these gaps and ensure equitable access to science education for blind students.

Interactive  math  study  systems  for  blind  students  are innovative, yet many systems are limited to currency recognition, which  restricts educational access. The  Sri Lankan Currency Recognition Device for Visually Impaired People demonstrates progress in the field of currency identification. However, it lacks real-time feedback systems, mobile applications, and interaction with IoT devices, which diminishes  its  effectiveness  in  creating  a  welcoming  and stimulating  learning  environment  [6].  Singh's  investigation into  mobile  phone  money  recognition  introduced  a  mobile application  for  blind  users  [2].  While  this  is  a  positive development, the study focused solely on currency identification and overlooked other crucial aspects of mathematics  instruction.  Without  mechanisms  for  real-time feedback, visually impaired students may face greater challenges in their studies [7].

A  comprehensive  study  introduced  a  system  capable  of recognizing  Euro  banknotes  and  providing  vocal  feedback, significantly  enhancing  the  ability  of  blind  individuals  to identify  currency.  Nevertheless,  this  study  did  not  leverage an IoT-based device and could not identify multiple banknotes simultaneously. Its potential impact on mathematics  education  was  limited  due  to  the  absence  of robust integration with real-world arithmetic problems [8].

Despite improvements in assistive technology for students  with  visual  impairments,  many  challenges  remain. Traditional  tactile  aids,  while  helpful,  may  cover  only  a limited  scope.  For  instance,  raised-line  drawings  can  be challenging to create and interpret, and physical models may not faithfully represent complex geometric designs.

Moreover,  existing  digital  solutions  often  fall  short  in providing  comprehensive  access  to  mathematical  content. Screen  readers  and  text-to-speech  software  might  struggle with accurately comprehending mathematical notation, which  is  essential  for  accessing  digital  text.  This  limitation can  make  it  more  difficult  for  students  who  are  visually challenged to interact with mathematical concepts, potentially leading to frustration and disengagement.

One  of  the  most  significant  challenges  faced  by  blind students is the time-consuming nature of the learning process.  In  the  absence  of  readily  available  educational resources  and  effective  teaching  strategies,  students  with visual  impairments  often  require  more  time  to  fully  grasp mathematical content. This discrepancy in learning time can hinder  academic  development  and  contribute  to  feelings  of isolation.

## III. METHODOLOGY

## A. Theoretical Framework

This  section  provides  a  comprehensive  overview  of  the theories  that  have  been  employed  throughout  this  research and highlights the significance and relevance of each theory.

In the realm of object identification models, three algorithms  stand  out:  Mask  R-CNN,  YOLO, and  Faster  RCNN. Each model has distinct features and suits a range of applications,  depending  on  its  benefits  and  weaknesses. YOLO, known for its real-time object detection capabilities, divides the input image into a grid of cells and predicts the bounding boxes and class probabilities for each cell simultaneously.  Although  YOLO  sacrifices  some  accuracy for  speed,  it  remains  the  preferred  choice  for  applications requiring fast processing. In contrast, Faster R-CNN achieves a balance between speed and accuracy by employing a twostage detection technique. It first generates region proposals using a Region Proposal Network (RPN), then refines these proposals with a Fast R-CNN network. This method excels when accuracy is more critical than real-time speed in object detection scenarios. Mask R-CNN extends the capabilities of Faster  R-CNN  by  adding  a  segmentation  mask  prediction branch, offering pixel-level precision. It performs exceptionally well in tasks requiring precise instance segmentation, despite its substantial computational demand, making it suitable  for  applications  that  demand an in-depth understanding of object boundaries.

As shown in Fig. 1, the YOLO algorithm processes the input  image  to  generate  a  grid  of  cells.  Within  each  cell, YOLO  simultaneously  predicts  bounding  boxes  and  class probabilities. Each bounding box includes class probabilities for  various  item  categories  and  a  confidence  score,  which indicates  the  likelihood  of  an  object  being  present  in  the predicted box. This  prediction  process utilizes a single convolutional neural network (CNN), which has been trained end-to-end  to  optimize  both  localization  and  classification tasks. During inference, the YOLO model predicts bounding boxes  and  class  probabilities for each  grid cell.  These predictions are then refined through post-processing techniques such as non-maximum suppression (NMS). NMS enhances detection accuracy by eliminating redundant bounding boxes, selecting the one with the highest confidence score among those that overlap.

Fig. 1. YOLO Architecture



When  it  comes  to  development  environments,  Google Colab and Jupyter Notebook each offer distinct advantages. Google  Colab  is  a  cloud-based  platform  that  provides  free access to GPU and TPU resources, thus eliminating the need for  powerful  local  hardware  and  enabling  advanced  deep learning  research.  Its  collaboration  features  allow  multiple users to work simultaneously on the same notebook, and its integration  with  Google  Drive  simplifies  access  to  datasets stored in the cloud. On the other hand, Jupyter Notebook is an  open-source  web  application  that  allows  users  to  create and share documents containing live code, equations, visualizations,  and  narrative  text.  It  can  run  locally  on  a user's computer, providing offline access and greater control over computing resources, making it the preferred choice for users who value customization and flexibility.

The  functions  and  applications  of  Raspberry  Pi  and Arduino  boards  are  distinctly  different.  The  Raspberry  Pi functions  as  a  single-board  computer  and  is  ideal  for  a variety of applications requiring substantial computing power, such as media centers and IoT applications. It boasts a robust processor, ample RAM, and a variety of networking options. In contrast,  the  Arduino's  microcontroller-based design, which offers simplicity and real-time control, makes it  excellent  for  embedded  systems  and  electronics  projects involving  sensors,  actuaries,  and  automation.  Although  the Raspberry  Pi  presents  a  steeper  learning  curve  than  the Arduino due to its more complex architecture and operating system  requirements,  it  also  offers  greater  flexibility  and  a broader range of capabilities, albeit at a higher cost.

As illustrated in Fig. 2, a mobile application was developed  using  Flutter  for  the  client-side  interface,  while the server-side logic was implemented using Python. WebSocket  technology  was  utilized  to  enable  real-time, bidirectional,  full-duplex  communication over a single TCP connection between the Flutter client and the Python server.

Flutter  enabled cross-platform  mobile  app development, ensuring  compatibility  and  a  consistent  user  experience  on both  iOS  and  Android  devices  with  a  single  codebase.  Its extensive widget library, expressive UI components, and hot reload feature expedited development and facilitated rapid UI prototyping. Python was chosen for the server-side due to its versatility,  robustness,  and  comprehensive  library  support. WebSocket  communication  was efficiently implemented using Python's asyncio package, which allows the server to manage multiple client connections concurrently while maintaining responsiveness.

## B. Proposed system

Fig. 2. System diagram



In this system, all functions utilized the YOLO algorithm, implemented using the OpenCV library in Python. OpenCV provides robust computer vision capabilities, enabling efficient object detection tasks. NumPy was also utilized for mathematical  calculations  and  array  manipulation,  which simplified  the  pre-processing  and  post-processing  stages  of the object recognition pipeline. The geometric shape detection capabilities were seamlessly integrated with accessibility features to support visually challenged students. The system uses the Flutter Text-to-Speech (TTS) library to provide audio feedback, enabling blind users to hear descriptions  of  recognized  geometric  shapes  in  real-time. Moreover,  for  every  detected  shape,  dynamically  produced descriptive text  is  generated  by  OpenAI  GPT-3.5.  The science equipment identification function incorporates several significant technologies to enhance accessibility and provide visually impaired students with an extensive educational  experience.  This  feature  uses  the  Flutter  TTS toolkit  to  produce  audio  outputs,  allowing  blind  students  to receive real-time audio descriptions of equipment in science labs.

Furthermore,  arbitrary  descriptions  for  these  items  have been generated using OpenAI GPT-3.5, enriching the educational content with dynamic and contextually relevant information. Additionally, blind students can guess the equipment  name  by  speaking  into  the  system,  with  the Flutter  Speech-to-Text  library  capturing  their  guesses.  Gen AI  is  utilized  to  create  random  questions  for  the  currency detection  feature,  while  Flutter  TTS  and  Speech-to-Text facilitate audio outputs and user interaction. Thanks to Gen AI's  advanced  natural  language  generation  capabilities,  a wide  range  of  contextually  relevant  questions  regarding money  and  transactions  for  visually  impaired  students  can now be constructed in real time. This system uses Gen AI to provide visually impaired users with engaging and instructional content, enhancing their educational experiences, engagement, and understanding. As depicted in Fig. 3, instance segmentation is utilized to accurately capture the  responses  of  blind  students  using  currency  notes  and coins,  ensuring  precise  interpretation  and  interaction  within the educational context.

Fig. 3. Instance Segmentation



## 1) User Interaction Flow:

The  user  interaction  flow  of  the  system  encompasses three key functionalities: Geometric Shape Detection Model (GSDM),  Scientific  Equipment  Detection  Model  (SEDM), and Currency Recognition Model (CRM), each designed to cater  to  the  unique  educational  needs  of  blind  and  visually impaired students.

Students  can  quickly  navigate  between  these  elements from the main menu upon launching the mobile application. In the Geometric Shape Detection, students select geometric objects to examine and capture images with cameraequipped smart glasses. The system uses the YOLO object detection  paradigm  for  real-time  detections  and  provides auditory  feedback  including  the  name,  characteristics,  and relevant  mathematical  equations  for  calculating  parameters such as area, perimeter, and volume. This interactive approach promotes independent learning and comprehension of geometric concepts.

Similarly, students can access the Laboratory Equipment Learning  from  the  application's  home  page.  Once  there, users can guess the name of the object by interacting with its interfaces and engaging with science laboratory equipment. Upon  accurately  guessing  an  object's  name,  the  system emits an alert stating, "You are correct." If the guessed name is  incorrect,  the  system  provides  audio  feedback,  "You  are wrong," followed by the correct  name  and  a  random description of the particular object.

The CRM  enables students to solve mathematical exchange problems from real-world scenarios. They calculate  answers  and  visually  demonstrate  their  responses using physical currency. Employing YOLO object detection, the system verifies the accuracy of calculations and provides real-time audio feedback. If the displayed answer is correct, the  system  displays  "Your  answer  is  correct";  if  not,  it specifies what the mistake is.

## 2) Types of Data Used and Data Collection Methods:

Images  of  geometric  forms  commonly  used  to  teach mathematics  to  blind  or  visually  impaired  students  are included  in  the  dataset  used  for  this  study.  These  images were captured at the Ratmalana Blind School, specifically in classrooms housing fifth and sixth-grade students. To ensure the  completeness  of  the  dataset,  photographs  of  various geometric forms, tactile aids, educational materials, science laboratory  equipment,  and  coins  and  currency  notes  used during instruction were taken.

Data collection efforts involved direct engagement with the classroom environment, enabling the capture of real and representative resources used in science and math classes for students  with  vision  impairments.  Additionally,  photos  of coins and currency notes were gathered from daily transactions  and  trips  to  nearby  banks,  ensuring  a  wide variety of denominations and variants commonly encountered in everyday life.

High-quality digital cameras were used to capture images of the objects, ensuring the images were suitable for subsequent  analysis  and  annotation.  The  primary  objective of this data collection approach was to obtain accurate and comprehensive  representations  of  the  geometric  shapes, scientific lab equipment, and currency used in instructional methods as well as those encountered in real-world scenarios.

Subsequently, each image in the collection was meticulously  annotated  using  LabelImg  software.  During the  annotation  process,  coin  borders  and  characteristics, banknotes, laboratory objects, and geometric shapes were all marked.

## 3) Tools and procedures for Dataset Creation:

To  enhance  the  quality  and  diversity  of  the  dataset, several  preprocessing  and  augmentation  techniques  were applied  after  data  collection.  The  labelImg  tool  facilitated the annotation process by accurately classifying the geometric  shapes  visible  in  the  images.  This  meticulous annotation enabled the precise identification and naming of every geometric item in the dataset.

After  annotation,  the  dataset  underwent  preprocessing using  Roboflow,  a  powerful  platform  designed  for  data preprocessing and optimization. Roboflow standardized and optimized  the  dataset  through  various  methods,  including scaling,  grayscale  conversion,  object  isolation,  and  static cropping. These preprocessing techniques were essential for improving  image  resolution,  standardizing  image  formats, and isolating geometric shapes for further analysis.

To increase the robustness and diversity of the dataset, augmentation techniques were also employed. These techniques, including flipping, rotating, blurring, and adding random noise,  were  used  to  simulate  variations  commonly observed in real-world scenarios, thus enhancing the model's generalization and performance.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

After  evaluating  different  versions  of  YOLO,  YOLOv8 was  selected  for  its  superior  accuracy  and  faster  training capabilities. Subsequently, YOLOv8 was used to train three object  detection  models:  the  CRM,  Laboratory  Equipment Detection Model  (LEDM),  and  Math  Object  Detection Model  (MODM).  This  approach provided a consistent architectural foundation across all models, facilitating efficient training and optimizing performance in their respective object detection tasks.

To  enhance  the  models'  generalization  capabilities  and improve object recognition under various lighting conditions and orientations, data augmentation techniques were implemented. These techniques included horizontal and vertical  flipping  of  images,  random  rotations,  and  color jittering, which adjusted brightness, contrast, and saturation. Roboflow, a user-friendly data manipulation library, facilitated the efficient implementation of these augmentations on the dataset. A crucial step in  the  training process  involved  splitting  the  dataset  into  distinct  sets  for training, testing, and validation. A 70/20/10 split was adopted, allocating 70% of the data for model training, 20% for  testing,  and  the  remaining  10%  for  validation.  This distribution  helped  monitor  the  model's  learning  progress and mitigated the risk of overfitting.

The training was conducted on the cloud-based platform Google Colab, which provided a convenient and accessible workspace.  The  availability  of  Tensor  Processing  Units (TPUs)  in  Colab  significantly  reduced  training  time  and expedited  results.  TPUs  are  specifically  designed  for  deep learning tasks.

To achieve an optimal balance between training efficiency  and  model  performance,  the  impact  of  three  key hyperparameters-batch size, image  size, and epochs-was investigated.  'Batch  size'  refers  to  the  number  of  images processed together during each training iteration, 'image size' determines the resolution of the images fed into the model, and 'epochs' represent the number of times the entire training dataset is passed through the model. Image sizes ranged from 480x480  to  1280x720.  Lower  resolutions  (e.g.,  170x170) might  limit  the  model's  ability  to  extract  crucial  features, while very high resolutions (e.g., 1280x720) could increase computational demands. Various batch sizes were explored, including 1, 8, 16, and 32, and different numbers of epochs, ranging from 10 to 50, were tested. Through this exploration, a  configuration  of  a  batch  size  of  16,  an  image  size  of 640x480, and 30 epochs was identified as delivering the best trade-off between training speed, model accuracy, and convergence. This configuration effectively leveraged computational resources while ensuring robust features were learned  for  accurate  object  detection.  Figures  4,  5,  and  6 visually represent the experimentation process and the optimal configuration.

To  evaluate  the  effectiveness  of  the  object  detection models, confusion matrices were utilized, as shown in Table 1.  These  matrices  provide  a  comprehensive  view  of  the models'  classification  performance,  detailing  the  number  of true positives, true negatives, false positives,  and false negatives  for  each  object  class  the  models  are  trained  to detect.  Fig.  7  and  Fig.  8  present  the  confusion  matrices  for the  CRM,  LEDM,  and  the  GSDM.  By  analyzing  these matrices, valuable insights into the models' ability to correctly  identify  various  objects  within  their  respective domains can be gleaned. This information can guide further optimization  efforts  to  enhance  the  models'  performance  in real-world applications.

## CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This research has developed a smart glass system poised to  revolutionize  the  education  of  blind  people  in  science, mathematics, and currency usage. Blind students are empowered through the use of YOLOv8, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech technologies, facilitating independent learning, accurate object detection, and comprehensive descriptions. Potential improvements could include providing audio feedback in multiple languages, reducing the weight  of  the  IoT  device  to  ensure  comfortable  wear  for blind  students,  and  enabling  standalone  functionality  that does not rely on a mobile application. This would allow the device to independently capture and provide voice commands.  The  findings  are  significant  for  educators  and technologists working on inclusive education and accessibility. This study underscores the necessity of offering equal learning opportunities for all blind individuals, regardless  of  their  visual  ability.  The  impacts  of  this  study extend  beyond  academia,  influencing  the  daily  lives  and future  aspirations  of  blind  people  worldwide.  By  aiming  to promote inclusivity and equity, this research seeks to remove barriers to education and independence for blind students.

## Enhancing STEM Education Accessibility for Blind and Low Vision Students

D. I. De Silva

Department of Information Technology Sri Lanka Institute of Information

Technology Malabe, Sri Lanka dilshan.i@sliit.lk

M. N. N. J. Jayasooriya Department of cSoftware Engineering Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

Abstract -This study focuses on enhancing STEM education accessibility for blind and low vision students through  the  development  of  innovative  assistive  technologies. The  primary  challenge  addressed  is  the  limited  engagement and  effectiveness  of  traditional  teaching  methods  for  visually impaired  students,  particularly  in  science  and  mathematics. Leveraging advancements in computer vision, machine learning,  and  internet  of  things  technologies,  the  proposed solution includes a mobile application integrated with YOLObased object detection and real-time audio feedback. Methods employed  involve capturing and preprocessing images of geometric shapes, educational materials, and currency, followed by rigorous model training using Google Colab. The system's architecture incorporates YOLOv8  for  real-time object  detection,  combined  with  text-to-speech  and  speech-totext technologies to provide comprehensive audio descriptions and interactive feedback. Results demonstrate significant improvements  in  detection  accuracy  and  user  engagement, with  YOLOv8  achieving  high  precision  in  object  recognition tasks. Performance standards were evaluated through confusion matrices, highlighting the model's robustness across various educational scenarios. The developed system effectively enhances independent learning and engagement among visually impaired students, promoting inclusivity and equity in STEM education.

R. A. K. M. Ranasinghe

Department of Software Engineering Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Malabe, Sri Lanka kushanmigara@gmail.com

D. K. S. Savishka

Department of Software Engineering Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

Malabe, Sri Lanka

supunsavishka2017@gmail.com

Enhancing the education system to better serve visually impaired students is crucial to making learning more accessible and engaging, thereby increasing their interest in education.  This  study  addresses  the  problem  of  developing assistive technologies to improve the educational experiences of  visually  impaired  students,  particularly  in  subjects  like science,  mathematics,  and  object  recognition.  Advances  in computer vision, machine learning, and accessibility technologies can be leveraged to create innovative solutions that enhance accessibility for blind individuals.

Keywords -assistive technology, STEM  education, object detection,  visually  impaired,  low  vision,  blind,  YOLOv8,  Google Colab

## I. INTRODUCTION

Eyes  are  essential  for  most  human  activities,  including learning, but some people are unfortunately deprived of this ability. According to the World Health Organization, approximately  284  million  people  worldwide  have  visual impairments, with 39 million of them being completely blind [1].  In  Sri  Lanka,  around  1.7%  of  the  population,  which equates  to  about  364,000  individuals,  are  visually  impaired [2]. A survey highlighted that 1.6% of this group have severe visual impairments, while 15.4% have some degree of visual impairment [3]. The Ceylon School for the Deaf and Blind, established in 1912, marked the commencement of educational efforts for the blind in Sri Lanka [2]. Despite a commendable  literacy rate of 92.5%, the country still struggles with Braille literacy. According to the Ministry of Social Welfare, 71% of blind or visually impaired individuals have attended school to some extent, yet only 6% have progressed beyond the General Certificate of Education (G.C.E.) Ordinary Level [4].

Currently,  visually  impaired  students  rely  on  tools  such as embossed images, real objects, and Braille books. Traditional  teaching  methods  can  be  time-consuming  and often fail to capture students' interest, leading to low engagement  levels.  Adapting  to  new  technologies  can  be challenging,  but  doing  so  can  potentially  boost  students' interest in learning. Compared to their sighted peers, visually impaired students often find learning more difficult. Teachers from schools for the deaf and blind have noted that subjects like science and mathematics pose additional challenges.  Enhancing  memory  retention  and  maintaining focus  can  be  more  effectively  achieved  through  engaging activities rather than traditional methods. However,  it's important to acknowledge the potential risks associated with tactile  learning  of  geometric  and  scientific  objects,  which may  cause  injury. Additionally, the discomfort  visually impaired students experience with money handling underscores  the  need  for  early  financial  literacy  education. Such programs can provide essential  skills  and  confidence, facilitating smoother financial transactions.

Recognizing the role of technology in education, a smart educational application combined with an Internet of Things (IoT) device proves to be a valuable tool for supporting the learning needs of visually impaired students. Object detection,  paired  with  a  user-friendly  mobile  application, offers an effective solution to enhance learning activities and outcomes  for  these  students.  Furthermore,  as  technology continues to advance, its role in education will only grow. It is  imperative that the younger generation not only learns to consume this technology but also understands and controls it, ensuring  they  are  not  left  behind  in  an  increasingly  digital world [5].

Section 2 details the background  and  the literature review,  highlighting  the  current  state  and  limitations  of educational aids for visually impaired students. In Section 3, the  methodologies  employed  to  integrate  and  test  these technologies are discussed, providing insights into the approaches used for system development and implementation. Section 4 presents the results,  followed by Section 5, where a thorough discussion interprets the implications  of  these  findings.  Finally,  the  'Conclusion  and Future Work' section reflects on the impact of these technologies on educational accessibility and outlines potential directions for further research to continue advancing this critical field.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Research  on  educational  systems  for  blind  and  visually impaired students has been a focus of scholarly interest for many years. Historically, the ancient Egyptians were among the first to address the educational needs of visually impaired learners  [1].  The  development  of  assistive  technologies  has significantly advanced the understanding of object detection for blind students. Early efforts relied on tactile and auditory modalities, such as raised-line drawings and tactile graphics, to help visually impaired individuals understand shapes and diagrams.  Over  time,  these  aids  evolved  to  include  3D models and embossed pictures, offering more tangible representations of objects [3], [13].

Despite advancements, only 6% of blind students progress beyond the General Certificate of Education (G.C.E.)  Ordinary  Level,  with  science  and  mathematics posing significant challenges. These students often excel in hands-on activities over traditional note-taking.[12].

The integration of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has improved the accuracy and efficiency of object detection  systems  for  the  visually  impaired.  The  advent  of the You Only Look Once (YOLO) real-time object detection system  has  further  enhanced  these  capabilities,  providing rapid and precise object recognition that is particularly suited for real-time applications.

Recent studies highlight the challenges of implementing artificial intelligence (AI) in education, particularly for multilingual  students,  and  emphasize  the  need for  balanced AI-teacher  evaluation  systems  [7].  Additionally,  systemic barriers faced by first-generation university students point to the necessity of supportive infrastructures to develop inclusive educational tools [8].

One major issue is the lack of infrastructure and financial resources in schools, which hinders the effective implementation of technology. This problem is compounded by  inadequate  training  for  teachers  and  staff,  limiting  the integration of technology into the curriculum and restricting visually  impaired  students'  access  to  essential  information [4].  Furthermore,  many  findings  in  assistive  technology research lack generalizability, contain methodological flaws, and exhibit biases, which challenge their credibility.

Interactive  math  study  systems  for  blind  students  are innovative but often limited  to  currency  recognition, which restricts  educational  access.  For  example,  the  Sri  Lankan Currency Recognition Device for Visually Impaired People [6] shows progress in currency identification but lacks realtime feedback systems, mobile applications, and interaction with  IoT  devices,  diminishing  its  effectiveness.  Similarly, mobile phone applications [2], for money recognition provide  some  solutions  but  often  overlook  other  critical aspects of mathematics instruction [9].

Dunai et  al.'s  comprehensive  study  introduced  a  system capable of recognizing Euro banknotes and providing vocal feedback, significantly enhancing the ability of blind individuals to identify currency [10]. However, this study did not  leverage  an  IoT-based  device  and  could  not  identify multiple  banknotes  simultaneously.  Its  potential  impact  on mathematics  education  was  limited  due  to  the  absence  of robust integration with real-world arithmetic problems [12].

Despite  improvements,  traditional  tactile  aids  such  as raised-line drawings and physical models often fail to fully represent complex geometric designs. Digital solutions like screen readers and text-to-speech (TTS) software also struggle with accurately interpreting mathematical notation, making it difficult for visually impaired students to engage with these concepts.

In summary, while significant strides have been made in the field of assistive technology for visually impaired students,  many  challenges  remain.  Continued  research  and collaboration among educators, researchers, and technology developers are essential to ensure equitable access to education for blind students.

## III. METHODOLOGY

## A. Data Collection Methods

Images  of  geometric  forms  commonly  used  to  teach mathematics  to  blind  or  visually  impaired  students  were included  in  the  dataset  for  this  study.  These  images  were captured  at  the  Ratmalana  Blind  School,  specifically  in classrooms housing fifth and sixth-grade students. Additionally, photographs of various geometric forms, tactile aids,  educational  materials,  science  laboratory  equipment, and  coins  and  currency  notes  used  during  instruction  were taken. High-quality digital cameras ensured the images were suitable  for  subsequent  analysis  and  annotation.  Photos  of coins  and  currency  notes  were  also  gathered  from  daily transactions  and  trips  to  nearby  banks,  ensuring  a  wide variety of denominations and variants commonly encountered in everyday life.

## B. Tools and Procedures for Dataset Creation

After data collection, several preprocessing and augmentation techniques were applied to enhance the dataset's quality and diversity. LabelImg software facilitated the meticulous annotation process, accurately classifying the geometric shapes visible in the images. This precise annotation enabled the accurate identification and naming of every geometric item in the dataset. The dataset underwent preprocessing using Roboflow , a powerful platform designed for data preprocessing and optimization. Techniques such as scaling,  grayscale  conversion,  object  isolation,  and  static cropping  were  employed  to  improve  image  resolution  and standardize formats. Augmentation techniques like flipping, rotating,  blurring,  and  adding  random  noise  were  used  to simulate realworld variations, enhancing the model's generalization and performance.

## C. Theoretical Framework

Three prominent object identification models were considered  for  the  development  of  the  proposed  system: Mask R-CNN, YOLO, and Faster R-CNN. Each model has unique features and is suited to different applications based on its strengths and weaknesses. YOLO, known for its real- time  object  detection  capabilities,  divides  the  input  image into  a  grid  of  cells  and  predicts  bounding  boxes  and  class probabilities for each cell simultaneously. Despite sacrificing some accuracy for speed, YOLO is preferred for applications requiring fast processing. Faster R-CNN balances speed and accuracy with  a  two-stage  detection  technique,  excelling  in tasks  where  accuracy  is  more  critical  than  real-time  speed. Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN's capabilities by adding a  segmentation mask prediction branch, offering pixel-level precision, ideal for tasks requiring precise instance segmentation.

## D. Development Environments

Google  Colab  and  Jupyter  Notebook  were  used  for  the development  of  the  proposed  system.  Google  Colab  is  a cloud-based platform providing free access to GPU and TPU resources, eliminating the need for powerful local hardware and enabling advanced deep learning research. Its collaboration features allow multiple users to work simultaneously  on  the  same  notebook,  and  its  integration with Google Drive simplifies dataset access. Jupyter Notebook, an open-source web application, allows users to create and share documents containing live code, equations, visualizations, and narrative text. Running locally, it provides  offline  access  and  greater  control  over  computing resources,  making  it  ideal  for  users  valuing  customization and flexibility.

## E. Hardware and Software Utilized

Raspberry  Pi  and  Arduino  boards  were  employed  for different functions due to their unique capabilities. Raspberry Pi, a single-board computer, is ideal for applications requiring substantial computing power, such as media centers  and  IoT  applications,  with  its  robust  processor  and variety  of  networking  options.  Arduino's  microcontrollerbased  design,  offering  simplicity  and  real-time  control,  is excellent  for  embedded  systems  and  electronics  projects involving  sensors  and  actuators.  Although  Raspberry  Pi presents a steeper learning curve, it offers greater flexibility and a broader range of capabilities at a higher cost.

## F. Implementation

A mobile application was developed using Flutter for the client-side interface, while the server-side logic was implemented  using  Python.  WebSocket  technology  enabled real-time,  bidirectional,  full-duplex  communication  over  a single  TCP  connection  between  the  Flutter  client  and  the Python  server.  Flutter  facilitated  cross-platform  mobile  app development,  ensuring  compatibility  and  a  consistent  user experience  on  both  iOS  and  Android  devices  with  a  single codebase. Python's versatility, robustness, and comprehensive library support made it the preferred choice for the server-side implementation.  WebSocket  communication  was  efficiently implemented  using  Python's asyncio package,  allowing  the server  to  manage  multiple  client  connections  concurrently while maintaining responsiveness.

## G. Proposed System

In the proposed system, all functions utilized the YOLO algorithm implemented using the OpenCV library in Python.

OpenCV provides robust computer vision capabilities, enabling  efficient  object  detection  tasks. NumPy was  also utilized for mathematical calculations and array manipulation, simplifying the pre-processing and postprocessing  stages  of  the  object  recognition  pipeline.  The geometric shape detection capabilities were seamlessly integrated with  accessibility features to support  visually challenged students. The system uses the Flutter TTS library to  provide  audio  feedback,  enabling  blind  users  to  hear descriptions  of  recognized  geometric  shapes  in  real-time. Additionally, dynamically generated descriptive text for detected shapes is produced by OpenAI GPT-3.5.

The  science  equipment  identification  function  enhances accessibility by using Flutter TTS  for real-time audio descriptions  and  OpenAI  GPT-3.5  for  dynamic,  relevant content.  Blind  students  can  guess  equipment  names via  the Flutter Speech-to-Text (STT)  library. Gen  AI  generates random questions for currency detection, with TTS and STT facilitating interaction. This system provides engaging, instructional  content,  enriching  educational experiences and understanding for visually impaired students.

## H. User Interaction Flow

As  depicted  in  Fig.  1,  the  user  interaction  flow  of  the system encompasses three key functionalities: Math Object Detection Model (MODM), Laboratory Equipment Detection Model (LEDM), and Currency Recognition Model  (CRM),  each designed to cater to the unique educational  needs  of  blind  and  visually  impaired  students. Students can quickly navigate between these elements from the main menu upon launching the mobile application.

In MODM, students select geometric objects to examine and  capture  images  with  camera-equipped  smart  glasses. The  system  uses  the  YOLO  object  detection  paradigm  for real-time detections and provides auditory feedback including the name, characteristics, and relevant mathematical  equations  for  calculating  parameters  such  as area, perimeter, and  volume.  This  interactive  approach promotes independent learning and comprehension of geometric concepts.

Similarly, students can access LEDM from the application's  home  page.  Once  there,  users  can  guess  the name  of  the  object  by  interacting  with  its  interfaces  and engaging with science laboratory equipment. Upon accurately  guessing  an  object's  name,  the  system  emits  an alert  stating,  "You  are  correct."  If  the  guessed  name  is incorrect,  the  system  provides  audio  feedback,  "You  are wrong,"  followed  by the correct  name  and  a  random description of the particular object.

The CRM  enables students to solve mathematical exchange problems from real-world scenarios. They calculate  answers  and  visually  demonstrate  their  responses using physical currency. Employing YOLO object detection, the system verifies the accuracy of calculations and provides real-time audio feedback. If the displayed answer is correct, the  system  displays  "Your  answer  is  correct";  if  not,  it specifies what the mistake is.

Fig. 1. User interfaces of the proposed system



## IV. RESULTS

After conducting a comparative analysis of various YOLO iterations,  YOLOv8  emerged  as  the  most  effective due to its heightened precision and enhanced training speed. It  was  therefore  chosen  to  develop  three  specialized  object detection  models:  the  CRM,  LEDM,  and  MODM.  This strategy established a uniform architectural basis that improved  training  efficiency  and  maximized  each  model's performance for its specific detection task.

To bolster the models' adaptabi lity and enhance detection accuracy across different environmental conditions and orientations,  various  data  augmentation  techniques  were applied. Techniques such as image flipping both horizontally and vertically, random image rotations, and color jittering to modify brightness, contrast, and saturation were utilized. The Roboflow platform, known for its intuitive data manipulation capabilities, was instrumental in applying these adjustments to the dataset effectively.

A pivotal element of the training methodology involved segregating  the  dataset  into  three  parts:  70%  for  training, 20%  for  testing,  and  10%  for  validation.  This  separation facilitated  continuous  monitoring  of  the  learning  progress and helped prevent overfitting.

The training sessions were executed on Google Colab, a cloud-based platform that offers an easily accessible environment equipped with Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). TPUs, which are optimized for deep learning tasks, significantly  diminished  the  time  required  for  training  and yielded quicker outcomes.

An examination of critical hyperparameters -batch size, image  size,  and  epochs -was  undertaken  to  find  the  ideal balance  that  would  enhance  training  effectiveness  without compromising  model  performance.  The  batch  size,  which indicates  the  number  of  images  processed  in  one  iteration, along with the image resolution input into the model, and the epochs, or the total number of complete passes through the training dataset, were adjusted. Experimentation with image sizes  ranging  from  480x480  to  1280x720,  and  batch  sizes from 1 to 32 over 10 to 50 epochs, led to the selection of a setup  with a 16  image batch size,  a  resolution of 640x480, and  30  epochs.  This  setup  was  optimal,  efficiently  using computational resources and achieving high levels of feature extraction  for  precise  object  detection.  Fig.  2,  3,  and  4

visually represent the experimentation process and the optimal configuration.

As  shown  in  Table  1,  the  performance  of  the  object detection  models  was  rigorously  evaluated  using  confusion matrices, which detailed the classification accuracy by showing  true  positives,  true  negatives,  false  positives,  and false  negatives  for  each  model.  Fig.  5  and  6  present  the confusion  matrices  for  the  CRM,  LEDM,  and  MODM.  By analyzing these matrices, valuable  insights  into  the  models' ability to correctly identify various  objects  within  their respective  domains  can  be  gleaned.  This  information  can guide  further  optimization  efforts  to  enhance  the  models' performance in real-world applications.
