## V. DISCUSSION

This research develops an advanced system to revolutionize education for the blind in science, mathematics,  and  currency  usage.  Using  YOLOv8,  STT, and TTS technologies, it empowers blind students to engage in  independent  learning  through  accurate  object  detection and comprehensive descriptions.

## A. Addressing Research Gaps

Despite  significant  strides  in  assistive  technology  for visually  impaired  students,  gaps  remain.  Traditional  tactile and  auditory  aids  lack  the  dynamic  interaction  of  modern computer vision and machine learning. Methods like raisedline drawings and physical models fail to represent complex designs accurately or provide immediate feedback. Existing digital solutions also struggle with mathematical content, as screen readers and text-to-speech software often misinterpret notation, hindering engagement. Moreover, traditional  learning  processes  are  time-consuming,  leading to slower academic progress and increased isolation.

## B. Innovative Contributions

This  study  introduces  several  innovative  aspects  that address the above mentioned gaps:

- Real-Time Object Detection: By employing YOLOv8, the system provides fast and accurate real-time object detection, enhancing  the  learning  experience  for  visually  impaired students by offering immediate feedback and interaction.
- Integrated Educational Tools: The development of a smart educational application combined with IoT devices offers a seamless and interactive learning environment. This integration facilitates a more engaging and efficient learning process compared to traditional methods.
- Comprehensive Audio Feedback: Utilizing TTS technologies, the system delivers detailed auditory descriptions of geometric shapes, scientific equipment, and currency, enabling blind students to receive contextual and comprehensive information in real-time.

- Interactive Learning Models: MODM, Scientific Equipment  Detection  Model  (LEDM),  and  CRM  provide specialized functionalities tailored to the unique educational needs of visually impaired students. These models not only assist in learning but also encourage independent exploration and problem-solving.
- Enhanced Accessibility  Features:  The  system's  ability  to dynamically generate descriptive text using AI technologies like  OpenAI GPT-3.5 adds a layer of contextual relevance and engagement that was previously lacking in educational tools for visually impaired students.

By  addressing  the  limitations  of  past  approaches  and introducing novel features, this research significantly contributes to assistive technology in education. The findings are crucial for  promoting  inclusive education, emphasizing  equal  learning  opportunities  for  all  students, regardless  of  visual  abilities.  The  study  aims  to  enhance inclusivity  and  equity,  removing  educational  barriers  and fostering independence among blind students.

## VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This  research  demonstrates  the  potential  of  advanced technologies to transform STEM education for blind and low vision students. The system, using YOLOv8, STT, and TTS, offers real-time  object  detection  and  audio  descriptions, promoting  independent  learning  and  engagement.  Despite progress, challenges like infrastructure limitations and teacher training remain.

Future  work  will  focus  on  developing  more  robust  and scalable  solutions  inspired  by  successful  models  like  iPAT [14] to ensure broader accessibility and inclusivity in STEM education. Additionally, integrating language translation technologies such as those discussed in sources [15] and [16] could further enhance educational accessibility for multilingual  students.  These  translation  tools  can  bridge language barriers, ensuring that students from diverse linguistic  backgrounds  can  benefit  from  the  educational resources provided by the system. This integration would be particularly  beneficial  in  multilingual  regions,  promoting  a more  inclusive  and  equitable  learning  environment  for  all students. Furthermore, integrating mobile and IoT technologies as explored in [17] can offer innovative ways to enhance  real-time  interactions  and  personalized  educational experiences  for  visually  impaired  students,  ensuring  they receive timely and context-aware educational support. Moreover, employing machine learning techniques similar to those  used  in  [18]  can  provide  deeper  insights  into  student learning  patterns  and  preferences,  enabling  the  creation  of more  adaptive  and  personalized  educational  tools  to  better cater to the needs of blind and low vision students.

By addressing these challenges and continuing to innovate,  future  research  can  further  advance  the  field  of assistive technology in education, ensuring that all students, regardless  of  their  visual  or  linguistic  abilities,  have  equal access to high-quality STEM education.

## Paper Source: EULER - Mathematical Editing by Voice Input for People with Visual Impairment

## EULER - Mathematical editing by voice input for people with visual impairment

Tribeth Rivas-P´ erez 1 , Abraham Meza-Vega 2 , Ver´ onica Mora-Lezcano 3 , Dionisio Palacio-Amador 4 , Mario Chac´ on-Rivas 5

Abstract -Access to mathematical content has been limited for the visually impaired population, since some of the technological tools to access information require specific skills, abilities and / or prior knowledge that exclude these people by impeding access to the tool. This paper presents a proposal to improve the accessibility of mathematics for people with visual disabilities, based on the use of information and communication technologies, that allows students to advance at their own learning style. This applied research in process has allowed us to identify alternatives to make mathematics accessible according to the needs of the population with visual disabilities, taking into account that the development is being carried out in a living lab of people with visual disabilities, so it is presented the implemented model of a voice input component in the mathematical editor called EULER, as an alternative to entering basic and compound mathematical expressions, which in turn are accessible in reading and editing. A learning model based on neural networks is used, for which voices of 145 volunteers were used for training. Currently three potential users have evaluated the development of the voice component in a functional way. As a result, opportunities for improvement are obtained in terms of accuracy and proximity when interpreting verbal commands. This research allows us to identify alternatives to make mathematics accessible.

Keywords -Voice input, Human Computer Interaction, Mathematical Editor, Visual Disability, Neural networks.

## I. INTRODUCTION

In the process of inclusion of people with disabilities, support products have been developed that facilitate their autonomy, which can be any type of product (including devices, equipment, instruments and software) specially manufactured or available in the market for people with disabilities [1]. This paper refers to a support product as a software component for people with visual disabilities.

The inclusion of Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) as a support product in education has favored the elimination of barriers to access information, because in this area if the student wishes, he can move at his own pace and learning style [2].

Regarding education, in Costa Rica Law 7600 in its chapter I, article 14 establishes that access to education must be guaranteed to all persons, regardless of their disability [3]. However, during the investigation and work with people with visual disabilities there have been deficiencies, specifically in the mathematics subjects.

On the other hand, the United Nations Organization (UN), in various communiques, has urged member states to recognize and promote the principle of equal opportunity for education at the primary, secondary and higher levels for children, youth and adults with disabilities in integrated environments [4].

The use of technological tools represents an alternative to provide adequate school material to the possibilities of each student [2], therefore, it is recommended for people with visual disabilities the conversion of text to voice and the recognition and digital recording of voice, in order to facilitate the entry and exit of information from technological devices.

In the case of mathematics, which is a pillar in current education, manipulate tools through voice, and that they understand and represent mathematical expressions, it can mean an important advance to make mathematics accessible which is one of the main objectives from EULER.

Within the literature there are several works that focus on supporting the visually impaired user for reading and representing mathematics [5]- [6], however, these systems have the disadvantage that they are not focused on people with visual disabilities, therefore, they omit aspect such as audio confirmation and / or only incorporate basic mathematics.

Consequently, in this work we focus on incorporating functionality through voice to a tool under development that allows ease of use, regarding the interaction and feedback between the user and the system (EULER).

The advantage of this system over similar works is that it offers the visually impaired user the option of creating verbally constructed mathematical expressions, which are represented as if they had been entered using the keyboard.

## II. TOOLS THAT ALLOW MATHEMATICAL EDITING THROUGH VOICE INPUT

Regarding digital tools that incorporate mathematical text input through voice, a literature review was made, as a result, Math Talk, VISO Calculator, EquatIO, Mathifier, CamMath and TalkMaths have been identified as digital tools designed to facilitate the editing of mathematical expressions.

Here are some features of these tools:

- MathTalk: Voice command dictation and use of lexical indicators for disambiguation [5].
- Viso Calculator: Scientific calculator VISO (Voice Input Speech Output), mouse interaction, keyboard and voice shortcuts, allows zooming, high contrast and narrating the expression [7], [8].
- Cam Math: Entering expressions by voice [9].
- TalkMath: Management of mathematical documents by voice, supports mathematical simbology for intermediate secondary level, for example, calculation and matrices, export expressions to MathML or LaTeX and detection of syntactic errors [10], [11].
- Mathifier: Edit mathematical formulas by voice input, recognize the expression and convert to LaTeX. It is a prototype and does not specify the population [12], [13].
- EquatIO: Entering expressions by keyboard, handwriting or voice, inserting expressions in Google Docs, Word, Google Sheets, Slides, Forms and Drawing [6].

A summary of the characteristics of each of the related works is shown in Table 1, there can be seen that EULER meets all the desirable characteristics in voice interpretation for a mathematical editor, thus achieving a useful system target users.

The characteristics evaluated in the different tools are represented as follows in Table I:

- Voice input = VI.
- Makes use of screen reader = SR
- Focused on visual disability = VD.
- It incorporates calculator = C.
- It is a mathematical editor = ME.
- Perform auditory confirmation = AC.

Voice input is an efficient input method for blind people [14]. In the incorporation of voice input of mathematical expressions for EULER, as main characteristics, focused for blind people and low vision, the following are available:

- Voice input of mathematical expressions, as an alternative to using the keyboard.
- EULER handles accessible reading of mathematical expressions with screen readers Non-Visual Desktop Access (NVDA) and Job Access With Speech (JAWS).
- It incorporates a calculator with auditory output.
- Confirmation of the expression that was inserted, this allows people who are blind or have low vision to corroborate if the result of voice entry is as expected.

As part of the development of this component of voice input, it is known the contribution for students who have visual impairment and also have some level of motor disability due to cerebral palsy or other cause.

## III. MODEL, INTERPRETATION AND REPRESENTATION OF MATHEMATICAL EXPRESSIONS THROUGH AUDIO FOR EULER

The editing of mathematical expressions through voice input involves the pronunciation of verbal indications (such as preset commands), the interpretation of the indications and the translation and visual representation of the mathematical expression.

For the above, a learning algorithm must be selected to define the prediction model of mathematical symbols and expressions. The task of the learning algorithm is to learn the weights for the model. The weights describe how the model have to behave in relationship to the data [15]. On the other hand, a prediction model is the result obtained from the training phase [16].

## A. Learning and training algorithm

To carry out the process of entry, interpretation, translation and representation in EULER, the learning algorithm had to be selected and then the training phase had to be executed to define the prediction model.

1) Learning algorithm selection: Convolutional neural networks work by dividing and modeling information into multiple layers, each of these layers has a higher level of abstraction compared to the previous one, which allows it to discern between basic elements or complex elements [17], [18]. Acoustic models or voice inputs have rapid progress using neural networks [19], [20]. In addition, convolutional neural networks work by converting audio inputs into spectrograms to make the classifications [21]. Based on this, the convolutional network algorithm was selected to be applied in EULER.

For the implementation of this algorithm we used the open source library TensorFlow developed by Google that is used to meet needs such as image recognition, voice, data prediction, decision making, machine translation, among others [22]. This library is selected because it offers robust models with very wide support for different platforms.

2) Training and model creation: Prior to the training stage, a set of data ( dataset ) is required to be supplied to the neural network, which is used to establish the parameters that will be used to make the predictions.

The dataset audios for the training were classified as: numbers, Latin alphabet, delimiters and mathematical symbols. The work is focused on the teaching-learning process of the area of mathematics for people with visual disabilities, so the prediction model that is sought must be mathematical.

For the construction of the dataset, support was obtained from volunteers, 145 people so far, 81 adults (20 years and older),

64 children (5-12 years), who agreed to record their voices for the dataset. The audios obtained were divided into two parts, 80% for training and 20% for tests and validation. The division is done in this way on the recommendation of TensorFlow [23].

The training audios are taken by the network to try to find patterns in them and generalize future verbal entries that have not been entered, distinguishing from the set of possibilities (moments of silence, nonverbal and background noises and accepted commands) to determine which interpretations are more likely to be the searched word [24].

The validation audios are used to verify that the network is not memorizing the training data, this is a usual process in this type of neural networks. Once the network complies with the training phase, one of the validation audios is supplied to verify that it is learning correctly, in advance the network is given the possibility to verify if it answer was correct with a file which it is created manually and contains the answers, indicating to which set the audio being tested belongs. Additionally, the training program automatically stores this data which the user can consult during the training phase of the network [24], as shown in Figure 1. The graph on the left shows how the network is improving accuracy and on the right it shows how the difference between the predicted result and the correct answer is reduced.

Fig. 1. Convolutional neural network training stats



In addition, to improve the recognition process, the neural network is trained with data that is not relevant for the interpretation of mathematical content, for example, background noises, moments of silence and involuntary errors in speaking, this is usual in this type of networks.

At the end of the training, the TensorFlow library indicated that the neural network has approximately 82% accuracy.

## B. Interpretation and representation of the input audio

The first step is to capture the audio, for this, the TensorFlow convolutional neural network, defines a time window in which a user is expected to enter some indication with the voice, the identified input audio is broken down into smaller samples than they are transformed into single-channel images, known as spectrograms [25], once this process is completed, the data is sent to the neural network and the word spoken by the user is inferred. For the interpretation and representation of the input audios, once processed, language models are established, these models define how the audio is processed, what elements are involved and in what order [26]. In EULER a language model is defined for simple mathematical symbols and another for compound mathematical symbols.

1) Language model for simple symbols: The simple symbols were categorized in numerical values and in operators, this classification is proper. Operators are interpreted and represented symbolically, as shown in the examples in Table II.

TABLE II OPERATORS REPRESENTATION

| Verbal input   | Representation   |
|----------------|------------------|
| plus           | +                |
| alpha          | α                |
| empty set      | ∅                |
| angle          | /measuredangle   |
| cosine         | cos              |

For the representation of numbers two cases can occur. The first case is when the number is only one digit, it is represented symbolically, similar to the operators. The other case is when the number is two digits or more, for this a syntactic analysis is performed to represent the number. In Figure 2, the process that is executed to represent the number is shown and Figure 3 shows the syntactic analysis performed to obtain the numerical value.

Fig. 2. Numerical value representation process



* This algorithm was developed for spanish language.

The parser takes the translation performed by the neural network and exchanges the equivalent numerical values, then concatenates them according to the positioning in base blocks 10. Considering the above, in EULER each value is added sequentially and visually displayed on the screen, also gives the auditory confirmation for the blind or low vision user.

2) Language model for compound symbols: The interaction with each compound symbol varies to avoid ambiguities, for example, if the user enters X raised to the n plus one, the editor could represent x n + 1 or x n + 1. To avoid this, a commandbased protocol was chosen, in which the user interacts with the editor. In Table III, the interaction with the editor for the entry of composite symbols is exemplified.

The interaction is chosen in order to keep the user located and do not miss or make mistakes when you want to enter a mathematical expression, in addition, possible ambiguities are under control.

## IV. EVALUATION AND RESULTS

With the data of the volunteers the training was carried out. For the evaluation of voice input, interpretation and representation, there have been three people, two with low vision and one with blindness.

## A. Evaluations

For the tests carried out on the current development of voice input in EULER, the following have been taken into account:

- Numbers
- Basic operators (addition, subtraction, multiplication and division)
- Composite symbols (fraction and exponent)

The steps implemented to test the voice inputs with the elements mentioned above, were performed as follows.

- Users are told what commands they can use.
- The user is presented with an exercise that involves the commands provided.
- The user is assisted in case of doubt.
- The record of the results obtained with respect to the commands used by the user is kept.

## B. Results

The incorporation of voice input functionality in EULER is still under development and testing, therefore, the results are in terms of changes and improvements. With the tests applied to the target users (blind and visually impaired), it was obtained that:

- The interpretation of the numbers was not always correct.
- Some symbols because of their similarity to numerical values are confused, for example, '%' represents it as '* 100'. The tests were applied in Spanish, for this reason it is this result. This is because the symbol '%' is pronounced in Spanish ' por ciento ' and the saying ' * 100 ' is pronounced ' por cien .'
- It depends on how the value or symbol is pronounced, represents a symbol or number that does not correspond, for example, the users pronounced 'uuuuno' 1 , EULER represents '11'.

From that findings, in development the following must be taken into account.

- It is necessary to improve the accuracy of numbers, for this you need to use another dataset with numbers.
- Initially a training method was used for word inferences, however, due to precision problems, a phoneme 2 training was chosen, with the aim of improving the proximity of the input audios.

For the other commands to be added to the voice input system, the results obtained with the target users must be taken into account and identify what new actions should be considered for the next tests.

## V. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORKS

The learning and development of mathematics for people with visual disabilities is complicated because it is very visual. The representation of mathematical expressions through voice recognition is an alternative for the development of accessible mathematics.

EULER, which is a tool focused on blind and low vision people, with a function of entering expressions by voice facilitates the process of editing mathematics, offering an accessible and autonomous environment.

The change from training by inferences of words to training by phonemes, allows to treat the problem of proximity in the symbols or numbers, and allow the target user to have no problems of incorrect representation of symbols or numbers.

In the future it is planned to integrate more composite symbols which correspond to advanced levels in secondary and university education, such as systems of equations, integrals and propositional logic, in addition to the integration of more voice commands for greater application control, to navigate between menus and to switch between editing modes. Also develop a voice recognition version for the web version of the mathematical editor.

1 Pronunciation in Spanish for the number 1

2 Defined as the phonological unit that cannot be broken down into successive smaller units and that is able to distinguish meanings, for example, the number '14' is associated with the word 'fourteen', and this in turn is associated with phoneme / f / / o / / u / / r / / t / / e / / e / / n /.

Another important project that could be addressed is to include support for multiple languages because there is currently support only for Spanish. To achieve this task, it is planned to look for people who are willing to voluntarily collaborate to record their voices and create the different datasets for different languages, it is also planned to use the databases offered by Google [27], since they contain a variety of audios compiled by the Google team such as music, speech, noise, among others.

It is necessary to expand the number of blind and low vision people to have more feedback on the functionality. Similarly, perform repeated tests with these people, to adjust to approach compliance to make mathematics accessible. Given the wide use of voice command functionalities, in the future, other types of users could be involved, for example, people with motor disabilities or elementary school children who have not yet developed the ability to write.

## Framework for Voice-controlled AI Teaching Assistant for Specially-abled

Tilottama Goswami Department of Information Technology Vasavi College of Engineering (A)

Hyderabad, INDIA

Shashidhar Reddy Javaji Department of Computer Science University of Massachusetts, Amherst

MA, USA

goswami.tilottama@gmail.com ORCID: 0000-0003-0665-5190

shashidhar.chintu16@gmail.com

ORCID: 0000-0001-7601-8504

Abstract -Recent advancements in technology have triggered a revolution in the education sector. One of the significant developments of this change is being granted access to vast online resources from various world class institutes. The motivation behind this paper is to be able to create a technological solution for providing equal opportunities to specially-abled online learners who may have physical disabilities such as visual impairment, loss of hands/weak hand motor skills, etc., and enable their participation for a more inclusive society. The paper uses a twofold approach. Firstly, it provides literature on various stateof-art assistive technologies for e-learning portals. Secondly, the paper proposes a learning framework as teaching assistant for specially-abled, which is artificial intelligence based and interactive voice enabled. The proposed framework has three modules completely controlled by voice commands for self-paced - reading, learning and auto-marking assessment. The assessment module generates fill-in-the-blanks and question-answers, which is a part of continuous comprehensive tests. As a case study, the proposed framework is prototyped on an e-learning platform DIKSHA, which hosts digital books from National Council of Educational Research and Training. Natural language processing toolkit based on Python libraries has been used. The results have been found encouraging. Extensions for future work are also discussed.

Index Terms -Natural Language Processing, E-Learning Portal, Voice-Based, Specially-abled, Inclusive Society

## I. INTRODUCTION

W E live in a digital era. Advancements in technology have seeped into various sectors of our life, and education has not been left behind. This revolution has eliminated the need to carry stacks of books to school, decreased the teacher's workload and has made learning more efficient. Massive Open Online Courses (MOOC) have transformed the education system, as its significant advantage includes both flexibility and affordability with unlimited participation - thus paving a path to career advancement. MOOC providers bring the best courses from the best schools (that includes reputed tech giants and world class academic institutes) at the learner's doorstep. Thus the learner's focus shift towards flexible schedule and self-learning at higher secondary and university levels. But at the same time, the specially-abled learners are not able to cope up with the same pace due to their physical limitations. The wide spectrum of disabilities include visually challenged, hand amputees, wheelchair users, Kapil K. Nagwanshi Department of CSE Central University Bilaspur Chhatisgarh, INDIA dr.kapil@ieee.org

ORCID: 0000-0003-3133-978X

weak hand motor skills, which hinder them from accessing the online resources. Research is going on to create technological solution for providing equal opportunities to the specially-abled, enhancing their experience using online elearning platform and enable their participation in an inclusive society. A large percentage of such learners lack employment as the resources are not easily available, the number of special institutes available are not enough to educate such a large population. Lots of research are conducted under the umbrella of assistive technology over the decades, which include wearable devices and mobile applications [1], [2].

The evolution of Natural Language Processing (NLP) is seen as an emerging field to interact between computer and human language, combining the concepts from subjects such as linguistics, artificial intelligence and computer science. The packages and libraries related to NLP helps to create models that can communicate and respond like humans. There is a great demand to serve specially-abled in the education sector [3]-[5].

The paper focuses on providing a voice enabled interactive learning framework creating an enabling environment for specially abled learners for their empowerment based on natural language processing , a branch of artificial intelligence. The paper is divided into following sections. Section 2 provides literature of state-of-art assistive technologies for e-learning portals. Section 3 puts forth the proposed methodology of Voice-controlled AI Teaching Assistant Framework. Section 4 details out the prototyping experimentation and results. The paper concludes with future work in Section 5.

## II. RELATED WORK

The following sub-sections showcase the literature survey of the assistive technologies used for specially-abled learners, especially the visually impaired as end users.

## A. Computer Vision for Assistive Technologies

The authors in [6], created a learning platform by combining deep convolutional networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks(R-CNN), and speech corpus models to provide an interactive learning experience for particular subjects. The authors in [7] designed an inexpensive wearable device that uses computer vision (CV) to read documents placed near to the user in various alignments and lighting conditions. The systems proposed by researchers in [8]-[10] use a combination of techniques such as machine learning, image processing and speech synthesis techniques.

## B. Text-to-Speech and Speech-to-Text

In the paper [11] the author explains different approaches for text to speech synthesis, articular synthesis and formant synthesis.The author in [12] explains the working of speech to text conversion using Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (MFCC) and support vector machine. The proposed model experimented on mix of couple of languages which includes English and Marathi, an Indian language of state of Maharashtra. The works proposed by authors in [13], [14], [15], [16] detail about using Digital Assistance for the Blind using the Text to Speech and Speech to Text libraries for tutoring.

## C. Mobile Based AI Applications

As technology advanced and the use of mobile phones became very popular, the presence of innumerable applications surfaced up, serving various purposes for the visually impaired such as color detection [17], motion marking menus [18], image recognition [19], [20], Google Vision APIs, Voice Dream Reader.

## D. Continuous Comprehensive Assessment (CCA)

Continuous assessment has become an integral part of any education system, which are usually short and concise in nature such as quiz, question and answers, fill in the blanks. Question and answers are mostly generated by the human experts in the respective subjects. There is a limitation in the number of human generated questions.

The author in [21] has built the model which is based on sentence selection, gap selection, distractor selection which includes semantic similarity, syntactic similarity, and contextual fit. Word2Vec library along with probabilistic functions is used to choose the blank generators in [22]. The model gave satisfactory results and the quality of the questions generated was evaluated. In paper [23], the author has used the wordembedding concept, sequence classification and sequence labelling. CoreNLP was used first to bring the sentences to wordlevel and thereafter for the sequence labelling and sequence classification. 2-layer bidirectional LSTM was applied, for training and evaluating the model using the data collected from user-interface. The authors in the paper [24], [25], [26] explain the concept of filling in the blanks and missing words in articles. Comparative study is done among the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), ELMo (context setting word embedding method) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) model. In the paper [27], the author uses WordNet library. The paper [28] proposes the state-of-art model for the question and answers generation, using the multi-flow attention model, transformers, word-byword generation. The author [29] has worked on a model for question generator. The paper [30] proposes a novel pretraining and tuning framework to generate and predict words closer to human writing patterns, which helps in achieving good state of art results in summarization, question answering, question generation.

To the authors best of knowledge, all these related works are not end-to-end voice assisted process for reading, learning and assessment taken together. The motivation of the paper is to develop a framework for reading, learning and assessment using voice assisted teaching assistant. Prototyping has been done for the school learners which features voice based easy selection of class, chapter and particular topic for reading and learning. The proposed methodology is detailed out in subsequent section.

## III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

Most of the related work mentioned are proposed keeping the visually impaired. The authors want to address wide spectrum of specially abled which includes visually impaired and other disabilities which restrict the usage of using the e-learning platform due to poor hand motor skills as well. In National Education Policy NEP 2020 (https://www.education.gov.in//en//nationaleducation-policy-2020-0), various new provisions for children with disabilities are encouraged to enable them to fully participate with regular schooling process.

The paper proposes a framework for Voice controlled AI Teaching Assistant built to mainly focus on helping speciallyabled learners using online platform based on natural language processing. The authors have considered an existing online portal 'DIKSHA' contents (easily accessible and freely downloadable) for prototyping the proposed methodology. DIKSHA is one of the online learning platform by India government for school learners (https://diksha.gov.in/ncert/). DIKSHA is developed on open source technology, made in India, which incorporates internet-scale technologies and enables various usecases and solutions for teaching and learning. The platform is being leveraged and developed for foundational learning programs, school education and to support inclusive learning for differently-abled communities of learners and teachers [31]. In the context of COVID-19 related disruption of schooling, DIKSHA made it feasible for all states and union territories to enable education at home through innovative programs. The platform works very well for normal learners (without disability), but issues are being faced by the specially-abled students as per their parents reports. The article [32] 'Visually impaired struggle with NCERT e-textbooks' published in a national newspaper in India, mentions the details of the issues faced by the specially-abled learners [33]-[35].

The strength of the proposed framework prototyping is that it does not need any supervision, specific dataset and covers holistically reading, learning, and assessing of any digital text content of the user's interest. In future the framework will be extended as a service plugged into any such e-learning portal. The framework has three modules : 1) Reading, 2) Learning and 3) Assessment as shown in Fig. 1. Firstly, the user needs to login to the DIKSHA portal and he/she selects the class, subject, chapter and after doing so, the user can choose any of the three modules from the framework. The user also has the option of choosing a language for any of these modules (by default, it is English). In future, the prototype can be extended to any language.

Fig. 1. Schematic Diagram of the Voice controlled AI Teaching Assistant



Detailed working explanation of the modules is discussed in the following subsections.

## A. Voice Controlled AI Reading Module

The following pseudocode depicts step by step process of the reading module, selects learner's choice of subject and lesson in the preferred language.

```

ELSE 19 SET sentence list index=0, para list index=0 and word list index=0 20. OUTPUT AND READ OUT \select the subject" 21. VOICE INPUT subject 22. OUTPUT AND READ OUT \select the lesson" 23. ```

The Table I provides information about the Python packages and functions used for the reading module.

The natural language processing libraries are extensively used for these modules. The model takes a word as input from the user and then the model gives some of the basic information about the word, such as synonyms, antonyms, word definition, an example sentence, parts of speech. Finally the user also has the option of getting the translation of that particular word in any preferred language. WordNet, a lexical database is used to get all the information of the words. It links words into semantic relations including synonyms, meronyms, and hyponyms. The synonyms are grouped into synsets with quick definitions and usage examples. Nouns, adjectives, verbs, and adverbs are assorted into sets of synonyms called synsets, each expressing a different concept.

## B. Voice controlled AI Assessment Module

The continuous comprehensive tests can be automated by creating quizzes including fill-in-the blanks, true or false, etc. The framework assessment module gives the learner the options of a) question and answer assessment b) fill in the blanks assessment, based on the choice of subject and the chapter. The methodology is totally unsupervised and is independent of any particular dataset.

Questions and Answers Assessment: The model prepares the questions from the given lesson. First, the sentences from the lesson are taken and then the sentences are further divided into words, then the parts of speech tagging is done onto those words. Constituency tree and the dependency graph of the sentences are drawn by the model, based on the main verb and main clause found in the sentence. Using the information of parts of speech and the information gathered from the trees, the 'Wh'word is applied in the sentence to generate the questions, such as 'What', 'Where', 'When', 'Who', etc. The questions are read out, and the user has to answer the questions, which will be recorded and then converted to text for further analysis and assessment.

Fill in the Blanks Assessment: In the present scope, the blanks are filled with nouns, can be either singular(NN), plural(NNS) or a proper noun(NNP). The appropriate noun is replaced with a blank. The sentences are spelt out for the user and the model waits for around 10 seconds to get the answer from the user. The answer is fed into the system in the form of voice and converted to text using the speech to text. The text is matched with the answer and upon matching the model increases the score count by appropriate value. The model spells out the final score without any human assistance.

The framework has been tested as a prototype case study on the DIKSHA portal. The experiments were conducted on intermediate physics, chemistry, biology and history subjects for school students of class 6,7,8 and 9.

## V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

The paper proposes an artificial intelligence based voice enabled teaching assistant which can be integrated with the elearning portals in future, to make the specially-abled learners and instructors fraternity to work independently. The paper provided a comprehensive literature on assistive technologies developed and researched on e-learning for specially abled, most of them focussed on visually impaired. To the authors best of knowledge, none of the related works are end-to-end voice assisted product which can be plugged to any of the MOOCs for reading, learning and assessment taken together for any learning context in general. The paper proposes a voice assisted framework to create a technological solution for providing equal opportunities to specially-abled online learners who may have physical disabilities such as visual impairment, loss of hands/weak hand motor skills, etc., and enable their participation for a more inclusive society. The three modules are based on natural language processing and speech processing. The reading module, learning module and assessment modules have been prototyped on one such publicly available online platform called DIKSHA, which hosts digital books from NCERT. The development is carried out using Python libraries for Natural Language Tool Kit (NLTK). The results are encouraging especially with no dependency on any special hardware, no dependency on screen readers, and without any supervised learning on any particular datasets. The proposed model is a simple to use and special-abled friendly. Finally, the model does almost all the work of human teaching right from reading to teaching, generating objective type assessment tests and finally automated assessment - totally voice assisted. The future work of this paper includes an improved version of assessment module with text summarization as the core engine. This will increase the efficiency of question generation. The reading of equations and images are still open areas of research. In the future, the improved version of the proposed framework will be extended as a service interface for any elearning portal to provide an inclusive learning ecosystem.

## Kanak: Automating the Generation of Accessible STEM Materials for Blind and Low-vision Students

## [Hari Palani](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3140-6359)

Research Scientist Northeastern University Portland, Maine, USA Principal Research Engineer UNAR Labs Portland, Maine, USA hari.palani@unarlabs.com

## Abstract

Blind and low-vision (BLV) students face significant barriers to timely access of visual STEM materials. Accessibility practitioners, such as braille transcribers and teachers of the visually impaired (TVIs), rely on manual and labor-intensive processes to produce accessible formats (e.g., braille, tactile graphics) of visual educational materials. To complement this effort and address ongoing accessibility gaps, we developed Kanak, an AI system that leverages generative intelligence to automate the generation of accessible STEM content, including text, math equations, and graphics. Through a comparative study with seven practitioners, we examined how Kanak supports traditional transcribing workflows and augments expert judgment. Our findings reveal how generative tools could complement practitioner expertise by providing context-aware formatting, proofreading support, and on-demand graphics generation. We conclude with design considerations for human-AI collaboration in transcribing work, positioning generative intelligence not as a replacement for expert insights, but as a catalyst for expanding equitable access.

## CCS Concepts

· Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in HCI ; Empirical studies in Accessibility .

## Keywords

Accessibility, STEM Education, Blind and Low-Vision (BLV), HumanAI Collaboration, Generative AI, Tactile Graphics, Inclusive Design

## 1 Introduction

In STEM education, visual educational materials (such as equations, diagrams, and charts) serve as foundational tools for conceptual understanding, problem-solving, and communication. However, blind and low-vision (BLV) students often face significant challenges in accessing these visual educational materials [22, 41, 66]. Achieving access to educational content for BLV students requires not only classroom accommodations but also systemic efforts to produce accessible instructional materials in formats such as braille, Nemeth or UEB math expressions, tactile graphics, audio descriptions, and accessible digital documents [3, 5, 23]. Producing such accessible materials involves the collaborative efforts of a range of accessibility practitioners, including braille transcribers, teachers of the visually impaired (TVIs), mainstream educators, and publishing institutions [16, 17, 35, 36, 38, 62]. However, these accessibility practitioners continue to face numerous challenges, including delays in educational material delivery and inconsistent quality of tactile resources [6, 16, 46, 76]. Further, while braille remains an important medium for accessing educational content in BLV education [3], there is a persistent shortage of certified braille transcribers, which often results in delays in delivering textbooks and other instructional materials to students [2, 16, 36, 77]. In many cases, braille textbooks are distributed incrementally (e.g., one chapter at a time) because the transcription process remains ongoing. These delays are exacerbated when teachers change course materials mid-semester, which leaves students without timely access to updated content [36]. These existing issues in the production of accessible educational materials negatively influence the learning experience of BLV students, often leaving them without timely access to educational content that their sighted peers receive in real-time.

While prior research [9, 16, 29, 56] has explored the strategies provided by accessibility practitioners to enhance accessibility in BLV education and the challenges they face, limited studies [40, 48] have captured the accessible material production workflows from the perspective of these practitioners. Further, we know considerably less about how technological interventions, such as generative AI tools, could be integrated into transcribing workflows to augment practitioner expertise and streamline accessible content creation. Responding to this gap, our study explores how generative tools could collaborate with accessibility practitioners to automate and reshape accessibility workflows for educational materials. To study this, we developed Kanak, a prototype AI system that extracts, converts, and generates accessible STEM content from visual formats, with flexible delivery across different platforms. We then conducted

Shivangee Nagar College of Engineering Northeastern University Boston, Massachusetts, USA nagar.sh@northeastern.edu a user study involving seven accessibility practitioners, including braille transcribers, tactile graphic designers, and TVIs, to examine how Kanak supports the transcription of visual educational content into accessible formats [49, 53].

The purpose of our study is twofold. First, we identify the challenges in the current process of accessible educational material production and how accessibility practitioners perceive the design of an AI-powered generation tool, Kanak, in their transcribing process, extending prior work [16, 46, 61, 76] on accessibility practitioners' strategies on adapting academic content for BLV students. In doing so, this study provides in-depth empirical evidence of practitioners' step-by-step transcription workflows and their multi-tool ecosystems, which reveal how practioners strategically select each tool based on the content type of educational materials and formatting needs. Second, we systematically evaluate the usability and efficacy of Kanak to support the generation of accessible educational materials through both qualitative and quantitative evaluation. This approach enabled us to capture and assess how an AI-powered generation tool like Kanak could be integrated into-and potentially streamline-current transcribing workflows. Based on our findings, we rethink the accessible educational materials' transcribing workflows and discuss design considerations to support accessibility practitioners, including providing context-aware formatting suggestions, supporting content verification and proofreading, enhancing the generation of accessible graphical components, and promoting human-AI collaborative interventions.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 describes the design and development of the tool; Section 4 outlines the evaluation method; Sections 5 and 6 present findings from the user evaluation; and Section 7 provides a discussion of the results.

## 2 Related Work

Our study is informed by prior research on accessible educational materials generation for BLV students and the practices of accessibility practitioners to support accessibility of educational materials for BLV students.

## 2.1 Accessible Educational Materials for BLV Students

A growing body of research has highlighted the accessibility challenges of BLV students when interacting with visual materials [14, 57, 61, 76]. For instance, Prakash et al. [57] found that BLV students often invest substantial time in accessing information from visual diagrams like bar charts. In response to these accessibility issues, there has been increasing research to improve the accessibility of visual educational materials for BLV students [5, 8, 23, 28, 42, 45, 60, 70, 75]. For example, Giudice et al. [23] introduced a tool that allows learners to explore visual graphics through vibration patterns and auditory feedback triggered by touch interactions. Similarly, Zhao et al. [80] developed TADA to enable BLV students to access node-link diagrams by engaging in open-ended touch-based exploration, node search, and navigating between nodes.

Relatedly, researchers [22, 31, 44, 59, 73] have also focused on improving accessibility for discipline-specific content. For example, in the domain of mathematics, Ge and Seo [22] developed an equation editor using spatial audio cues to support intuitive navigation for BLV students. Likewise, Knaeble et al. [31] created AutoChemplete, an interactive tool for generating accessible representations of chemical structural formulas. Others [28, 64] aimed to improve accessibility of data visualizations. Sharif et al. [64] proposed VoxLens, which enables BLV learners to explore visualizations through voiceactivated commands and obtain holistic summaries of the data. Hoque et al. [28] designed Susurrus, a sonification-based tool that integrates keyboard interaction and text-to-speech feedback to present data through natural sounds. In addition, to support access to various chart types, Moured et al. [45] introduced Chart4Blind, an intelligent interface that converts bitmap images of line charts into accessible digital formats (e.g., SVG, CSV). Zhang et al. [79] developed ChartA11y to provide accessible interaction techniques for making line charts, bar charts, and scatter plots.

While impactful, much of the existing work has centered on making specific types of visual content accessible in isolation, such as charts or discipline-specific graphics. In contrast, accessibility practitioners must routinely transcribe entire documents containing diverse visual elements, such as charts, diagrams, equations, and more, which requires a more holistic approach. Our study addresses this overlooked need by examining the end-to-end workflow of practitioners and exploring how an AI-powered generation tool can support the holistic transcription process of educational materials as they occur in real-world contexts.

## 2.2 Practices of Accessibility Practitioners

Inclusive education continues to face challenges when teaching methods in classrooms fail to address the diverse needs of all learners. This is often due to the inadequate teacher preparation and a lack of both human and material resources [25]. Among the key stakeholders of BLV education, teachers of the visually impaired (TVIs) face several challenges in providing accessible learning experiences to BLV students due to the inaccessibility of mainstream learning resources, which often rely heavily on visual representations and are not designed with non-visual accessibility in mind [4, 29, 30]. For instance, Stefik et al. [68] noted that when adapting a computer science curriculum, TVIs expressed concerns about the heavily visual learning materials, the absence of braille-compatible practice exams, the omission of visual graphic-based exam questions, and the implications of such omissions on educational equity for BLV students.

To address these inaccessibility challenges, TVIs provide considerable effort by adapting academic content to meet the accessibility needs of BLV students [9, 56, 61]. In doing so, they consider strategies to enhance the accessibility of learning materials for their students [21, 65], such as the use of tactile resources for interpreting visual information non-visually [56]. Hayes and Proulx [26] showed that TVIs consider classroom adaptations, such as handson activities and increased lesson time, important for topics like science and mathematics. Rosenblum et al. [61] found that TVIs provided a range of strategies to help students access and understand information presented in graphics. These included aligning instructional language with that used by general education teachers, simplifying complex visuals, for instance, by reducing data points in scatter plots, and tailoring instruction to meet students' individual learning needs. Likewise, Zebehazy and Wilton [76] reported that TVIs faced numerous challenges related to the preparation and instruction of tactile graphics to support accessibility for BLV

students, including limited time for material production and lack of standardization in how tactile graphics are designed. TVIs expressed concern that learning materials often arrive late for timely transcription or modification into accessible formats [36]. In addition, classroom support staff were sometimes unfamiliar with how to properly convey graphical information or felt rushed to keep pace with the lesson, further hindering the delivery of accessible learning experiences [76]. Corn and Wall [16] found that braille production systems often rely on volunteers, which leads to inconsistencies in the availability and quality of accessible educational materials. As such, there is no guarantee that students who use braille will receive the appropriate quantity or quality of accessible materials corresponding to the mainstream educational curricula.

Extending this prior scholarship, our study captures the current transcribing workflows of accessibility practitioners and their challenges, investigating how AI-powered tools can be integrated into this transcribing process, and identifying opportunities to optimize workflows for efficient and effective production of accessible educational materials for BLV students.

## 3 Tool Design and Development

To explore how generative AI can be embedded into practitioners' workflows for generating visual educational materials (e.g., worksheets, handouts, quizzes) into accessible formats (e.g, braille, tactile graphics), we developed Kanak, a web-based tool that supports automation with human-in-the-loop control. As an initial use case, we developed and deployed a prototype version of Kanak that focused on SAT test preparation materials, which enabled practitioners to generate accessible equivalents of the visual SAT paper (in scanned PDF format) that can be instantly delivered to students as accessible versions, such as BRF for braille and DOCX for screenreader access. The tool enabled users to generate accessible materials through a range of integrated features and supported flexible delivery of the accessible content across multiple hardware and software platforms, which we describe below.

## 3.1 Dynamic Visual-to-Tactile Transcribing and Editing

We designed Kanak to support end-to-end transcribing of visual documents into accessible formats. The tool begins with a document upload interface similar to file-management systems like Dropbox, which allow users to manage multiple uploaded documents, preview and edit contents, and download outputs. After the file upload, the backend engine of the tool processes the uploaded document and initiates a visual-to-tactile transcribing process. The tool automatically extracts (Figure 1 (d)) textual, math, tabular, and graphical elements into editable blocks from the uploaded document. It provides users with an in-browser editor (Figure 1 (e)) where different content types (e.g., text, table, math equations, graphics) are made interactively editable.

## 3.2 Inline Editing for Multiple Content Types

To provide accessibility practitioners with flexible and intuitive editing methods, Kanak incorporates a multi-pane preview editor that presents the original and transcribed document contents sideby-side. Users can directly edit all extracted document contents, such as text, math equations, tables, and graphics, within the interface. Users can also rearrange the editable blocks to customize the flow and order of the content as needed (Figure 1 (d)). These features enable practitioners to correct the content extraction errors across diverse content types and refine content within a single platform, which eliminates the need to switch between multiple tools. For example, when users click on a text block, it activates a standard text editor. When they interact with a math equation, it launches an equation editor. Likewise, tables open in a dedicated spreadsheet-style table editor, which allows users to perform celllevel modifications. For graphical content, such as bar and line graphs, users can adjust data labels, axis values, and other visual attributes through a built-in graphic editor.

## 3.3 Custom Graphic Redrawing Feature

Kanak allows users to manually revise or recreate graphical content, given that automated graphics extraction is still evolving and often inaccurate [15, 71]. This feature enables practitioners to retain control over the tactile interpretability of visual graphics. Users can use a built-in graphic editor within Kanak that supports drawing with different shapes and line textures. For instance, users can specify properties, such as line style (solid, dashed) and line width.

## 3.4 Output Generation in Multiple Accessible Formats

Recognizing the diverse range of assistive technologies used by BLV students, including notetakers, refreshable braille displays, and screen readers [6, 21, 43], Kanak supported the export of transcribed documents into multiple device-compatible formats. While audio-based output is under development for future iterations, the supported output formats include BRF (braille ready format) for embossing or use with braille displays and DOCX for further editing or embossing. The prototype also supported Nemeth 1 codes for mathematical content. Additionally, users have the option to specify if they require contracted braille 2 or not in the transcribed document.

## 3.5 Prototype Architecture and Workflow

The Kanak prototype was designed to align with the structural and content-specific ways of standardized assessments, particularly the SAT, which comprises four distinct sections: reading, writing, math with calculator, and math without calculator. Implemented as a webbased application, the tool used ReactJS for the frontend interface and NodeJS for backend operations. Kanak leveraged computer vision and deep learning techniques to analyze visual documents and automate their transcription into accessible formats, facilitating non-visual access for BLV learners. The underlying models and backend services of the tool are proprietary to UNAR Labs [32]. The tool architecture consists of five key modules, each focusing on a specific stage in the accessibility conversion pipeline, which we describe below:

1 Nemeth Code is a braille code which is developed for writing mathematics and scientific notation in braille [1].

2 The shorthand combinations of braille characters, that are used to represent common letter groups, syllables, or whole words to make braille compact and efficient, are called braille contractions [18]

Figure 1: Steps of Kanak's workflow: (a)-(f)

- Pre-Processor: Extracts embedded images and text from PDF documents and stores them as temporary assets for modular processing.
- Text Processor: Parses, formats, and semantically classifies the extracted text to ensure compatibility with non-visual consumption tools.
- GraphicProcessor: Uses custom scripts in conjunction with OpenCV's EAST text detector to isolate graphical elements (e.g., charts, diagrams), identify their spatial attributes (type, size, color, and location), and convert them into structured spatial objects.
- Reconstruction Module: Translates these spatial objects into perceptually optimized representations for tactile access, such as braille and raised-line graphics, guided by tactile perception research [12, 23] and compliance with BANA guidelines [52].
- Cross-Platform Delivery Module: Compiles the structured accessible content into platform-specific output files (e.g., BRF for embossers, tagged HTML for screen readers, SVG for tactile rendering systems). This module ensures that content is tailored to the technical and usability constraints of target devices, including embossers, notetakers, refreshable braille displays, smartphones, and tablets.

Through this modular pipeline, Kanak could automate the task of transcribing diverse visual educational materials into standardized accessible formats for real-world educational use. By supporting the accessibility of multiple content types, including text, mathematical expressions, and graphics, Kanak addressed the core components of most educational materials, which provides an approach that could be expanded to support accessibility in other contexts (e.g., workplace, professional certification).

## 4 Tool Evaluation: Method

To uncover the challenges in current accessibility workflows and assess the usability of Kanak in generating accessible educational materials, we conducted a comparative and within-subjects study with seven experienced accessibility practitioners, with approval from the institutional review board of our university.

## 4.1 Participants

We recruited seven participants (1 Male, 6 Female) who had prior experience in transcribing visual educational materials into tactile formats. Participants were recruited with a study announcement distributed through an organization that works with blind or lowvision individuals. All participants were from the US. Two participants belonged in the age range of 45-50 years, two were 51-55 years, and three were 60-65 years. The sample size is considered reasonable in this context, as prior literature [63, 67] demonstrated that five to six participants are sufficient for assessing the usability and identifying the majority of issues in novel human-computer interaction (HCI) systems. Table 1 provides details about each participant's occupation, years of experience in material conversion, and the tools they currently use (e.g., Word, Firebird, Duxbury Braille Translator) for visual-to-tactile conversion.

## 4.2 Materials

For our study procedure, we prepared four sample PDFs (included in the supplementary materials), each consisting of modified version of the freely available SAT test preparation materials. Each document comprised four sections: reading, writing, math with calculator, and math without calculator. The documents were four pages long and included a range of content types (Figure 2 and 3), such as textual questions, bar plots, tables, mathematical equations, and graph-based math problems. We selected these sample documents because they reflect real-world learning materials commonly encountered in educational settings. The material's breadth of content and multimodal structure made it an ideal testbed for evaluating the system's ability to address varied visual and textual formats across academic contexts. The math sections included various difficulty levels of math questions ranging from quadratic to linear equations, as well as graph-related questions, geometrical figures, and tabular data. This diverse set of questions aimed to represent the typical content encountered in educational settings and provided a comprehensive way to evaluate the usability of the Kanak in converting different types of graphical content into accessible formats when compared to existing methods.

During the evaluation sessions, participants also completed three questionnaires: two System Usability Scale (SUS) [34] questionnaires to assess their experiences with Kanak and existing methods, and one Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) questionnaire [39] specific to Kanak.

## 4.3 Procedure

Prior to the study session, we emailed each participant two modified SAT test papers as PDF. The evaluation sessions had two conditions: a control condition and an experimental condition. In the control condition, participants walked us through their existing workflow by transcribing one of the provided PDFs into a tactile equivalent format. In the experimental condition, participants used the Kanak tool to transcribe the other PDF. At the beginning of each session, we obtained verbal consent from all participants. We first asked them to describe the tools they typically use for transcribing visual content into accessible formats. We then requested them to walk us through their process of transcribing visual materials using one of the provided sample PDFs that we sent via screen sharing. This live demonstration included copying content from the sample PDF, pasting it into different platforms such as Microsoft Word or Duxbury Braille Translator, and transcribing graphical elements, such as graphs, bar plots, and geometrical content. Participants also provided approximate estimates of the time they would typically need to complete the full conversion of the PDF contents. Throughout the demonstration, we probed participants for deeper reflection on the challenges they encountered during the transcribing process.

Following the demonstration of participants' existing transcribing workflows, we introduced participants to the Kanak tool via screen sharing. Using a separate trial sample PDF, we provided a demonstration of Kanak's core features, including how to rearrange content, edit textual elements, modify tables, and update graphical content such as bar plots using the tool's built-in editors. We also showed participants how to export the transcribed materials in accessible formats such as BRF and DOCX. After this demonstration, we provided participants access to Kanak via the website URL and login credentials. We then requested them to use the tool to transcribe one of the PDF documents into an accessible equivalent. Throughout the session, we offered reminders to participants as needed about Kanak's available features. As participants shared their screens and walked us through their use of the tool, we prompted them to interact with various features, including content rearrangement, text and math equation editing, table formatting, and plot editing through the built-in graphic editor. We asked them to share their thoughts on these features and whether they found them useful in their workflow. After the conversion, we requested participants to download the transcribed files in both BRF and DOCX formats, open them, and discuss their opinions on the transcribed materials. Further, similar to the earlier part of the session, we asked participants to estimate the time they might need to transcribe educational content in the PDF using Kanak.

Next, we asked participants to reflect on their experience using Kanak for the visual-to-tactile conversion process and probed for any changes and challenges compared to their typical conversion workflows. Finally, we collected their feedback through the questionnaires that included Likert-scale items from the System Usability Scale (SUS) for both Kanak and existing methods, and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) specifically for Kanak. Each evaluation session lasted approximately 90 minutes. Participants
